div.head: CHAINED DOGS IN WINTER.
div.p: CHAINED DOGS IN WINTER.

Sir,—May we call special attention to the sufferings of chained dogs in cold weatheir? In many cases the chained dog has to endure not only the mental and bodily misery pro- duced by loss of liberty and exercise, and all that makes life worth living, but is also much neglected; his sole abode being a leaky tub or box in ti bleak backyard, exposed to bitter winds. Often the tub has no bedding, and the -only lace where the dog can sit or stand out- side his prison is on the wet ground; the cold stones, or even in a puddle of water, and he can- not run about to warm himself.

We hear of dogs in farmyards always chained, sometimes to a fence or post, without pretence at shelter, sitting and lying day and night on mud, snow, or the frosty ground. And the condition of dogs in allotment gar- dens is pitiable in the extreme. In addition to all the sufferings of captivity, they are some- times left unvisited—and therefore presumably without food or water—for days together. If it is not possible for a dog to be always at liberty, he should at least have a sound. dry, comfortable kennel, raised from the ground, so that its floor may not become damp, and pro- vided with a bed of clean, dry straw or shav- ings, placed in an enclosure where he can be loose and move about.
Dogs need liberty, comfort and warmth in order to be happy. _ _
_ C. R. JOHNS, Secretary. National Calline Defence League.

div.head: IRISH DIFFICULTY.
div.p: THE IRISH DIFFICULTY.

Sir,—l am sorry Mr. .O'Brien is displeased with ray description of his attitude toward the .prison van outrage, but I cannot see it in any other light, and must leave the verdict of whether I am right or wrong in the hands of your readers. I see no further useful object in prolonging this correspondence, which was started to show the impossibility of Home Rule in existing circumstances, and not to discuss the rewards of orime and outrage. I have endeav- (mired to keep to the point, but, I regret to say; ray would-be critics have wandered far afield from the subject matter at issue: _ _

In my opening I endeavoured lo show that Home Rule was impossible and inimical to the interests of the Empire, so long as there were two opposing parties in Ireland. I further showed that Home Rule would not be a step forward in federating the Empire, but would retard it. I sketched out a plan that, if carried out, would not only solve the Irish difficulty, but would be a step on the way to Federation. I stated, and I still believe, that what is now taking place in Dublin is only a phase of what will become chronic under Home Rule. I think that Larkinism is only another phase of the Invineiblism and Fenianism of the past, and that Britain has no right to pass a measure of Home Rule, and then stand idlir by watching the factions exterminate each other. Let me also point out the ridiculous- nature of the 'Government policy that, while they levy war on a few crazy suffragettes because they are women, they show their bravado in committing Larkin to prison; and then show their abject cowardice by letting him out, and, while they talk of the arming of Ulster, they have not the courage to restrain it- I maintain that when there is a considerable and substantial minority of intelligence and wealth, that they are justified in objecting to be put under the heel of a less advanced major- ity. It has been my object and aim in this cor- respondence to advocate the formation of an homogeneous vationality, that the four races that form the inhabitants of these isles, while proud of their individuality, should coalesce in -forming one national whole; that Dublin Castle government should be abolished, and that all local matters devolve on provincial assemblies; that at least there should be two provinces in Ireland, north and south; that Wales and Mon- mouth should form another; Scotland another, whilst England might be divided into the pro- vinces of York and Canterbury, leaving the Imperial Parliament free to deal with the ques- tions of Empire. Since my critics fight so shy of the real points of issue I may as well consider this my closing -letter on the subject. PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: LICENSED HOUSES AND DRINKING.
div.p: LICENSED HOUSES AND DRINKING.

Sir,—ln a letter in your issue of the 11th inst., Mr, J. T. Rh ys endeavours to show that the "Licensing Statistics, 1912," supports the theory that a reduction in the amount of drunkenness is brought about by.a reduction in the number of licensed houses. - - .

An examination of the statistics referred to will reveal the fact that counties like Northum- berland, Durham, York (W.R.,), Glamorgan, and -others, which have the highest proportion "of convictions for drunkenness, are just those which have the fewest public-houses in propor- tion to population. On the other hand the counties like Oxford, Cambridge, Wilts, Hert- fordshire, Somersetshire and others, which have the smallest proportion of drunkenness convic- tions, are those which have the greatest number of public-houses in proportion to population. On contrasting the figures relating to the -inty borolighs, practically the same state of things is revealed, 6.g., Middlesbrough, with 9.74 public houses per ten thousand of the popula- tion, having 117.88 convictions for drunkenness, while 'Wolverhampton, with 35.98 public-houses, has bnly 19.41 drunkenness Convictions. With regard to the increase of drunkenness in 1912, the Blue Book says: "It is sufficient to point out that not only the total number of convictions, but also, in spite of the increase of population, the proportion of convictions to population was higher in 1912 than in any year since 1908."

These two statements very aptly suggest a new and opportune version of an old theme, which might easily become very popular and useful at election times; as a sort of antidote to the Tories everlasting use of :the original.

div.head: QUAKERISM AND NATIONAL SERVICE
div.p: QUAKERISM AND NATIONAL SERVICE

Sir,—Mr. Graham, in his reply to my letter on the above subject, quite confirms that I. Pennington and G. Fox were ready to stand up to defend their own country in their days, and that G. Fox recommended a vigorous foreign policy, and one Edwards Burrough, advised the Ironsides to march to Rome. These things happened in the early days of Quakerism, but in later years the Society has modified AS views, and do not now believe in 'war under any circumstances. Our friends are mistaken if they think that we are out to cause war, or that we recommend a vigorous foreign policy. We are out for home defence only, and we believe that if every able-bodied man was prepared to defend his own country it would be the best guarantee we could have for peace. Mr. Hampson asks, Do I infer that because I. Penniegton had no personal objections to any- one taking up Arms in defence of their country, the proposals °Me N.S.L. are necessarily, right, and that those who subscribe to the religious formula propagated by Pennington, must, as a consequence of such allegiance, accept with- out ,quastion his opinion upon a totally differ- ent matter?- My sole reason.for quoting I. Pen-, nington was to point out to present-day Friends that their early leaders believed in being pre- pared for .war. The fact that they follow his religious teaching does not necessarily mean that ' they must agree with his opinion on national defence. On the other hand, because a man is , a Quaker,. it need not mean that he is against 11 every form of national defence. He also asks if I am quite. sure that if I. Pen- nington was alive to-day he would accept the proposals of the N.S.L. I would not like to say ,that. ;But I •do think that he would support some such proposals for the bettermint of home defence.
T. R. ASHWORTH.

Sir,—What an extraordinary mixture of argu- ments local correspondents put forward last week against a citizen army! First, Mr. J. A. Ransoms lamented that he should have been drawn into publicity, for he protested, "I have made no public statements of my views regard- ing national service." Many will appreciate his modest shrinkirig from public attention, but surely when a Christian body, of whom Mr. Ransoms is the leading spirit, develops such sudden pugnacity as to bring a lady from Bir- kenhead one Sunday and a gentleman from Manchester the next Sunday, for the sole appar- ent purpose of a tirade against the National Service League, 'he must expect a public reply. As for his denial of a public statement, he for- gets a public speech which he made on Decem- ber 9th last. However, I have no wish to press unduly so public-spirited and genial a gentle- man as Mr. Ransoms. We, of the National Ser- vice_League, thank him for his letter, and the interesting information gratuitously given, that many Quakers go so far as to "lose valuable business" by refusing to manufacture goods needed by soldiers, but we look in vain for an answer to the original question, "Is it not as worthy to risk your life for a cause as to pay someone else to do it for you?" Miss Thompson next took up the pen. Her words were eloquent, but the only solid state- ment contained in her letter was indiscreet. She asserted that some of the highest military authorities were against national service. I ask Miss Thompson to name one living English soldier in a -reSOonsible and high position who has consistently declared against national ser- vice.

Mr. Gray then tried his skill, and wrote with 'sublime inaccuracy about Australia. He actually wrote that parents in the Antipodes are allowed no voice in the "Defence Acts." But the parents, lather and mother, too, are the voters; they voted in Australia for the Labour party, which introduced national ser- vice; and in New Zealand for the Liberal originators of the Defence Act; they continue at various General Elections to support univer- sal military training. If the majority of the parents really objected, they would show their objections by their votes. Mr. Gray is not usually credulous, but in this case he has swal- lowed the exaggerations which a loisy but small band are proclaiming. Last came Mr. Graham, the Manchester Quaker, eager, not to turn the other cheek, but to hit out at his wicked opponents! Alas! he, too, like Miss Thompson, had to disown the early utterances of the founders of the Quaker movement as heresies.

Personally, I must thank him for, the valuable information that many of the original Quakers served in Cromwell's Army! We will even wel- come Mr. Graham's abusive letter, containing such wards as " ill-considered," "reactionary," "NVorthless promises," "slippery organisation," if he will only continue to provide us with facts about the Quakers as soldiers. Mr. Graham is a living illustration of the instinct of com- bat, which is so often responsible for those horrible wars, which we of the National Service League are striving to prevent. I dare not trespass further on your space in replying to your correspondents. If they really wish to hear the truth about the system which they denounce, we invite them to attend our annual' meeting in the Bold-street Schools on November 27th, when we will answer their ques- tions as fairly as we can. Truly, if we have this quartet of military critics to "heckle" us, the ninth annual meeting of the Warrington Division- will not be devoid of interest.
B. S. TOWNIIOE.
Mere House, Newton-le-Willows, November 13th, 1913.

Should a case attract con- siderable attention, the Church will institute au -official inquiry lest the faithful be deceived. , This is the Church's duty as "a guide. The whole thing is gone into, independent courts sift the evidence over and over again—nothing is done in a hurry, and it is Proverbial that no tribunals are harder to satisfy than these. Miracles are generally looked for in confirma- tion, and again the 'evidence for these is min- utely examined. In the end,:if all prove satis- factory, the Church says 'people may safely -be- lieve. But she never obliges her children to believe in any of these private apparitions', and none of her doctrines depend upon them. They have to do purely with the devotional side of a Catholic's life.

(b) Quite different is the conduct of Spiritual- ists. Their whole religion (in so far as it can be called a religion) is to try to get into direct communication with the world beyond. They want to live by sight and not by faith. They deliberately form a "circle," with a medium, and invite the spirits by " mind-passivity " to manifest. This surely is quite a different thing from what we have been considering above. It is ray old distinction between spontaneous and induced phenomena. As to the evidence for the reality of spirit manifestations at these seances, think it has proved satisfactory, at least in sßme cases.: But*what, has- not,,been iproyecl in that the spirits- are what they declare them- selves to be, and what Spiritualists think them to be, viz., the spirits of the dead. In all real test cases, as the best scientists admit, they have failed to prove their identity. On the otherland, #there -arekstrong. reasons for believ- ing that it is the wqrk of masquerading evil spirits of the devil. The reasons for this opinion were set forth by Mgr. Benson in his lecture, and will be found in a popular form In his most interesting novel, "The Necroman- cers," which can be purchased anywhere for Is. I hope this letter will help Mr. Chrimes also. I have no desire, and neither have I time, to continue this controversy further; this letter will close it as far as I am concerned. (Rev.) P. L. BUGGINS, 0.5.8. St. Alban's. Bewsey-street. -

is somewhat on the Point o, letter:of 11.41 Squod. "in your nder discussion, .1 should be glad of a little • -A - point. siuspslui —oifnAlSawA:liScahtutordareyply. 1. But first let me deal with a part of his letter that is somewhat off O Why. Phil sg uod introduces Joan of Arc is not clear to me. The whole tone of his letter seems to imply that he does not believe in the reality of any spirit phenomena. One would have thought, then, that he would hardly have cham- pioned Joan of Arc. However, let that pass. But it is his statement that the Church of Rome was responsible for her death that I am con- cerned • to deny. • It was the English—deter- mined before any trial had taken place that she should die—and Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, ?who were responsible for the passing of 'that unjust sentence, and as an Englishman, and as a Catholic, I blush for their conduct. It was a cruel and bigoted local tribunal, entirely under the control of an unscrupulous and vio- lent political partisan, that condemned her. Over and over again she appealed from that court to the Pope, but access to him was denied her. 'News travelled slowly in those days, and Martin V. heard nothing of her story until too late. His successor, Calixtus IIL, however in- stituted a new trial and cleared her ,name of slander, and Pius X. (the present Pope) has declared ,her virtues heroic, has given her the title of Blessed, and soon we hope to be able, to call her Saint. It is no more true to say .the Catholic Church, properly speaking, consented to Joan's burning, than it is true to say the Apostolic College crucified Christ, because one of its members was a traitor. 0. Now, as to Mdlle. de Lamerliere's. connec- tion with the apparition at La Salette. - This is, as. far as I can gather., the true history of it: Father Deleon, a priest of the diocese of Grenoble; who was in difficulties with his superiors, made up his mind to oppose them by publicly denying the apparition at La Salette: He, in conjunction with another priest,' Father Cartellier, having failed to disprove it by honest means, had recourse to a very unworthy and dishonest method. He Persuaded Mdlle de Lamerliere, a good, but somewhat eccentric lady, to' say she impersonated the Blessed •Virgin on the day of •the apparition. The Bishop of Grenoble examined the whole thing afresh, and was obliged to refute the errors of Father Deleon in a pronouncement dated November 4th, 1854. Mdlle. de Lamerliere was somewhat offended by some true expreasions, which the Bishop mode use of on the subject; in order to explain how the opposition had been able to employ her for the purpose of giving some semblance of truth to their case. She threatened a law suit against the Bishop, but it did not come off; instead she turned on Father Deleon and brought a civil action against him for defamation of character. She lost the case, and a later appeal. on the ground she had •suffered no loss. The judgment in no way re- ferred to the apparition at La Salette, but it was fully proved incidentally at the trial- that -Mdlle. de Lamerliere was at home 75 miles away on the-date of the apparition,. September 19th, 1846, and that she visited La Salette for the first time on July 16th, 1848. None of this, I know, proves the genuineness of the appari- tion, but it shows that deceit was had recourse to, not by those who wished to prove it, but by those who, for sordid motives, wished to dis- ' prove it. - 3. As to positive proof for La Salette, Lourdes, lor any other apparition, I cannot be expected to enter into it here. There is aocumentary evi- dence. and I may mention that in .34:4Bertrin's Lourdes'," the whole of the evidence for and against that particular apparition is set out l'scientifically. I should be delighted to lend "Phil Squod " a copy, if he cares to read it. But if you can, spare me a little More space, 'Mr. Editor, I should like to show "Phil Squod" how entirely different is the practice of the Catholic Church from that of the Spiritualist with regard to spirit phenomena in general, since he says he does not see any difference. (a) Catholics do not believe that God's ordin- ary mode of dealing with us, is through spirit anparitions, &c. •He has left His infallible Church to be our guide in all matters of faith and conduct; we are to live by, faith and not by sight. However, if from time to time God does choose to manifest to us by means of an appari- tion, who shall say nay? But when such a thing is alleged to have happened, all sensible •Cntholics. and still more the official Church, knowing that this is not God's ordinary way,
REGINALD GOODWIN.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
BOROUGH POLICE COURT
SATURDAY.
Before Mr. R.
T. " Feirelqugh, Alderman
Tinnion and Mr. T. Pemberton.

THE SEAMY Fudge, a labourer, giving an address at a lodging-house in Ship- yard, was sent to prison for three months on a charge of assaulting Louisa Ann, Singleton, also of a lodging-house in Ship-yard, but a charge against nim of living wholly or in part upon the woman's earnings was dismissed.—Detective :Reddington saw the accused strike and kick the woman, and when questioned the man replied: "I did it because she had not got my food ready." The couple had been living together in Liverpool, and towards the end of October, when the prisoner was in gaol, the woman came to Warrington, hoping to get away from him. However, a day or two later she saw him in the town and he followed her to her lodgings, and later assaulted her.—The prisoner, in declaring his innocence, stated that he had sold a home up in Liverpool, through the woman, and that his Insurance Card would show that he had been working. This led to the dismissing of the second charge.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.
Before the Mayor, Councillor Peacock (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton and Smethurst, and Messrs. T. Locker, G. Pilling, S. Wright and W. Roberts.

A Rua TRICIL—An, ingenious trick that was 'attempted once too -often was related when Patrick R. Moran, no fixed abode, was charged with loitering with intent.—The police evidence showed that accused had been going about the town and saying to innocent-looking customers, "Here is a splendid 22-carat ring; give me is. 6d. for it. I want to go to Manchester, out of the way of the police." On Saturday he attempted this with a man, who stated that he only had 6d., and on the pretence of going for another is. he informed the police.—The Chief Con- stable said the ring was, worth about 6d.—Pris- oner was sent to gaol it, three months. THE MUSICIAN'S EXPEILIENCE.—The sequel to an exciting affair in a lodging-house in Stanley- street on Saturday was told to the Bench, on the appearance of William Blanchard on a charge of damaging a bed and assaulting an aged street musician named Bell.— The evidence showed that the old man retired to bed about 10 o'clock. and about an hour later the prisoner went into the same room and threatened to throw the 'old man out of the window. The musician informed the prisoner that there was a vacant bed in the room, where- upon he was violently assaulted, and in the strnggle had his shirt torn from his back, and Ithe bed was bicken.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for one month. A 16-STONE CONSTABLE.—Thomas Page, giving an address at a lodging-house in Barbauld-street, was charged with being drunk and assaulting a policeman and doing damage to the extent of 10a. to the constable's overcoat. The pris- oner struggled with the officer, who received a nasty cut over the left eye. In Court he said he hardly remembered anything, and he was sure a 16-stone policeman would not let a drunken man knock him about.—He was fined etl and costs, or one month. TUESDAY. Before Councillor Roberts (in the chair), Messrs. J. Rymer Young, C. Jackson Holmes, Ar• Richardson, slid Colonel Edelsten. KEPT BY HER S6N. 1.--tA separation order was made against Patrick Donoghue, of 18, Melville- street, on the ground of persistent cruelty to his wife, Mary.—Mr. Browne stated that the couple's son, Steve Donoghue, the jockey, had Promised to keep his mother. He asked for no alimony.

div.head: WOMEN'S OUESTMRS.
div.p: WOMEN'S OUESTMRS.
Fashionable Plumage Mounts that
are Innocent of Feathers.
WOMAN " CHIEF " OF GREAT CITY.

Chicago, always to the fore in matters of social reform, is about to appoint Mrs. Ger- trude Howe Britton its chief of police, an inno- vation even in America. The lady is familiar with police work, and a member of the exam- ining Board for the Civil Service. Mrs. Brit- ton is a wealthy woman, .and has for years taken a prominent part in social work. Chicago has for some time had its corps of policewomen, but In Europe, Germany and ' Norway are the only countries that so far hay followed the lead of the American Porkopolis ; although it is admitted in this country that such a corps would meet a need felt by all who deal with women and children in. our police courts. It is impossible to predict with any degree of certainty what the luture.holds in store .for corn- munities'Or for'indiVldual; but Wl§ quite within the range of possibilities that in this country , the pOwers that be will shortly recognise the need for policewomen in connection with criminal courts.

The London Needlework Guild. Queen Mary has always taken a keen interest in the London Needlework Guild, and lately spent three days at the Imperial Institute, assisting to apportion the 60,270 garments sent in this year. The ,King is a generous suppor- ter of the Queen's group and his contribution includes not ,only serviceable suits and boots for the unemployed men, but flannel shirts,-and pretty frocks for. little girls,- both of which are made to his Majesty's orders by the wives of soldiers and sailors, who thus earn welcome ad- ditions to their husband'. pay. The Royal children 'are also interested in this admirable charity, , and the . first ,official position .occupied by the Princess Mary was that of president of a group composed of young ladies of her-oWn age. Last year she, sent 2,800 garments. The ,Princess has contributed to the Guild from the time ,she learned Louse a needle, and is quite deservedly proud of the successful work her group has accomplished.

The Origin of the Charity. Like so many of, our important charities, the Guild had a small beginning, and is provincial In origin. Its inception was due to the first Lady Wolverton, who started it in the early 'Eighties in Dorsetshire. It now exists in a number of counties, and flourishes exceedingly in Middlesex, ,where the Duchess of Albany is the president. Working girls in London con- tribute voluntarily and handsomely to this ad- mirably organised charity. One city church opens its churchroom to the girls who arrives by the workmen's trains, and have no place in which .to spend the tune between their arrival and the opening of offices or factories, &c., where they are employed. Last year no fewer than sTx fiundred garments were made by working 'girls in one churchroom during this interval. The idea of the Guild has been adopted in pur overseas dominions,, and gifts have frequently been sent to London from Australia. Many welcome orders are forwarded by the various presidents to East End work- rooms, and agencies employing widows with families to sup Pert, or unemployed husbands. Boots and blankets are always in great demand and are widely distributed by this useful organisation.

Luxurious Linings. This season linings are much used, and never were they more luxurious. The stiff glace silk, once prized for its rustling propensity, has gone, and its place has been taken by exquis- itely soft brocades, satins and figured silks. Clinging and soft Japanese, silks in white or colours are also in demand as linings of a less expensive kind. British silks, too, are holding, .their own, for they have been found to be ex- tremely- durable. The Japanese also wear well. Some of the designs for this season's linings are bizarre in the extreme; these belong to what is known as " futurist " and "Post Im- pressionist" art, and They certainly afford a change. and perhaps add more or less origin- ality to women's dress. But the wall-paper effects in poor qualities of materials should he avoided, they are at the best very poor substi- tutes for a good 'plain soft colour at a lower 'price. Only in the most "e*nensive materials are the colours of eccentric designs of the new Ftrt in any degree beautiful.

The- Smaii Set of Fur. For girls' smart morning wear, nothing is near than the quite small ties and cravats of good fur, and they are comparatively low in price-. In ermine these ties are delightful. Less seal-dyed furs and American opos- sum, and all give a neat finish to a plain cloth expensive, necklets tailor-made. In the shaping, of the newest stoles, Much ingenuity is displayed. Some are the new white coney have deep bands of skunk with muffs to match, long, ucr u. t square,.ilose and bordered with a contrast- ingof also finished with deep bands of the same fur. For young girls ,these are most suitable and becoming. Some of the new stoles drape the shoulders more like mantles' than:anything known by the name of stole, others are made like an old-fashioned pelerine. It is. almost a relief to see a coat of the wrap variety without fur trimming of some sort, for even the cheapest ready-made has at least its collar of some kind of pelt. • The Newest Hats.,

The very latest hat from Paris is that known as a Tyrolese hunter, "with conical crown, sur- mounted by a bunch of curled and crested feathers, giving an idea of a volcano in action, for the thin plumes suggest nothing So ,Much as a cloud of smoke. The crowns ,of coloured hats match the dresses with which they are worn, and may be of brocaded crepe, duvslyn, satin; velvet or "any handsome material. The mount usually tones with the costume, and its 'stem is frequently covered with the same material as that of which the crown is built. The most fashionable plumage mount is inno- cent of feather frouds of any description, except at the top, where, the quaintest ..tufts give a rather comical effect. The most suitable use for this curious plumage is with satin or velvet butterflies, for as \ antenna% they do not look quite so much out of place.

div.head: Brocaded Footwear.
div.p: Brocaded Footwear.

This season's new boots are- quite novel as far as the uppers are concerned. These have been made for quite a long time from white kid or cloth, which in its turn has been superseded by heavy brocatle or tapestry, in. colours to Lone with the costume, worn at the same time. The fashion is a pretty one, and quite becoming to the. -appearance of the ankles The buttons match the prevailing , tone of the material em- pio,yed. The toecap and surround are of black patent leather. Such dainty, thin-soled,. Ilar- row-welted fOotWetir is, however, -hardly suit- able for the Weather at this time of year.- The stout " mannish " kind of boots and shoes which women adopted the last winter or two is more suitable for this purpose, but there is now a decided. reaction in favour of lighter feminine footgear. It is of little use in keeping out the water in bad weather, and it is said that it is the habit of. sitting about with damp feet that makes neuralgia so much more prevalent with women than among men.
On Saturday Lord Mostyn presided over a conference of women from North Wales, Che- shire and Shropshire for the purpose of organ- ising to receive women and children in case of civilhwar in Ulster..

THE EGGS IN WINTER.

Probably there are mi-.1-e extremists in feeding fowls than in any .other detail of management,. rthei.e?- 4re those'. who roundly:- abuse wfndian corn, and condemn it, not only as worthless, but positively as a. danger to fowls. Again, there are many who hardly use anything else but -Indian corn, and certainly if their state- ments are authentic the egg yield is wonderful. flowevee, both forms of bigotry—this word ex- presses it better than any other—are bad. Indian corn has its good .and its bad qualities. In -Whiter it is excellent.; in sitininer it is in- jurious. For chickens it is better than for old .stock. It is very good in colds cxpOSed places-,.; but it ean be dispensed viUi under.more congenial conditions; ,it may be given in mudi ; larger .quantities when fowls are kept on a heavy clay .soil ,than if the -soil is light and of a sandy nature, since under the former condi- tions the birds require more &eating matter. ,In addition, they can elimpato more fat, and in these two elements Indian corn is particularly strong.

div.head: WINTER EGGS.
div.p: WINTER EGGS.

Winter egg-production is, perhaps, the most profitable branch of industrial poultry-keeping, and fortunate is the pdultry-keeper who -can persuade-his hens to lay well during the next few ,weeks. Feeding and housing are both matters requiring careful attention, for if they are neglected, the egg supply is likely to be' small. Warm food should be provided in the morning, grain in the afternoon, and at mid- day some green stuff-; this last to keep the fowls .in good health, as without it their blood be- comes heated, and their internal organs refuso to work satisfactorily. The morning rations - should consist of three-parts barley meal, two- ' parts middlings, and half a part meal The best grains are wheat, barley, and, during cold- weather, a little maize. The sheds in which the birds sleep should be well constructed, free front draughts, well lighted, and perfectly dry. A scratching shed attached to the roosting „conk partment is :a great boOn,:as on wet-days, when the birds are much better under cover, they are debarred from exercise. The floor should blit littered with straw or chaff, and the afterno.o. grain srattered th.ereamong, instead of being fed from 4 roughs. A great difficulty with stoCk birds during the winter months, When 'there 0( little temptation for them to wander about out,: 'side in search of worms, grubs, &c.., is to pre- vent them becoming too fat, but this must be _ prevented at all costs, as fat:heni7 or fat male" birds are rarely profitable. Ther:4 is probabbt no more common cause of indifferent laying than, want of exercise.

KNOWING TRW BMW. AGES* - A ...;;Itiffidirtiiiit m'etter at ine-:,lyrese.in is the tweessity for studiously recording the eq.° of both cockerels and pullets. Of course, 17 Jim(' and July, and with some breeds in Angus" no dilliollty is experienced in knowing the age, at ally rate to within a week or so, but by the end of the year, when the flock is all gathered together for inspection, it is no easy matter tit kn'Av with absolitte accuracy, without 'sour' dis- tinctive mark, the chickens that were halche4 in February and March from those of later. date. If one cannot discriminate between the April' chickens and those' hatched in March, it is of no importance, since the former are equidlY suitable 'for breeding purposes as those hatched earlier, but when it comes to May hatched chi,•kens it is quite another matter, and, one which later on may have disastrous resnlts. An eN tic knowledge of age is more important whcro ho heavy, slow growing breedspare eon" cerned, The question is one rarely regarded yet almost- every'poultry keeper who real' large numbers of chickens extending froll . the beginning of February to the end of MO' has experienced the difficulty of knowing their exact ages when the birds are ahnost NW • grown. There are, however, many simple.' devices by which the risk of breeding froliT immature stock, with its Subsequent dangerS, may he .ob-viated.

INTERESTING BUTTEU TEST.

The results of the butter test of the Royal JerseY Agricultural ,Society have ,just been 'Wiled. In the class for cows under five years of age, the first prize goes to Mr. T. Vibert's Belle of Jersey, which calved April 9, 1913? and after having been 182 days in milk produced in the twenty-four hours 311 b., giving a butter yield of 21b, .40z., judged as- being pale and -,of fair quality,' ratio 13.45.. The second prize animal, Mr, E. E. Leonard's Golden Drop, after 1 thirty-live day's milking, gave 321 b. Boz., which yield 31b. of butter, or a ratio of 10.83. The colour and quality were good. This cow ob- tained a total of 48 points from butter only. Belle of Jersey's total of 48.75 included 12 for period of . lactation. The third was also an animal belonging to Mr. Leonard. After sixty- three days' milking it 'gave 381 b.. 4oz. of milk yield, 21b. 12oz. of butter, good in colour,. but poor in quality. Its ratio was j 3.9; total points. 46.30; including 2.30 for period of lactation. Twenty-SIX other animals received certificates of merit. In the class for older ,cows, Mr.. F. H. Le Bontillier's Bonne Brune obtained the first prize with 371 b. 4oz. of milk, after 147 days' lactation, and 21b. 9oz. *of butter, a ratio of 14.53; total points, 51.70. Second went to Mr. 1-?.' J. Pree's Stephanotis, 291 b, 40z., after 178 'days, butter k 211.); 1-oz., ratio 14.07; to,tal points 45.25. Third was won by Mr. C. Fossey's Jap's Pallas, 301 b. 4oz. milk after 166 days, 21b. Oloz. butter, .ratio 15.0; total points -44.25. Twenty other animals were awarded certificates of merit. The quality of the Jersey milk is Shewn by the ratios, which varied, being 13.28 to 22.80, and only eight cows out of the number in both classes exceeded the 20.0 limit, while the major- ity were far below. The summary shows that seventy-six cows averaged 152 days in Milk. 281 b. 4oz. of milk, 11b. 9-ioz. of butter: and gave a ratio of 18.7.

div.head: PLANTING ROSES.
div.p: PLANTING ROSES.

Bose bushes are now so cheap that they are worth growing, even if they only last one or two seasons. But if they are purchased from a re- liable nurseryman and properly planted in suit- able soil, there is every reason to expect good growth for many years. The month of Novem- ber is the best tune of the whole year for plant- ing, but before confining them to their beds an examination of the roots should be made, find all damaged growths cut off. , Make each hole wide enough to take in the roots spread out fully. If manure is required dig it into the lower layer of soil, so that none of it can come in actual contact with the roots. If the soil is rather wet have some dry loam at hand to place around the roots, and then no harm will result. If the soil is light, add clay and cow dung; if heavy, add road grit, leaf mould, burnt refuse, horse dung and lime. Plant bushes about le inch 4 apart, at a depth of from 'four to six inches, or up to the mark of the soil shown on the stem. Firm the soil well right U!) 19 the base of the stem.

A dressing of basic slag may be : given to established roses, and will give good results next summer. The quantity to use will be about six ounces to the square yard. Dig up the surface soil round roses and leave it rouglr through the winter. It is not always the number of degrees of frost that does harm to roses as the condition of the wood,' and at the present time this is rather sappy. Some protection should be given to the teas and hybrid teas by sticking clippings of hedges around the stems. Set rather close around the bushes, the clippings break the wind and make good shelter for the trees. A great future is predicted for a new climb- ing rose, a sport from Paul Lode. This new :rose has been given the same name, with the ;addition of the word climbing. The rcise is identical in every way with its parent, except that it is of a vigorous climbing habit. The colour is bright rose-shaded yellow, and the flowers are large and of good shape. Two good autumn roses are General Macar- thur and ,Mrs. Arthur Mint. The blooms of the latter are borne; on long, stout stems, - which make. It an ideal rose for cutting. The colour is ivory white, with a very faint blusitt showing through the petals. The former is reckoned one of the best red roses we have, and is deli- ciously fragrant.. ,

div.head: —Aire
div.p: —Aire
A Question of Fusion.

At the conference on Saturday Alderman McCabe, the Lord Mayor of Manchester, said in looking over the list of branches he had found that, with the exception of about two in York- shire, they belonged almost exclusively to Lan- cashire and Scotland. lie trusted that eventu- ally they would unite the whole of the country, and so grow in power and helpfulness to the members of their community. The President, Mr. T. Wilkinson, of Leigh, explained that a start had been made in the direction indicated by the Lord Mayor. At present there were about a dozen or sixteen Catholic societies which did cover tile country. They had been requested to form a group of Catholic societies, and eight had responded. During the last nine•months meetings had been held and a regular association had been formed, comprising the whole of the country from the South up to Scotland. Aims of Catholic Laymen.

The President said that the aim of the Catho- lic layman should be .to get Catholics ade- quately represented on every public body. This had not hitherto been ,the casein . all ,their cities and towns. They boasted of Lancashire as the most Catholic count-, yet they had not one member on the Lancashire County Council, and the same might be said ;Of many large towns. On 'Boards of Guardians their full strength was not felt, though Catholic members were especially needed there to watch, over the interests of their numerous poor. But it was on Trades Councils, Committees of ,Trade Unions, Associations of Shop Assist- ants, Clerks, and .kindred associations, and on the Committees of Co-operative Societies that the presence of earnest practical Catholics was greatly needed. Resolutions were being con- tinually passed by those bodies which were con- trary to the ideals of the Catholic members. * Catholics did not sufficiently work together to secure representation. (Hear, hear.) There was still in many localities that national antag- onism which had enormously hindered the development of religion. Suspicion of each other's motives had kept English and Irish Catholics from working together, but perhaps the present political situation would band them stronger together and give them freedom in future to join forces for the common good. (Applause.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1913.
Great Crowds elloome igin Mew Wvio Head, Councillor,. Pete,r Peacook.
MAYOR ADDRESSES YIS BRETHREN.

The Mayoral Sunday in Warrington proved the most imposing function of its kind ever since Warrington became a borough. The customary procession was greatly aug- mented by the support given to it by the various friendly societies in the tcwn. Thus the spectacle was made more remarkable and was witnessed by crowds of spectators, who lined the route. The Mayor, as he passed 'along the streets, was cordially greeted by the citizens, and the event all through was a memorable one. After the visit to the ancient Parish Church, the procession returned to the Town Hall, where the Mayor briefly expressed his thanks to the Council. In the Drill Hali the members of the Friendly Societies assembled, along with the Terri- torials. The Mayor visited the Hall, and addressed his thanks to the brethren.
The oldest inhabitant, that useful person who remembers everything, has been interviewed on the. subject of the Mayoral procession on Sunday. • .

. . ese "It's doivnreight t' best' I've' seen, th Many years.'' Thus the oldest resident chuckled: "It- war'n't half a show, but a reight good 'lin." For once, perhaps, the more modern residents will be in unanimous agreement with the oldest inhabitant. It was conceded upon every side that Sunday's function was not only the most 'memorable, but the most ' picturesque witnessed in the history of Warrington since it first, aspired' to the. dignity of a borough. From the spectacular standpoint it was a success. The pronounced foreground of the picture was provided by the scarlet-coated "Terriers," and their blaze of colour was toned by the more naval-like garb of their brethren of the Army Service Corps. Then came the distinctive colours of the police uniforms, while topping all, reminiscent of the days of the Roman soldiery, flashed in the fitful burst of sun rays the highly-polished helmets of the firemen.

The Mayor was conspicuous in his robes and chain of office, with a setting supplied by the officially robed and dignified mace and sword bearers. Then came the sombre tone in the picture, the aldermen, councillors, officials, &c. Dignified England does not maintain gorgeous robes for these, as happens in Continental towns, and also a few Scottish cities, .hence the frock coat and silk hat were the chief 'article's of adornment. In the rear came a long array of friendly society members, with their char- acteristic regalias and jewels.

We had, he added, from the Romans, the splendid roads, along which Came the Church frOm the Continent to this.country. • In those days of old He used strange instruments, and now He- used sometimes strange instruments for the accomplishment of His ends. He nSis War, and why? In order that we shall, through the horrors of war, be prepared to maintain and defend our land.

He uses pestilence in order to teach us to have our dwellings clean and pure, oar' streets clean .and pure, and our liver—which, I trust it will be in time—clean and pure. God sends us drought to teach us the storage .of water. You know how important that is to us in England. He sends floods to teach us how to make em- bankments and waterways for the _ surplus waters to pass through, and there are earth- quakes to teach those whose duty it is to live in these dangerous localities that we human beings have no abiding city here and that our true home is in heaven.

The scarlet tunics of the South Lancashire Territorials and the neat uniform of the Army Service Corps lent a dash of colour to enliven the sombre shades worn by the rest of the largo congregation. The Mayor, escorted by the sword and raacc

div.head: TOWN HALL CEREMONY. Mayor's Message of Thanks.
div.p: THE TOWN HALL CEREMONY. Mayor's Message of Thanks.

On the return to the Town Hall, the Mayor, the aldermen, councillors and officials adjourned to the Council Chamber, where refreshments Were provided. Councillor JOSEPH (deputy mayor) said it did not need any Words of his to point out that the omens for the future were most favourable. They might congratulate themseltes that they had had the opportunity of walking .with the Mayor in the bright sunshine, instead of the deluge of the previous day. He had great pleasure in, proposing the health of, the Mayor and Mayoress; ,and wished. them haPpiness and prosperity. (Loud applause.)

_ The 'MAYOR, in reply, said: I .thank you very heartily for the way you have drunk my health. It has given me very great pleasure to. have such a large and representative gathering fol- lowing me to-day. I shall always look back with great iride to this day. I did not think the weather would have been so favourable as it is, but everything seems to augur well for my year of office. I thank you most heartily, and I hope my year of office will be successful for all concerned. (Applause.) I feel that my thanks are due to the Town Hall and Friendly Society officials for the help, assistance and !upport they have given me. They have worked splendidly, and I thank them. (Applause.)
A HORSE SHOE FOR LUCK. Master Cunnington's Unique Gift.

Towards the end of the proceedings Council- lor CUNNINGTON announced that his little boy, James, desired to make a present to the Mayor. Master JAmns, approaching his Worship, said in a clear voice, which could be heard all over the Council Chamber: . . . "Mr. May6r, will you allow me to present your Worship•with a horse shoe as a token of pod luck for the coming year?" With this

the Mayor was decorated, amid applause, by the little man with a miniature horse shoe on ribbon, the ceremony being performed with an amount of confidence remarkable in one so young. The MAYOR, who was delighted with the little incident, afterwards went .across to the boy, shook him heartily by the hand, and spoke to _ ....... him in a kindly manner.

div.head: WITH THE BRETHREN. Friendly Society Enthusiasm, A POPULAR MAYOR.
div.p: WITH THE BRETHREN. Friendly Society Enthusiasm, A POPULAR MAYOR.

Evidence of the Mayor's popularity with the Friendly Society members was manifest in the Drill Hall, when his Worship, along with the Mayoress, returned thanks for the way •the;. members of his own and kindred societies • had suppbrted him. Many congratulatory speeches were made by Friendly Society members, and cheers were lustily given for the Mayor - and Mayoress, Councillor Dr. Joseph and others. Refreshments were provided. ' The MAYOR, said: Alderman , Tinnion, Mr. Bradshaw, Bro. Chrimes, Brethren and Ladies— I feel very proud of this day, the 16th Novem- ber, 1913, because, brethren, I thank you, and; you alone, for putting me into this exalted position as Mayor of this great and ancient borough. (Cheers.) It gives me especial plea- sure to tell you that my dear and respected brother, Alderman Tinnion, proposed me. (Cheers.) He is a Forester like myself. He has done a lot to sweep away the opposition that sometimes creeps in. I have been supported 1?y Bro. Chrimes and supported by Bro. Archer, and supported •by all the Friendly Society movements in Warrington. (Cheers.) lam proud of the grand gathering to-day, and more than pleased to be .a member of a Fritndly Society, and I thank you heartily. (Loud ' cheers.) I owe a big lot to Friendly Societies, and I have had great support from the Various sections, and sincere and devoted support from my friend, Councillor Joseph.. (Cheers.) • 'He has stood by me, and has promised to support me during my term of office. (More cheers, and a ;Voice '`Three cheers for C,ouncillor Joseph," compliment in Which the Mayor joined heartily). I might tell you that Councillor Joseph put off an 'important engagement ip. London on .Friday rather than that any sug- gestion of lack of support might creep in, and he had purposely foregone that engagement to attend the on the Bench., on Friday 'morning. , . .(C4eers.) .

div.head: "My Duty Is With You."
div.p: "My Duty Is With You."

There was'n-o reason why he,should not have, kept away. I told him to go, but he said, "My duty is with you," and he would not go, and I take this opportunity of thanking him rery sincerely and pul)licly. (Loud, cheers.) From the expressions and congratulations and sup- port from all quarters, I think my year of office cannot be anything but a successful one. (Cheers.) In this act Alderman Tinnion has i)ecn my godfather. (Laughter and cheers.)

div.head: ONLY HONORARY FORESTER.
div.p: ONLY HONORARY FORESTER.

Alderman TINNION, who had a hearty recep- tion, said he was very proud to be there that day. lie had been an honorary member of the Foresters:, for some .cdnsiderable time, .and he was the only 'honorary member they had. When they asked him to attend that day and wear his collar, he did so. with very great, pleasure. When he had the honour and pleasure of pro- posing Brother Peacock for the Mayoralty, he thought he was prophesying with very great truth, when lie said that Brother Peacock's eleb::. tion as Mayor would be one of the most popular the borough had ever known% .They had giv`eii him a good send-off; and they must see to'it that he kept to the kigh-Nvatpr Mark. If ke ,4;14* not,, it would not •be-becanse they 'had not given him, a good send-off. (Cheers.) Everything augured well for a successful year, and he hoped. that twelve months hence they would be able to congratulate themselves. (A Voice: "And elect him again.") That is a matter, answered the Alderman, I have nothing to do with to-day,, but I hope•he will have a successful year, not successful solely for himself, but successful to the workers and those who- live and have so much at stake in the good old, town of Warrington. (Applause.)

div.head: DR. JOSEPH WELCOMED.
div.p: DR. JOSEPH WELCOMED.

Councillor G. W. JOSEPH was very popular, and when he rose to address the gathering there were loud cheers. He said that he must thank them first of all for the very cordial reception of ,himself. He had very great pleasure indeed in appearing there to say a few words about his successor, although, perhaps, he was better known there than he (Dr. Joseph) was himself, and he thought he could say with regard to Councillor Peacock's commencement of office, that nothing could be more auspicious. He wished Councillor Peacock and his worthy help- meet, the Mayoress, a very successful year. (Cheers.) lie knew that during the last week it must have been a very busy time, and he was very • pleased to see the Mayor and Mayoress looking so well after the strenuous week they had had. He-knew all present were friendly dispof;ed towards his Worship. (Cheers.) They had been Instrumental in lifting him to that high position, and they would be strong sup- porters of him during the years and they, with the speaker, wished the Mayor and Mayoress a happy and successful year, of office. ~(Cheers.)

div.head: PROUD MOMENT FOR BRO. CHRIMES.
div.p: PROUD MOMENT FOR BRO. CHRIMES.

Bro. CHRIMEB said it was one of the proudest moments of his life to be able to congratulate Councillor Peacock 'on being promoted to the chief 'magistracy of the borough. (Hear, hear.) There was no one in the friendly society move- ment who deserved it more than -their highly respected brother, and he (the speaker) felt sure that the training the Mayer had had in the friendly society movement enabled him to take on that responsible position. With the training he had received he would be able to maintain the dignity of the Mayoral chair. They looked to him to conduct his dtities with all decorum and respect, so that at the end of the year they could say, "Go forward and do another year." (Applause.)

div.head: CHIEF MARSHAL GIVES THANKS.
div.p: CHIEF MARSHAL GIVES THANKS.

Bro. P. P. BRADSHAW said he was the chief marshal of the procession organised by the friendly societies, and he would like to take that opportunity of thanking all the members who had turned out, considering that the weather was not so propitious as it might ltave been. The Mayor and the officers of the socie- ties greatly appreciated the members coming that day. (Hear, hear.) The marshal's duties had been very light. They in the friendly socie- ties knew' how to conduct themselves, even if they did not attend the Council meetings. (Laughter.) It was a great day to have a friendly society worker risen from the bottom of the ladder, through all the chairs of office, to the position of Mayor, of the borough. When the Mayor 'presided over the Council, the train- ing he had had in the friendly so'ciety move- ment would stand him in good stead. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) He (the speaker) looked to the Mayor having a successful term of office. He had the whole-hearted support of the friendly societies, who fully intended to see him through. They had an example on the -occasion of the first official visit to church, and they would stand by him all through. (Loud cheers.)

div.head: R.A.0.8. TRIBUTE.
div.p: R.A.0.8. TRIBUTE.

Bro. JOHN HOLDEN (R.A.0.8.) commented on the enthusiastic manner in which members of his Order had rallied round the Mayor. It was also gratifying to know that the new chief magistrate was a member of their ancient Order, all the members of which would do all they possibly could to support the Mayor in his work, so that Warringtonians would be able to say, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant," and at the end of his year send him back for another period. The Mayor had a splendid helpmeet in his wife, a fact which would make the success of his Mayoralty doubly sure. (Loud and prolonged cheers.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1913.
DOMESTIC SMOKE.
Now Warr* ton Householders Could
Save £24,000 a Year
WITH LESS SMOKE. BETTER FIRES.
TO THE EDITOR OF "THE EXAMINER." _

-- Sir,—l have been interested in reading the article on domestic smoke in your last issue. I wonder if the writer is acquainted with the tests made by the. London Smoke Ab4terae4t. 'Skiety.? /Thictlisttest was cotiiicied With six different forms of grates. Manufacturers of all modern economical grates were asked to send a grate for the pur- pose of experiment. It is not necessary to narrate- sin the' details of this ca efiilly eon- ducted investigation, but it is worth noting the fact that the result confirms your article about economy and smoke consUmption going to- gether. The tests were conducted on each grate for three days; the conditions of the outside atmosphere, as well as all others, were prac- tically the same during the period of test. Among the many tabulated points the three of special importance were : First,- the amount of.,coals _consumed. Second, the rise of temperature, in' room. • •Thir& the intessity.-of smoke given :off. The coal consumption over. the three days Of eight hours varied from 191 b. per day in the best grate to. 35,1 in the worst. The mean tern- perature of the room in which the trials were made was raised in the case of the best 17 degrees F., and in the case of the worst only 13 degrees F. Taking the heat given off in relation to ceelk.;.ciinsnililltiTl,T the, coal ,nper pound in the best did twice as inucli 'work as -at that of the worst. In smoke intensity, measur- ing by Bryan Donkin's smoke chart, the smoke giventhotoffo fbtyli et the beator st, grate was only one-fourth clearly indicatingth the of _ loss of heat was due to the unconsumed fuel going up the chimney in smoke. A later_ test was made of 24 grates under like conditions. We select two of the best all- round (A and B) and the worst (C).
Average amount of Temperature coal in lbs. of room Average per day. raieed. smoke. A. 22.81 8.3 1.02 B. 27.13 9.3 1.01
Average of the two 24.97 8.8

The grates 'that burnt the .251 b. coals took 2.81 b. of coali-Per day to 'raise ttig room one degree in temperature, while the grate burning ll 's . took nearly double, namely, 4.41 b ' in smokeb the bad grate emitted 50 per cent. more 4. than tha,,betteir.ones.. ' The significantpoint :abOut both test is that these grates were all supposed to be the most economical of their kind, and were sent in by ' the makers with the expectation that they would give good results. If, therefore, we find between such grates such a wide difference, what must be the difference between the best and the old-fashioned grates still in use in so many of our houses. -

-- - A further careful test illustrating this point was made by an expert independently alto- gether of those above-named. In this test there were also six grates. Number 1 was an ordinary heavy cast-iron grate of an old- fashioned' pattern. The. one that gave best results was a Bowes' Patent Well Fire. The test period extended over -sixty hours, the rooms were identical, and the temperature taken each hour.
The following was the result of the worst and the best :
Pounds of coal con- sumed per average de- gree of in- Coal constimed. creased tern- Total..
No. 1. Ordinary old pattern grate 1961 b. 3.2661 b. No. 6. Well Fire ll2lb. 1.8331 b.
It will he seen that the coal consumption taking the ordinary grate as it hundred was
vork :logra VOW VIM VSIIk Ng"

reduced •to fifty-seven, a saving of forty-three per Cent. Correcting it by the increase of. tem- perature the reduction is fifty-two per cent., a net gain of forty-eight per, cent. No smoke record was taken in this test.
If there is anything like .this difference be- tween the worst form of grates and one of the best, it reveals the enormous possibilities in L.,:onomical fire-places.

div.head: Local Possibilities.
div.p: Local Possibilities.

Applying the above facts to local conditions I we have 14,505 inhabited houses in the borough. Taking large and small houses together we may assume that the average consumption, of coal per house is 4 cwt.. per week, which-works out to an annual domestic coal consumption in War- rington of 150,852 tons. The all-round price can at present be taken at 21s, a ton equal to £158,394 per annum.. It is not safe to assume .that, what we have,ealled the good grates. and 'the bad grates would Show the same 'extreme differences under all conditions. It would de- pend upon.a great many circumstances, chiefly on the firing, and the heat wanted at particular times. For instance, if these grates had been :banked up with 'cinders, or small coal when a slow fire was wanted, the result might have been very different. But if through an im- provement in grates, and more intelligent fir- ing we could save, not 48 per cent. as indicated in above test of extremes, but one-third of this, say, 15 per cent., the saving in coal value would be £475E. But the proportion of saving in smoke production would be much more because the saving in coal. would be brought about mainly by hatter combustion of the smoke, tar, and gas, which .at present escapes unburnt up the chimney. Fifteen per eent—in-,coal saving might 'effect ,40 per cent, in knoke reduction.. and this is niore than confirmed by the results of the first test mentioned. It is well worth while.
CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, November 20th, 1913.

div.head: WAR ON SMOKE.
div.p: WAR ON SMOKE.
How Cities Can Be Clean and Prosperous
AN EXPLODED SUPERSTITION.

Every Sheffielder is interested in the preser- vation of a pure atmosphere, and all share, in varying degree, responsibility for its pollution. Everybody will, consequently, derive no little benefit from a visit to the Fuel, Light and Power Exhibition, which has been opened at the City Exhibition Hall ,(late ." The Jungle"); and is to remain open for three weeks. The biggest manufacturer in the city will have demonstrated to him how he can not only avoid the unsightly and unhealthy. clouds of black, smoke from his factories, -but 'at' the same time effect a considerable economy, for the old super- stition that Sheffield smoke is synonymous with Sheffield prosperity has long since been ex- , ploded, and it is now recognised that black smoke means incomplete combustion, and in- , omplcte combustion means wasted money. The ordinary householder can also contribute towards the attainment of the ideal of making Sheffield a smokeless city, because in the aggre- gate the product of tens of thousands of house- fires means a very appreciable addition to the city's smoke-pall. At the '_exhibition the latest 'devices for cooking and heating by gas .or elec- tricity are to be seen, and these show conclu- sively that from every point of view, comparison with the old-fashioned coal-fire is all to the 'favour of its twentieth century rivals. Fol. illuminating purposes "tile very latest" is demonstrated, and the numerous stalls which fill the spacious hall seem to the visitor to be set in a veiitable palace of light. . div.head: UNHEALTHY SMOKE.
div.p: UNHEALTHY SMOKE.
A Sheffield Protest Against a Polluted Atmosphere.
WASTE ON MAKING SOOT.

The Fuel, Light and Power Exhibition, which was opened recently in Sheffield, again calls attention to the smoke problem. It is a proplem- that has - never yet .been tackled with the seriousness it deserves. There is too general a disposition to take the smoke pall for granted. It has always been hanging over the city (except after holidays, when people are sutprised by the features -which suddenly come into their view), and therefore it is assumed 1 that it is necessary to Sheffield's industry_ " Sheffield stands on smoke" is the sort of take- things-as-they-are doctrine which has been preached whenever a few have tried to bring about an improvement in the condition of the atmosphere. The smoke pall is typical of Eng- lish lack of method. It is so much easier to tr Pour. clouds of smoke into the atmosphere than it-is e k e. to • it ta kdee,e- te n 0 h e necessary matter that ub aot thele •-tporepverenvteienn't sle ot smoke would result in the saving of money. The average Englishman is sceptical. He thinks there is only sentiment behind the agitation; and -that smoke cannot represent hard cash. The authorities, too, are slow to move. They shrink from doing anything that would inter- fere with industry. Most of the men on public die. ARe-quite convinced that if you stop smoke you stop trade. it has been demon- strated times out of number that exactly the opposite is the case; and that the tall chimneys in Sheffield and other large cities are scattering ' money as:Nvell as smoke, -Taking the country as a whole, it has been estimated that nearly 2.1 million tons of coal are every year wasted in the form of soot. And yet nobody gets excited. Manufacturers smile a knowing sort of smile when such facts are laid before them, and go on in the same old way. The Government is as hard to move as are the local authorities. We wonder if among all the many departments at Whitehall there is a smoke prevention depart- ment. There are smoke inspectors in large towns; but they are not taken, as, seriously as they ought to be. The people themselves, al- though their health is affected by living con- stantly in an atmosphere charged with smoke, do not appear to trouble. If they did, we should find smoke playing a considerable part in the municipal elections. Like the manufacturers, the ordinary residents are so accustomed to the smoke that they take it as a matter of course. Consequently nothingis done, and-an unhealthy indifference to most insanitary conditions reigns supreme. The only person who really complains is the housewife, who protests against having to wash the window curtains so often; and who, consequentlY, makes the home unhealthy by stubbornly refusing to open the windows. _ . _ . .

There Is less ex-cuse than there was for the wholesale creation of smoke. Now that gas- engines and electric motors are coming into common use, the number of fires ought to be lessened. So far we must confess no improve- ment is visible in Sheffield. Perhaps some day public opinion will be so educated that it will compel electrical energy for all the works to be taken from one great central station. When that day comes a new generation of manufac- turers will probably have opened their eyes to the "by-product waste" which now escapes from chimneys in the shape of smoke; and will have discovered how to utilise it wherever coal has to be burnt. We are still in the dark ages of smoke. We hope the country will emerge from them before smoke has utterly destroyed all its natural beauties.—" Sheffield Telegraph " lead- ing article.

WHAT SMOKE DOES. It has been said in defence of soft coal smoke in the air that Pittsburgh lips less tuberculosis than other cities similarly situated in which theie-is rritickless smok. But the Journal of the American Medical Association points out that this, if true, is offset by the fact that catarrh, pneumonia and other "bad air" dis- eases are prevalent and that "the Pittsburgh ophthalmologists are said to he busiest after a heavy fog accompanied by smoke."

div.head: WYCLIFFE 1,3 A.
div.p: WYCLIFFE 1,3 A.

There was an interesting paper delivered at the 'meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. on Sunday afternoon on the subject of • "Living in the sufferings ,of Christ" by Mr. Billingham. He took Paul as an illustration .of how he, in body and mind, lived a Christlike life. Christ in joy. suffering or pain, took hold of the sufferings of others.- Because Christ passed through a life of suffering, privation and shame, he was the more able to see and feel with others in the sorrow they experienced. The lesson was read by Mr. C. Cotton. and Mr. Wright led in prayer. The Rev. T. T. James said the P.S.A. movement stood for the help of humanity., If it did not it stood for nothing. The Secretary Of the P.S.A. expressed the meeting's deepest sympathy with Mr. Prin- cep, a member, who is in the Infirmiry through an actident to his eyes.

div.head: BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH.
div.p: BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH.
" The Virility of Christianity."

Choosing as his text "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth," the Rev. H. Williamson, h3f what at first sight might appear a paradox, preached a sermon on Christianity as .a virile, manly and energetje life. The .preacher pointed out that the common conception of a Christian was that he was a person lacking all the characteristics. that go to make up a man in the real sense of the word. Christ was frequently referred to as the "meek and lowly Jesus,". but the New Testument re- vealed on many occasions a Christ Energetic, active and virile in every way. The apostles, often regarded as saints of a onict. patient, sweet-tempered order, were freque.utly portrayed as ,veritable lions facing -tremendous odds, with a real bravery and the truest heroism. The Apostle Paul was a man who, in the face of many adversaries, and despite a of adversitics,.przwed himself a man of tremen-. dons power; rejoicing in Jinfirmities and ove:e- coming obstacle p that Weruld have crushed tint average ineavidual. _

div.head: CALL OF THE MISSIONS.
div.p: THE CALL OF THE MISSIONS.
An Appeal for the Lonely Workers.

The anniversary services of the Warrington and District Auxiliary of the 'London Mission- ary Society were celebrated last week-end, when there were large attendances at every meet- ing to hear the deputation which consisted of the Rev. Arthur N. Johnson, home, secretary of the society, and the Rev. W. W. Stephenson, who .has been out in the mission field in India. A cpinmendenient was made on Saturday at the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings, where a very 'good muster gathered to bid welcome to the deputa- tion. Prior to the addresses the ladies con- nected with the sewing party .served refresh- inents, and this was voted a success.

Mr. J. Longland presided, and on the plat- form supporting him were the Rev. T. T. James, Rev. A. N. Johnson and the Rev. W. W. Stephenson. The CHAIRMAN said they were interested in mission work for various motives, some of them from personal interest and some from other motives: It would be extremely ungrateful on the part of the English if they did not take a warm interest in missions, when they owed all they were to the fact Of missionaries having -been sent to their-forefathers. He thought that they did not alWaYs *give quite all the synipathy ,they -Might do to those- men and women .who went out, and he. was sure it would be of very great assistance to the missionaries if they could feel that they were receiving the direct sympathy of the brothers- and 'sisters in the Churches at home. It was altogether too late in the day for anybody to apologise for Mis- sions, but he did sometimes feel that they were apt to think that after they had given their contribution they had done all that was asked of them. It was not all, by a viry long way, and he thought they should trY all they could to infuse a little more missionary. spirit into .their meetings and churches at home. (Applause.)

div.head: LONDON, NOTTINGHAM, CARDIFF.
div.p: LONDON, NOTTINGHAM, CARDIFF.
OWN ARCHITECTS PREFERRED.
No Free Trade in the Designs for
New Council Schools.
A DECISIVE VOTE.

There was another lively discussion at the Warrington Education Committee ,on Monday over the question of whether new schools pro- posed to be erected should be thrown open to the country or confined to Warrington archi- tects. Mr. A. J. Jolley presided. A resolution was defeated by one vote at the October meeting to keep the competition closed to Warrington, and the matter was returned -to the Buildings Committee, but the committee brought back their old scheme to confine com- petition to Warrington architects. Alderman BOLTON moved the adoption, of their recom- mendation.

Mr. R. T. PAnteLordl in secondijig, said when the matter was sent back, that step was chiefly supported by Councillor Pemberton and Mr. C. E. Parker. Also Councillor Pemberton had argued in favour of the appointment of an independent assessor, as required by the Insti- tute, but if he himself • were building a school he would be the last man in England to pay an assessor. Mr. C. E. Parker had a good local reputation—he was "a bit of a kifig " at Pen- keth—(langhter)--and he had gained that repu- tation.because when he.went to Penketh he took a brewery and spent thousands of Pounds on converting it into a works. He .had been largely his own architect, and it was not likely that he would pay for an assessor in his own business. The same remark would probably apply to every member of the committee. It was' not the school, but the master, -i-ho made the scholar: Some masters would turn out better scholars, teaching in a barn, than others who were housed in palaces. Therefore, if the com- mittee had any money to spend, they should spend it upon the schoolmaster, and not upon the palace.

MANUFACTURERS' ANNOUNCEMENTS.

Again we give a collection of atlvertisementsn which show conclusively that black smoke can be prevented by mechanical means, and that great economies can be effected in the process. Where stokers can be employed we are advised, as will be seen by an expert opinion given below, that all black smoke is an indication of low efficiency and waste of fuel, and is totally unnecessary.
THE TRIUMPH STOKER. Perfect Combustion Without Smoke.

The Triumph Mechanical Stoker, manufac- tured by the Triumph Stoker, Ltd., Kirkstall- road, Leeds, is of the Sprinkler type. , The coal, in small quantities, is thrown or sprinkled over the fire by the automatic shovel at intervals of a few seconds, and no two. successive charges ever fall in the same place. The result is a clear, bright fire of a uniform thickness of a few inches, allowing a proper ad- mixture of the requisite amount of air with the gases given off by the fuel, thus ensuring per- fect' combustion without smoke.

The furnace is self-cleaning, consequently the fire-doors rarely require °veiling.; This, prevents the inrush of cold air, with consequent drop- ping .of steam pressure usual when firing, by hand; orcleaning out the clinker in the ordinary manner; it also prevents the sudden stresses on the boiler caused by fluctuating temperatures. During the, ten years it has been in, use, it has been proved to posses q many, decided advantages over the older stokers, whether of the Coker or Sprinkler variety.

Triumph Stoker, Limited, Kirkstall-road, Leeds, send us a catalogue descriptive of their " Triumph " Mechanical Stoker, and a list of users which includes, amongst hundreds of others, such well-known names as the Bradford Dyers' Association, the Fine Cotton Spinners' and Doublers' Association, the British Cotton and Wool Dyers' Association, the English Vel- vet and Cord Dyers' Association, numerous Cor- poration Electricity Works, including Bolton, Ashton-under-Lyne, Eccles, &c., and also some of the most prominent chemical works. The firm show their confidence in the machine by fitting the stoker on approval for a free trial, and also give guarantees covering smokelessness, increased steam raising, and saving in fuel.

div.head: MELDRUM FORCED DRAUGHT
div.p: THE MELDRUM FORCED DRAUGHT
FURNACE.

Cheap Fuel, More Steam, and No Smoke. Messrs. Meldrums, Limited, have for a num- ber of years specialised in machinery for util- ising as fuel, trade waste, _ and low grade materials, such as coke breeze and ballast, colliery waste, &c., and many other materials not otherwise combustible.

The Meldrum Forced Draught Furnace enables this to be done in the most efficient manner. Over 15,000 of these have been sup- plied for burning every 'description of fuel on every type of boiler, Lancashire, eornish, Watertube, Vertical, Locomotive and Marine. This furnace has also been successfully applied to all forms of kilns, stills and brewers' coppers, also thetallurgicar!,furnaces, and indeed every- where where solid fuel is used. A special fea- ture of the furnace is the device employed .to ensure smokeless combustion. This consists of a special valvular dead-plate, which auto- matically opens when the furnace door is shut, and is closed when the freshly-addtd fuel is burnt off. It is frequently- the case that from 25 per cent: to 50 per cent. more steam can be obtained from the boilers, even though the cheapest fuel is used. As 'an instance of the value of the furnaces in

reducing .fuel coots, the installation at the "Sheffield Telegraph" Office is a good one. These furnaces are fitted on all their boilers, both Lancashire and Watertube, and coke breeze, only costing a few pence a ton, is util- ised exclusively. During the thirteen years in which these furnaces have been fitted, the pro- prietors state that £12,000 has been saved and that the chimney is smokeless. . .

In another case the firm are obtaining valu- able steam from smithy ashes. These were formally discarded as useless, and Is. per load was paid to have them carted away. in many other such instances the " Meldrum" Furnace has proved of immense benefit in generating steam from waste and very low grade coal. For extreme economy and smokelessness the "Meldrum" Mechanical Stokers "Koker " and "Sprinkler" types are unequalled. These are made in a variety of designs to suit the condi- tions obtaining, in each individual installation. This "Koker" stoker an be made' for either forced or natural dimaught, and the "Sprinkler' with either fixed or moving bars. For many fuels the fixed grate is better, and for burning coke breeze there is no better machine. A test oi this type of stoker at the Nine Elms Gas Works shows an increasdd'evaporation of 65 per cent., and an improvement in efficiency of 10 per cent. Refuse Destructors.

The problem of utilising town's refuse as fuel 4xlil generating steam from it was solved by Messrs. Meldrums, and the continuous grate destructor, with the "Meldrura" forced draught system, was the bases of all modern destructors. Frequently from 2 to 211 b. of steam have been generated per lb. of refuse:, At Preston million units are generated per annum from ,the town refuse, and the entire tramway system is run by steam from the destructors. Over 150' installations of " Meldrum" destructors are at. work in all parts of the world generating steam for electric lighting and tramways, sewage pumping, heating baths, clinker crushing; and mortar making, &c., drc. For burning low grade fuels smokelessly on an ordinary,,hand-fired.grate, the ." Meldrum" Regenerative Dridge is an indispensible adjunct to the ordinary furnace fittings. This is an apparatus-to 'deliver heated air at the bridge in a Lancashire boiler just in the correct propor- tions for smokeless combustion. In view of the increasingly '''string,ent requirements Of the municipal authorities this -apparatus is almost a necessity, if the boilers are at all heavily worked. It is independent of the chimney draught and is suitable for natural, forced, or induced draught.

To sum up,, there is a vast .amount of fuel wasted in almost every boiler house, through exude methods of firing. All black smoke is. an indication of low efficiency and waste of fuel, and is totally unnecessary.
SMOKELESS AUTOMATIC STOKERS. Efficient and Noiseless.

Messrs. James HOdgkinson, Pendleton, Man- chester, produce stokers which guarantee- not only smokeless and gritless combustion with the maximum of efficiency, but noiseless in running, there being no Springs or shovels or wasteful steam jet forced blast apparatus, which have a tendency to injure the boiler flues. The grates being self-cleaning,, steady steaming is assured. there being no necessity to open the fire doors for any purpose during working hours; all clinker and ash are removed from the Pit at end of bars. This stoker is suitable for most classes of boilers, and all steam users. .

The stoker is proved absolutely smokeless in working, as may be 'seen at a large soap works, where a typical installation 'of 10 Lancashire boilers is. fitted. throughout, the chimney being only 40 feet high, situated close to a model vil- lage. There are over 70 boilers fitted at this firm's works.
