div.head: THORNTON CONSUMER.
div.p: THE THORNTON CONSUMER.
An Experiment at Oldham.
fr`VAck `Milk NiVIIN VISIk VianN Wik NscsN Vazk Nagik VOW Viak *IOW Valk Valk

An interesting demonstration of the consump- tion of 'smoke in the boiler fires of a 'big cotton factory was given recently at the works of Messrs. Murgatroyd Brothers, at the Boyd Mill, Hollinwood. The smoke-consuming plant, which had been fitted to the fire-boxes and which has now been in use at the mill for some months, is known as Thornton's Patent Smoke Consumer and Fuel Economiser, and is manufactUred by lir, J. T. Thornton, of Huddersfield. It has already been successfully adopted in several Nook

large industrial undertakings, and at the demon- stration a number of manufacturors, who have still to solve the problem of smo'kekonsump- tion at their own factories took a keen 'interest in its work. The fires to which the new appli- ance has been fitted have caused a good del of trouble during the last two years by the quan- tity of black smoke they have emitted from time to time. For the purposes of demonstration the smoke-consuming plant was first of all put out of action to give the visitors an opportunity of seeing the smoke usually sent up when the tires were stoked. There was a strong southerly wind blowing at the time and the smoke was therefore not so black as it would otherwise have been. To the eye of the layman it cer- tainly seemed " black " enough, as did most of the smoke coming from the neighbouring mills, but the local smoke inspector, who was there, described it as quite a "medium smoke." If that were taken to be black, he said, there woula be nothing for it but,to fine all the owners in Oldham. The smoke was not, therefore, black enough to incur a fine, but it was far from transparent, and when, almost immediately, the smoke consumer was put to work there was a remarkable change. In a few seconds the smoke coming from the stackoras no more than a thin transparent film, blown rapidly along on the wind, and scarcely to be distinguished from the grey clouds behind. Half 'a minute later there was not a sign that the boilers were in use.

A SMOKELESS COK:NG STOKER That Fieduces Labour 50 Per Cont., With Greater Efficiency. In these days of fierce competition, it is neces- sary for every manufacturer to reduce the -cost of production to a minimum, and his attention is called towards the boiler plant. It is not a dry subject, as many imagine; it is not a diffi- cult one to understand, although there are a good many conditions ;;o conform to before one can obtain the highest efficiency from the fuel burnt. It is these elements that make the sub- ject of interest to the one who is stiiving to produce the greatest economy in the operation of his boiler plant. Thousands. of pounds are spent on engines, and engineers spend hours indicating, setting and re-setting valves, getting rid of friction here and there, and the boiler furnaces are forgotten. This is just what is being done in a lot of instances, and everybody concerited-seems to be satiSfied that-no f aither economies can ,be effected. Do, not be satisfied with a smooth-running and -economical engine. but see that the best results are being obtained from the fuel in the furnaces. The day has arrived when Manufacturers, engineers, &R., must produce cheap steam, and abolish the smoke, grit *and smuts nuisance, and this can only be scientifically accomplished by ins,talling good-designed, powerfully-built mechanical stokers of the coking type. The very limit in machine firing is The Whittaker" Patent Smokeless Coking Stoker, made at Yorkshire- street Iron Works, Burnley. There is smokeless, combustion, no grit or smuts, and the highest efficiency is attained at 50 per cent. less labour. The upkeep is stated to be the very lowest. Other special features include the following: The coking plate is made on an entirely new. principle, being inclined instead of being • placed in a horizontal position, thus causing the coal to ignite more quickly, which is absolutely essential for a coking stoker. The grate is absolutely self-cleaning, all clinker being deposited into a closed chamber at the back of the bars, and is withdrawn underneath the grate by a special shovel at intervals.

div.head: ANTHRACITE STOVES.
div.p: ANTHRACITE STOVES.

The burning of Anthracite Smokeless Coal in a closed stove, having a door fitted with trans- parent mica, through which is seen the bright fire,glowing like a coal fire at its best, is a sys- tem that has come to us from the Continent and has only been of comparatively recent importa- tion. With this method of heating fully 85 per cent. of the heat generated is utilised; every •part of a 'roam, is warmed equally, even to the farthest corner;, perfect ventilation is attained, as even in the depth of winter a window may be kept open without causing a draught; uniform- ity of heat •is secured by a simple adjustment of c regulator, by which the exact degree of warmth desired is obtained and remains constant. There is no smoke, no dust, no fumes, no smell. The stoves are labour-saving and money-saving. Agents: Pendlebury's, Central Station.

div.head: WAGE-EARNING CHILDREN.
div.p: WAGE-EARNING CHILDREN.
Should the Education Committee Grant Exemption From School so Easily?

div.head: PRESENT SYSTEM CHALLENGED.
div.p: THE PRESENT SYSTEM CHALLENGED.

Should children be exempted from school attendance in order that they may become wage earners before the age of 14. years? Was the subject of a somewhat lively discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Education Com- mittee on -Monday evening.. Mr. -Upson pre- sented, amongst other arguments, the view of organised labour, which was against such ex- emptions, and, curiously enough, ,this • was scouted by Councillor Broadhurst, who poses as a " Labour " authority. The matter came ui on the minutes of the School Attendance Com- mittee. Mr. A. J. Jolley presided at the meet- ing.

Sir. UPSON said it would be noticed from thf summary of the weekly rota meetings 54 chil dren applied for exemption from school, and that was granted in 53 cases. If they referred to the preceding month they would find 871 applied and 84 were granted exemption. Tht by-law said that a child shall attend school from the. age of five to 14 years, but to meei eases of children where no provision was mad( for :their edUcation after they had passdd Standard VII. they could be allowed, if they satisfied the inspector, to leave before 14. The law assumed that there were some children not normally gifted, and that provision shpuld be made for them in cases where real hardship would be inflicted by their detention in school until the age of 14. years. Poverty Problem.

He knew the difficulty of the Committee, and he knew the great social problem concerned the men earning wages of from 18s. to 255. per week, in whose homes there was not .sufficient income to properly feed, clothe and maintain a family of young children. He admitted when such a case -came before the Pchool Attendance •Com- mittee they naturally leaned to what they con- sidered the side of mercy. He did not think the function of the Committee was to remedy social injustice and to right an economic wrong. He held that was going the wrong way to work. Many of the men did not geto living wage, but they were not going to remedy such an economic wrong by adding a juvenile wage earner to the family. It was simply an attempt to solve the ques- tion of poverty by relieving the man who °begged from door to door, or attempting- to cure -a cancer in the bowels-- by putting sticking plaster on the neck. (Laughter.) The exploita- tion of the child in the interests of the home income was a thing which ought not to be en- couraged by the Committee. There were other ways, for which some of them were working and for which all ought to work, by which economic wrong might be righted, but he maintained they had no right to imperil the future of the child by making him a wage-earner before he had reached the age of 14.
The " Dunce's Certificate."

The School Attendance Committee went fur- ther. No one would be prepared to maintain that 136 out of 137 cases, in which exemptions had recently been granted, were cases of sheer necessity, and that the childreiP must be

exempted from school to maintain tile family income. Surely that proportion was altoifether beside the mark. The Committee even ex- 3mpted those who did not fulfil the old condi- :ions of the "dunce's certificate."

lie knew a case in which 'a child wha ex- fmpted when he had made only 2,327 attend- tnce out of a possible 3,360; he had been in standard VI. three months and fulfilled the law in no single particular. Such was quite alien :•-,o the spirit of the Act which compelled chil- dren to attend school from the age of five to 14 years.

The speaker further complained of the im- mense amount 'of clerical work uselessly put ipon headmusters in getting out particulars And returns -in applications for exemption— work that should be done by a junior clerk. These were 'often left unnoticed when the appli- ihtion came before the Committee. Great Educational Loss.

lie would point out the great educational loss ;bat' was suffered hy the withdrawal of 'the. thildren at the age of 13. All educationists were agreed that the year from 13 to 14 was the most valuable in the child life and the one in which he could most readily receive instruction. The most valuable work wds done then, and he urged that greater caution should be exercised in withdrawing children from school at the age of 13. He had behind him not only all educa- tionists, but the representatives of the workers themselves.

Every Trade Union Congress, almost every Trades and Labour Council, with the exception af those in the cotton districts, had urgently tsked the Government to raise the school age. ehe representatives' Of labour in the House of :loin:moms were also unanimous in urging the Board of Education to take that step, but, in ;pito of that, the School Attendance Committee iad leaned so much to the side of mercy that Ivery child who reached the age of 13 and made ‘pplication for exemption was granted the .xemption. "EDUCATION GONE MAD."

Councillor BROADHURST said he must answer some of Mr. Upson's statements. Mr. Upson had claimed that the Trades Congress and the Trades Cowincila supported him,- but that was not o. .The whole, of Britain—the whole of the ftritish working classes—were entirely opposed fb the spirit shown by the Trade Union Con- gress. Why, it was education gone mad. tLaughter.) They had to consider what the boys' future was to be. In doing so, they had to come down to common-sense. If a boy of 13 remained at school until he had passed the ex-seventh standard and then entered an iron works, of what practical use would his education be in his employment? In most phases of his work figures would not count; the "rule of four did not count." (Laughter.),
The CHAIRMAN: Keep to the subject of exemp- tion.
Col.lllCillOr BROADEMRST : You allowed Mr. Upson to make a statement charging the School

Attendance Committee with negligence to their duties. I am showing they are not negligent, but take into consideration the whole of the points which must bear upon the question of exemption. If you rule me out of order, then I close.
The CHAIRMAN: No, I don't do that, so long as you stick to the main point and not get too far away from it. Councillor BROADHURST : Thank you, sir! (Laughter.)

div.head: LIVELY EPISODE.
div.p: A LIVELY EPISODE.

Mr. J. JARMAN : Is it quite fair that he should defend the School Attendance Committee when, to my knowledge, be has only been to one meet- ing for months? Councillor 13zoAnunnsT (passionately): No, and why? It is for this reason. I cannot, like Mr. Jarman, leave my employment at any time I like, I have to work for my living and every hour I am away from work means a loss of wages. Unfortunately, I have not got such a deep pocket or the capital that Mr. Jarman has, and that is why.,l'cannot always be there. I think Mr. Jarnian might have thcitight twice before making a remark of that description. It is my humble position in life that will not allow me to spend from two till five o'clock in the afternoon discussing whether a child shall be exempted. It's shameful of you, Jarman! Mr. JARMAN : I never mentioned anything of that.

Councillor BROADHURSI : I hope you will not interrupt. I was saying it was shameful— Mr. JARMAN : Nothing of, the kind was in- tended. I look exception to anyone defending a committee who did not attend the meetings. "Keep the Widow Out."

Councillor BROADHURST : It is sufficient for you that you do know. I:know what I am talking about; I have gone through the mill. If a boy was sent to a wire works like Rylands' or to Crosfield's . soap works—unless he entered the laboratory it would be useless for him to con- tinue his education to the age of 16, if he then only had to‘undertake work like carrying soap. Let th'e Committee consider the case of the poor widow with five children. The CHAIRMAN The poor widow is not on the minutes:, (Laughter.) _ _ _
Mr. H. KINGDON : As far as one of the firms mentioned is concerned, I• must dissociate my- self entirely from .what Councillor Broadhurst says. .
Councillor BRO.kontilLST : If you have a widow who requires an exemption, is not that in order?

The CHAIRMAN : No, it is not.. Councillor BROADHURST : Then 'why allow Mr. Upson to go on as he has done? The CnktßmAN: Don't argue that point. Councillor BROADHURST : I know the reason why I am to be ruled out of order; 1 know it quite well. The CHAIRMAN: I Will do the ruling out when the time icomes. I want to give you as much latitude as possible, but you must stick to the point.

div.head: EDUCATION OR POOR RELIEF.
div.p: EDUCATION OR POOR RELIEF.

'Mr. C. E. PARKER said it was the duty of the Committee to consider the objects of education in Its simple form: were they educating the children merely that they might •go into the soap works or the iron works, or was there something in life a great deal larger than the mere question of employment? If the sole ob- ject of education was to get the children into the works it would be better to reduce the age to 11, but inasmuch as the true object of educa- tion was not merely' to get the children into public works, but really to enlarge their minds so that the children would have an opportunity of living a larger and fuller life, that was the chief point the Committee had to consider in
keeping the children at school to an older age. (Hear, hear.) . .

He agreed with what Mr. Upson said about the School Attendance Committee taking .upon themselves the. responsibilities and duties which did not in any way .belong to them, that was taking upon themselves the duties of the reliev- ing officers or the Poor Law Committees. This brought about confusion, and they had no real guiding principle. He thought the School Attendance Committee should remember that they Were first of all an Education Committee, and that the child should be the first and only interest, and leave to other agencies the ques- tions of. poor relief. (Applause.)

Noticing a light I;urning in a tenement in a Wirksworth court on Saturday, Police-Constable Outram, opening the door, found the dead body of William Spencer, aged 64, who had lately lived the life of a recluse.

div.head: BABY ONE MASS OF ECZEMA.
div.p: BABY ONE MASS OF ECZEMA.

Race Horse Cottage. Llanelly Hill, Aber- gavenny; S. Wales.—" I have a' little. girl gone eight years old, and when a baby five days old eczema started to come. She was one solid mass from head to. foot. I had to carry her on a pil- low for such a time. It started on her eye and worked round to the ears, neck and head, and then started on her little back. She had-to wear gloves so that she could not scratch it. She was nearly blind for four or fire days- " The eczema was like a little boil and then discharged and then formed a scab, and when it was dry and mending it would shell off. I had. to make caps to put on her head so that she could..not.scratch it. It waa so irritating for-her and made her so cross that she could not sleep at all. We were up hr night for three or four weeks. I first washed her with the Cuticura Soap and then put the Cuticura Ointment on after, and the eczema was cleared away. She has not had anything Since. My baby, now ten months, was very near the same, and she is quite cured from the eczema by Cuticura Soap and Ointment." (-Signed) Mrs. Alice Aylett, February Ist. 1913. div.head: SIMILES IN COMPARISON.
div.p: SIMILES IN COMPARISON.

Councillor ihnsaia.i. questioned Mr. Upson's remark that they, the Committee, leaned too much to the sideof mercy, and referred to his illustration of applying sticking plaster to the neck to cure cancer in the bowels. " Well, Jeremy Taylor says you might as well try to core colic, by brushing a man's clothes. That is an improvement, I think, Mr. Upson. (Laughter.) t Mr. UPsos: Mine was original. (Laughter.)

Councillor HENSHALL : That accounts for mine being an' improvement (Laughter.) Alderman Bovrox : That is not on the minutes. (Laughter,) Councillor HENSHALL, after this bit of humour, said Mr. Upson and Mr. Parker said confu- 'sion had arisen through the School Attendance Committee misunderstanding their functions. He was sure they must know under what diffi- culties the work was carried, on. There was a, variety of grounds on which the Committee might relieve a child from attendance between the ages of 13 and.. 14. One was the ground of necessity, and he submitted that the judges of liecessity!were'the sub-committee. At the pre- sent time sticking plaster was all they had got —(laughter)—and he asked the members to assist the School Attendance Committee with something more effective. It was not for the Committee to -say whether the position was economically-. sound. If they were satisfied there was a necessity they had nothing else to do but to relieve it. It was a disaster they had not the power to help a Child more, but they did what they could. (Hear, hear.) ALDERMAN BENNETT DISAPPOINTED. Alderman BENNETT was extremely disappointed at the attitude. of Councillor litroadhurst, Who proved more retrograde than could have been imagined, and he was glad Mr. Parker "went for" C,ouncillor, Broadhurst. The idea that a lad was sent into the world to be a sort of'aux- iliary machine or an aid to mechanical appli- ances used in their industries was an utter falsification of every true ideal of life and edu- cation. He did not think that Councillor Broadhurst himself, quietly and calmly, would stand by the way in which he had put the mat- ter. How could they have anything approaching "equality of opportunity" under conditions such as those Councillor Broadhurst had been defending. Alderman BOLTON: You are all in a fog. (Laughter.) NO FUNCTIONS ASSUMED. - -

. _ Father Wnsos generally agreed with Mr. Upscrn, but had to say that the Committee had not assumed functions which did not belong to them. They had been thrust upon them by the Education Committee. There had been several attempts to solve the question in the only way in which it could be solved, and that was by raising the school age to 14. If someone would again propose that solution he would be delighted to vote for it. -
Councillor CHRIMES said as a trade unionist of 2.5 years' 'standing and as an official also, he could tell Mr. Upson that what the leaders had done in the Trade Union Congress had not

been backed 'up by the rank and file. Until a ballot was taken they could not say what the trade unionists of the country would desire to be done on the question. They could not pos- sibly keep children at school until the age of le unless they gave the working man more money. (Hear, hear.) # The School Attendance Cora- mittee were doing what was right and just.

Councillor PE3II3ERTON objected to what 901120 speakers had said. If some of the, gentlemen who had never had the experience of being hungry or of not having a bed on which to lie could be placed in the position of the poor people there would be a great change in their sentiments. The future success of a child did not depend so much upon his education as upon, the grit he possessed.

div.head: TO PAUPERISE THE PARENTS.
div.p: TO PAUPERISE THE PARENTS.

Mr. E.t PLINSTON; the chairman of the School,' Attendance COmmittee, in winding up the debate, said he agreed with Mr. Upson as to the real' solution of the difficulty, but he would ask Mr. Upson what was to take place in the inter. ml before that solution was arrived at? Would Mr. Parker like the Committee to refuse to allow a boy to earn ss. a week, when by doing so they were compelling the parents to be pauperised'? The Committee based their deci- sions on the question of whether the child would be necessarily and beneficially employed.' He, resented the charge that they did not give sue- dent consideration to the cases. He knew of a case in which the income of a family was 225. a week, out of which 4s. went in rent, and there were five people to maintain. When appliCation was made for exemption were the Committee to place education before the necessities of such a family?' (A Voice: Yes.") Well, he wouht very much like the gentleman who said "-Yes" to take up such an attitude on the Committee and then face the people of Warrington for their votes.

The CHAIRMAN said he entirely associate& with what had been well said by Mr. Upson and Mr. Parker. He felt very strongly that it was the duty of the Committee to turn out strong and healthy citizens rather than cheap drudges. The blame did not lie with the School Attend- ance Committee. The Education Committee were morally responsible, and he hoped they would take steps to amend the system of exemption. The minutes were adopted.

he reasons which seemed to make it there reossvibelethat if "an overture of such a kind" were made, the Opposition should decline alto-

div.head: TALE OF TWO COUNTRIES.
div.p: A TALE OF TWO COUNTRIES.
Protectionist Germany.

"Burdened with heavy and increasing taxes, the German upper and middle classes are economising this year," said a London fur buyer. "The big market of the choicest furs at Leipzig has !leen practically a failure as regards home sales, with the result that Ger- man merchants are 'dumping' furs into England." _ _ _
Free Trade England.

A West End furrier said,: "The buying has been heavy, because the demand this year is abnormal. Everybody seems to be buying furs, and I am afraid there will be no'reduction in prices, at any rate for the better qualities." The above examples were printed together in the "Daily Mail" of November 10th. We do get the truth, sometimes.
MAYOR'S YOUNG ADMIRER.
Photograph by Parkinson. MASTER JAMES CUNNINGTON, who presented the Mayor with a golden horse shoe as a token of good luck.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY 'NOVEMBER 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY 'NOVEMBER 1913.
"FHEP 'OG AVEEIi
A TOKEN OF GOOD LUCK. When the flow -tr of good feeling

was at its height in the Council Chamber on Sun- day at noon, after the Mayor and his many well- wishers had re- turned from church, it was suddenly an- nounced that a boy wished to make a presenta- tion to the Mayor. There was immediate silence and Master James Cunnington, son of Councillor and Mrs. Cunnington, • 32, Longford- street, steppt,. Joldly- up to his Worship and, in a clear treble voice, which could be heard by all, asked his acceptance of a horseshoe as a token of good luck. He also indicated, as he did so, that he was desirous of pinning the token op the Mayor's breast himself, and his Worship bent down .so that his .yOuthfUl admirer Could do as he wished. When the little unexpected ceremony was complete,• the company ap- plauded, and the Mayor stepped over to the boy, who had retired, and shook hands with him, engaging him for a few moments in con- versation.
Master Cunnington, who is only nine years, of age, not only conceived 'the idea himself, but paid the money iecessary for carrying_ it

into execution. Having an accounl at, the Post Office, he "drew " the requisite cash to buy the horseshoe, which is solid gold, and a sketch of which we give at the head of this note. One of the chief things said about the young gentleman was that he is already a.' better public speaker than his father.

div.head: GENTLEMAN.
div.p: A GENTLEMAN.

The late Mr. Edwin Woods, who, having made a gallant struggle with Death for just over twelve months, only to 77e—defeated in the unequal contest last Tuesday, was a true gentleman in every sense of the word. Keen to a degree in upholding the principles he held and in the prosecution of his many-sided busi- ness, he could still look the whole world in

the face and claim its unstinted respect. He did all the good he could privately, without making a noise about it. What he did in this way was known only to a few, but it was the more effective for that reason. The funeral service will take place at Christ Church, Latch- fold, at one o'clock this afternoon, and the in- terment will follow at Daresbury at half-past two. The Mayor has asked his brother borough magistrates to accompany him to the service, "so that a fitting tribute of respect may be paid to the memory of the deceased gentle- man."
ANDLORDS, TENANTS, RENTS AND RATES There Was a marked change in the tone o

the speech of the President of the Warrington Property Owners' Association, made at their annual meeting last Wednesday night. At a former meeting he spoke of the "unforltmate lot" of the 'properly owner—now his note was one of " hope " in the future, and he evidently could see the "clouds lifting:"- We ought to say that during the past few years the proPerty owner in Warrington alleges that he has not been receiving a fair return on his investment— .

Unit whilst the rates were increasing the rents remained stationaryrand therefOre the increased rates were paid by the property owner and not by the tenant. Probably a great deal of light might have been thrown on the question of rates and rent if the property owners had only thrown - open the meeting to the Press, but, unfortunately, we think, both for the property owners • and the public, after the President had given his address, the Press, despite the , remonstrances of several more enlightened gentlemen, were requested to leave.

It is our intention later on to say a good deal on the question of rents, rates and housing— because it is a most acute one. On the one hand, the public are faced with two very serious problems, affecting them in a most vital Way. In the first place, a shortage of houses is aris- ing; in the second place, high rents are loom- ing. The remedy is obvious—more houses must be built, and the money to build these houses, failing to be found by the private purse, will have to be found by the public purse. The recent inquiry in Dublin showed the appalling fact that over 3,000 families were living in one room each family. This is a condition that is prevailing in other parts of Britain, and ,we learn on good authority that even in Warring-

ton there are already in many cases several families living in one house, and that this system, owing to a shortage Of houses, is in- creasing. What does this mean? That not only will the health of the public be 'affected, but that both the moral and physical welfare of the .people are at stake. It behoves every- one who thinks well of the community to assist in combating the evils that are beillg presented before* us. '

div.head: Reason Why.
div.p: The Reason Why.

--A- man does not mind paying for the things he wants, but he hates 'paying for the things he only needs; that is why the water rate is so much more obnoxious than the champagne bill. --" The Tatler."
, THREE THINGS. Three things I ask for, as I go Along the uncertain path of Fate; With these equipped, past many a foe, I hope to reach the Golden Gate.
The first is Happiness: if I Learn not to love God's gift of Life, That gift is void, and Victory Can never rise from out the strife.
The second, Ftrength to overcome The foes that lurk along my Way, To harm; and having these o'erthrown, Strength once again, the more to slay.
And lastly, Faith. Life's use is gone If I can never hope to gain The Holy Place (by Faith alone), And follow in the Angel train.
These gifts I ask for. then I may The narrow path advance along, With confidence, from day to day, Until I join the Heavenly Throng. S.J.

div.head: ROARING COMEDY SKETCH.
div.p: A ROARING COMEDY SKETCH.
George Abel's Show at the Hippodrome

One of the smallest, cleverest and most ludi- crous sketches that have ever been at the Hip- podrome! is "Three of a Kind," presented so excellently by George Abel and Co. this week. In his desire to obtain his matrimonial partner, a young man disguises himself with a red wig and heard in order to "get round" the irate General, the father. Two other gentlemen visit the house, and, strange to say, the three are exactly alike. Those who have not seen the sketch can readily imagine the .humorous complications which accrue; as one of the three is married and is returning to his wife, and the other two are most ardent lovers of two sweet maidens. Mr. Abel, as the General, is the lead- ing comedy plan, and his company well support him. Bert 'Terrell has established himself as a Warrington favourite, his songs and comedy being excellent. The American Kyasas give exhibitions of strength of the teeth, and Miss Kyasa, whose hair is insured for ,tl,OOO, lifts weights of 1751 b. with her hair. Other excellent turns are given by Frank Nava and Dorothy Minton, in a comedy sketch; The Warrington Trio, gymnasts and equilibrists ; Raymond Trio, musical and dancing act; Dot Fm, vocalist; and Ida Ball, staircase dancer.

div.head: MAYOR'S SUNDAY.
div.p: MAYOR'S SUNDAY.

The good fortune which has invariably fol- lowed Councillor Peacock through life did not desert him on Sunday. It was a typically dreary November mornirig early, but no sooner did the crowds of people, who were intent on accompanying him to church, begin to assemble near the Town Hall than the clouds repented, and the rain ceased to fall. The great proces- sion, said to have been the biggest Mayoral procession on record, was • favoured by fine , weather, and after the service the return was made in actual sunshine, a happy omen which was naturally seized upon by his Worship anaP others who subsequently had to make speeches. The Parish Church is built to accommodate 2,000 people comfortably, but on Sunday every available inch was called into use, and it was estimated that the congregation numbered no fewer than 2,500, of whom nearly 1,500 were Friendly Society inembrs: So large was the procession ;that althougt the Mayor entered the church soon after 101% the service began five minutes late, and even then the end of the pro- cession had not entered the building. The church authorities maintained perfect order, and had made. the 'best of plans,- but it took twenty minutes to allow all those forming the procession to reach their seats. Large as the crowds lining the streets were on the journey to the church, they were much larger for the return journey, when the tram and motor 'bus traffic was held up, and the streets wore a Walking Day appehrance. At many points the fact- that it was Sunday did not deter the spectators from applauding as the Mayor passed. The ThePPularity of Councillor Peacock wasdemonstrated, and he once more ex- pressed his intention of doing his utmost to show that the ,confidence reposed in him has not been misplaced.:'-'

The best cheer •of-i The day was given to the ex-Mayor (Dr. 'Joseph), when he, told the Friendly Society memberS in the Drill HaII that he intended to stand by the new Mayor and give him all the help he could. Mr. T. P. Bradshaw, as chief marshal of the Friendly Societies, is to be congratulated upon the suc- cess with which he and his colleagues carried out their duties. •
The Parish Church collection on the occasion of the Mayor's visit, amounted to £l2.

MR. A. IL CROSTIELD AND THE BOWLERS. Mr. Crbsfield was among his good friends, the bowlers, at the Cemetery 'Hotel on Friday and Saturday nights of last week. We hear that On the latter occasion, after the reporters had left, there was some rare fun in the speech- making line, and that Mr. Crosileld's humorous and good-natured remarks were greatly. appre- ciated and ?loudly cheered.

div.head: SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.
div.p: SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.

Mr. Upson and others who look at the ques- tion from the educationist point of view, raised an ,objection at Monday's meeting of. the Educa- tion Committee against the present practice of exempting from attendance at school after the age of 13 almost every child for whom an ex- emption order is asked. There may be cases of hardship in which the small earnings of these Premature toilers are necessary to assist &poor home, but even so, the assistance is dearly bought at a price which is paid partly in loss by the State and partly in the sacrifice of the child's own prospects in life. Mr. UpSou's argument was that the Education Committee have to do with education and not the solving of social questions, which lie beliind the shame 7 ful starvation wages that many heads of families receive. The sub-committee very properly pointed out that they are carrying out the policy of the Education Committee, and ask to be protected by an instruction fixing the leav- ing age at 14. That would solve the educational side of the question--but not the poverty side. Perhaps we shall have decent living wages some day, and our civilisation will not need the sweat of children and the Wreck of their future to' keep it in position.

div.head: MUNICIPAL OFFICES AND LIBRARY,
div.p: MUNICIPAL OFFICES AND LIBRARY,

The Mayor has quickly brought his mind- to bear upon two most iniportant questions— Municipal Offices and the Library. At a meet- ing of the Warrington District Bowling Associa- tion last Saturday his Worship said What he would like to have, and. liking .to have with

Councillor Peacock is a good -piecb upon the way towards having. He wishes to see all the public offices concentrated at the Town Hall, nt, he would save the present building intact. That will have secured the adhesion Of Alder- man Bennett at one stroke. But he would build out wings at each side and make a quad- rangle where he would have the Gas, Health, Education and all the other officials of the town, who are now scattered in all quarters. He would invite the co-operation of the Guard- ians and have the Officials of the Union in the same group of buildings. We are advised by inen •of business and property that there is money in the scheme for the town, as well as convenience for the townspeople, because the present scattered offices could be made a Source of considerable income. The Guardians are on the look-out for a site for offices, °so that the 'present seems to be an opportune time for the powers-that-be to get together and evolve a workable scheme. _

We have an .excellent Library, so far as it goes—but it does not go far enough. .Council- lor Peacock suggests that we might approach Mr. Carnegie \ and improve the Library, which appears to be as good a suggestion as the other. A few years ago we rejected " Car- negie's monby for library extensions,' but if we asked the great man of iron and gold again he might forgerpast years, or, at all events, remember that the old Council .has very largely given way to a new one. Those who most vigorously opposed accepting the money are now gone—one to a place where the getting and spending of money am matters of no account.

div.head: ER ALFRED .111011 D.
div.p: ER ALFRED .111011 D.
Great Free Trader with Brilliant Record.
HIS SERVICES TO LIBERALIEI2II.
The Right lion. Sir Alfrod -Hond,_l3:trt., M.P.,

the principal speaker at next Frida,y's demon- stration in Parr Hall, has been an ardent Liberal and a promoter of political and social reform throughout his whole career. He is now recognised on all sides as one of the leading men of his party. lie is equally effective on the fluor of the House and before a popular audi- once, being a lucid, vigorous and exceptionally well-informed speaker. It is characteristic of him that his maiden speech in Parliament was delivered within a week of his election, during

the debate on the Address in 1906. He speedily got to grips with the ablest of the Tariff. Reform-, ers, subjeCting Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberi lain to most damaging criticism, in a resolution in favour of Free Trade, which he himself intro- duced in March, 1908. His interest extends from foreign affairs and. national defence (he is a vise-president of the Navy League) to, inter alia, Land Reform and Taxation, the position of the Lords, the creation
THE RIGHT HON. SIR ALFRED MOND BART., M.P.

of an elective Senate, and the prevention of Parliamentary deadlock, working-class insur- ance, Welsh Disestablishment, and Home Rule. His readiness of retort and the skill—and glee —with which he metaphorically wipes the floor, for instance, with an incompetent Tariff Reform "economist," delights his Parliamentary col- leagues._

Still in the prime of life—he was born in Lancashire 45 years ago—his record thus far fully justifies the expectation that he has higher tasks and greater opportunities awaiting him at no distant date—a confidence shared by lead- ing members of his party and by his numerous friends. Sir Alfred Mond' A political life began in South Salford, where, in 1900, he put up a good fight. Though unsuccessful on that occasion, hfs cap- ture at the following General Election of thel Tory stronghold of Chester attracted the atten- tion of the whole country. He afterwards accepted the invitation of the Liberals of Swan- sea Town to represent the party in that consti- tuency in succession to the late Sir George Newnes. The appreciation of his services to the Principalityp and his position in the Welsh party is indicated by the fact that he has been made chairman of the Welsh Land Inquiry, and by the importance attached to his co-opera- tion in all efforts to improve the condition of the Welsh people. Needless to add, he has played an active part in the work of the Welsh Disestablishment Campaign Committee. As a member of the Board of Trade Railway Conference of 1909, and of the Mansion House Association on Railway and Canal Traffic, of which he is now the President, Sir Alfred has missed no opportunity of calling the attention of the House of Commons to the grievances of the public and of the trading community against the railway companies. He was the official sec- onder of the "Parliamentary Franchise (Woman) Bill," introduced last year, and no member on either side of the House has been more consistent and energetic in his support of the claim of equal rights for women. Among the most valuable services wfiTch he has rendered to Liberalism has been his un- wavering advocacy of Free Trade, both by speech and pen, together with the work he has done in connection with the Free Trade Union, the Cobden Club, the Liberal Publication De- partment, and the " Westminster Gazette," of which he is chairman of the Board.

One of our most prominent captains of indus- try, Sir Alfred Mond is engaged in the man- agement of a number of important firms, in the founding of which his father, Dr. Mond, played a leading part. Sir Alfred, who has also inherited Dr. Mond's love of art and letters, is not only an active patron of literature—for a few such still exist even in our days—but is himself an effective writer on political, economic and social subjects. His book "Questions of To-day and To-morrow" (Methuen) bears witness to his acumen, inde- pendence, wide sympathy and extensive know- ledge.

div.head: "BABY MINE "-GREAT.
div.p: "BABY MINE "-GREAT.
Sound Comedy at Royal Court.

rt would take a stronger word than " fastidious" to describe anyone who cannot enjoy and set down "Baby Mine," at the Royal Court Theatre this week, as one of the best of farces. It has been enjoyed by thousands of audiences, and Warrington folk have shown their appreciation of sound comedy by filling the theatre nightly and laughing heartily at the droll situations. Miss Margaret Mayo's play is done ample justice to by Mr. Herbert Jay's company of talented artistes, and they have such a storehouse of humorous material at their disposal that they make the farce go with a swing. As the hubby, Mr. W. Kershaw is funny even in his serious moments; while, when he is making fun, he does it at a whirlwind rate. Miss Fay Temple daintily fills her part, and all the company do their utmost to make "Baby Mine" one of the best farces ever seen in Warrington. "THE PRIDE OF THE PRAIRIE" NEXT

div.head: WEEK.
div.p: WEEK.

Messrs. Travis Green and Graham Winsford are sending their original company to the Royal Court Theatre next week,, when, for the first time in Warrington, playgoers will be afforded an opportunity of witnessing this breezy and exciting drama of life amongst the famous Aztec Indians, one of the oldest and most pic- turesque•tribes in Mexico. A pretty love story is written around Clattering Kate (who, as a baby, was found on the Sierra Slopes, and who, 17 years afterwards, finds herself the•idol of the camp and the pride of the prairie) and Dick the Dandy, a young English cowboy. The wellbeing of the pair is materially inter- fered with by the machinations of. Carlos Durango. "Great Storm," seeking vengeance on Carlos, participates in a thrilling fight, dur- ing which Carlos escapes, to continue his un- scrupulous dealings. The whole of the original production will be transferred in its entirety, including the beautiful and realistic scenes,. typical of the grandeur of the scenery. in Mexico. Included in the cast : Miss Ethel Bickham, Miss Elsie Dene, Mr. Graham Wins- ford and Mr. Percy Morton Wright.

div.head: Caledonians to Dine.
div.p: Caledonians to Dine.
, The 27th annual dinner of the Warrington Caledonian Association will, as will be noted from our advertising columns, be held at the Red Lion Hotel, on the evening of Thursday.

Sales by Auction. Mr. Robert Lowe on Wednesday will sell rope trees, plants, &c., at Market Gate Sale Rooms at three p.m., and on Saturday next at 11 o'clock. On December 3rd and 4th he will sell carpets and rugs.
Municipal Officers' Guild Debating Society.

At a meeting of the above, held at the Educa- tion Office, Mr. A. S. Elliott in thg chair, a liter- ary evening was spent. Papers were given on Thomas de Quincey " and " Hilaire Belloc" by Messrs. Hands and Price. Discussions fol- lowed each.

div.head: AVveliffe Headmaster.
div.p: AVveliffe Headmaster.

Canon Morley Stevenson, at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday, congratulated Mr. Sydney W. Jeffery on his appointment as headmaster .of the Wycliffe School. He had known Mr. Jeffery for many years, and lie appreciated the beneficent service Mr. Jeffery had rendered to the cause of education in Warrington.

div.head: Regular Occurrence.
div.p: A Regular Occurrence.

At the Warrington Juvenile Court on Wed- nesday afternoon'three young boys were charged with stealing money from the till in the shop of Mr. Hall, 133, Sankey-street, amounting to 3s. old. One was discharged after a caution, and the other two were committed to a reforma- tory school until 14 years of age. The police stated that thieving by 'young Ws was becom- ing a regular occurrence.

div.head: Strike Settlement.
div.p: Strike Settlement.

As we intimated last week, the apprentices who struck work a week ago at Messrs. Rylands Bros. agreed to the terms offered by the manage- alAent to a deputation from their trade union. The boys struck against a system whereby each one would be required to fill in a sheet showing the amount of work done, and in addition to charges that the firm were going to a rush " them they believed that this system would eventually have led to piece work, to which they are opposed. They returned to work last Monday, on the understanding that the charge hands would fill in the sheets and that piece work would not be expected of them.

div.head: After 43 Years' Service.
div.p: After 43 Years' Service.

An interesting gathering took place on Sat- urday evening at the Royal Oak Hotel, on the occasion of a presentation to Mr. John Humph- reys, of the Bank Quay goods staff, who has retired after 43 years' service. Between 60 and 70 persons sat down to a hot-pot supper, after which Mr. J. E. Waddington, goods agent, made the presentation, consisting of a splendid bureau in oak, with name-plate suitably . in- scribed. Speeches eugolising and reminiscent of the good work of the recipient were made by Chief Foreman Mr. W. Gleave, and other mem- bers of the indoor staff, Mr. Humphreys respond- ing in a very efficient little speech. Mr. Wad- dington, in his remarks, referred to the good feeling which existed between all grades and the .company, as evidenced at this gathering. Topical songs, composed for the occasion, were sung by Mr. J. J. Kite, also songs and instru- mental solos given by other members.

div.head: Causeway Lawn Tennis Club.
div.p: Causeway Lawn Tennis Club.

The President, Lady Greenall, was re-elected. Vice-presidents elected: The Mayor, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, Mr. Harold Smith, Mr. W. P. Bylands, Mr. Walter Milner, Mr. J. H. Clarke, and Dr. Ogilvie. Committee: Messrs. J. W. Davies, Henry Hope, W. Woods, E. Hawkes- worth, H. Bibby, W. Greene, S. Woods, W. J. Isaac and W. Templeton; hon. treasurer, Mr. J. Cox; hon. secretary, Mr. Henry Sutton; Ladies' Committee, the Misses A. Wilson, G. Wilson and E. White, Mesdames Bowen, Woods, Cox, Bibby, Greene and Hope; captain, Mr. J. Bowen; hon. auditors, Messrs. E. W. White- house and W. Pickles. It was resolved to arrango five ho3ne and home matches for each team (first and second), also to have American tournaments on local holidays.

div.head: National Service League.
div.p: National Service League.

There will ke preliminary meetings on Thurs- day at 7 p.m., open-air, if fine, at Bridge Foot, Latchford, Sankey Green, and Cornhill. At Bridge Foot the speakers will be Captain Cros- field, Messrs. Needham and Ashworth, and Mr. Prost in the chair. At Cornhill, Mr. J, H. graethurst in the chair, Messrs. B. S. Townroe and E. Ball will be the speakers. At LatchfOrd the meeting is being organised by Miss S. Broad- Lent The chairman will be Mr. Bellian and the speaker Captain Crean. At Sankey Green Mr. Dale takes the chair, and Messrs. Elwell, Brirae- iow and Long will be the speakers. The Main meeting will be at 8 p.m. at the Bold-street Schools. The formal business connected with

the Warrington Division will be quickly trans- , . acted. The only epeaker will be Mr. Coulson Rernahan, one of the most versatile a modern authors, whose writings vary from imaginative spiritual work like "God and the Ant" to the sensational novel "The •Dumpling. Recently he has devoted practiCally all his time to writ- ing and speaking for Lord Roberts' crusade. In order to speak at Warrington he leaves his home at Hastings early in the morning of the 27th, and has to speak at Brighton on the following night. His work has been mainly for the Free . Churches, so Warring-ton Free Churchmen are likely to find food for thought in his address on National Defence. A further novelty of the Meeting will be the arrangements made to give ample opportunity to all who care to attend to atk questions. Supporters of the National Ser- vice League will be present, prepared and glad to answer questions. These are to be sent up in writing, but those who wish Will be allowed three minutes in which to explain the question, subject to the discretion of the Chairman. This departure certainly shows the fairness of the League and the belief in their own cause.

div.head: Councillor Dirties' Illness.
div.p: Councillor Dirties' Illness.
Councillor Birtles, who has been ill, showed signs of improvement during the week, and that condition was reported last night to be main- tained.

div.head: From Railway to. Education Office.
div.p: From Railway to. Education Office.

The Warrington Education Committee on Monday unanimously appointed Mr. Joseph Dutton, of 21, Battersby-lane, as stores clerk in the Education Office. Mr. Dutton, who is to take up his duties on December Bth, has been employed by the Cheshire Lines Railway for the past 16 years, over half of which have been spent in the company's chief stores offices in Warrington, where he has gained valuable knowledge in his business. Ile has for a num- ber of years been actively, associated with the Railway Clerks' Association, and at present he occupies the vice-chair of the Warrington branch, whilst he was chosen as a delegate to attend this year's conference at York. Mr. Dutton was the successful candidate of eight, who appeared before the committee.

div.head: Warrington Philomathie Society:
div.p: Warrington Philomathie Society:

At a meetilig of the society, held on Wi;dnes- day evening, the question was debated, "Should the land Policy of the present Government be discontinued?" For the affirmative;- Mr. W. B. Forshaw condemned the principles of land taxation embodied in the Finance Act of 1910, and gave examples of alleged injustices which had already resulted, from the applica- tion of the Government's lend policy.—Mr. A. Rathbone, for the negative, contended that the tax On the "unearned increment" in land was justified because the community were en- titled to a share of what they had created.—A discussion ensued, in which Messrs. N. Nield, P. Chadwick, R. M. Monk, Dr. Mellor and T. E. Knowles took part.—The affirmative was car- ried by a majority of three Votes. Mr. J. Walsh presided.

Municipal Cricket Fields. In connection with the Warrington and Dis- trict Amateur Cricket League, the annual pre- sentation of the shield and medals took place on Tuesday evening at Rylands' Recreation Club, Mr. J. W. Travis presiding. Mr. J. Ful- ton-Smith presented the shield and gold medals to the winners, Rylands' Recreation Club, the members of which were Messrs. 11. Booth (cap- tain), E. Sanders, A. Renwick, J. Waywell, J. Barton, T. Knight, T. Newton, F. Jolley, G. McGowan, G. Williams, S. Carter, F. Horrocks, and A. Bramhall. The Conservatives were the runners-up. Mr. Fulton-Smith said the .great difficulty in Warrington was to find an open space. Whether they Would be able to induce the Town Council to provide cricket grounds he did not know. With a great deal of persua- sion it might be within the range of possibility to induce the Corporation to provide cricket fields as well as bowling greens.

" EVeryWolllall. "The Theatre in the day of Shakespeare " was the title of an interesting paper given by Dr. Law to members of the Shakespearean Society in the Cairo-street Schools on Thurs- day evening. Mr. A. Perris presided over a moderate attendance.—Dr. Law said his object in giving the paper was to awaken a new interest in the great national poet.—Mr. R. 0. Riche, special representative of Messrs. Milton Bode and Edward Compton's Company in "Every- woman," spoke of the much-discussed play, and said it was coming to Liverpool on December Ist. " Everywoman " was an earnest endeavour to combine the old and modern stage produc- tion, and that was why they showed in the abstract, characters in the concrete form in men and women. It was not a drama, a musical comedy, nor, was it, strictly speaking, a moralit play. There were 45 characters, and "Eery- woman's" search for "King Love" was the prin- cipal theme, and the play showed how " Every- woman " was saved from pitfalls by "Con- science." It was not a preaching play or a sermon in disguise, but something which cry- one ought to see.

Daintily-dressed Dolls. The Council Chamber at the Town Hall was yesterday afternoon transformed into a nursery, for numerous " babies " were arranged on chairs and tables—but they were silent! The event was in connection with the Cinderella Doll Club, when over 200 dolls were on view, all of which had been dressed by local ladies, schools and in- stitutions, and these dollies will eventually find a place of repose in the arms of the poor little mites who abound in our big towns. The dolls will help to brighten and cheer the Christmas these children are forced to spend.—During the afternoon Mr. Murray, on behalf of the 'Mayoress, expressed her thanks to the ladies who had so kindly dressed the dolls. He ex- plained that this was a new idea in Warring- ton, and their thanks were due to the Deputy Mayor and Mrs. Nield, through whose thought- fulness the scheme was initiated. He was de- sired by the Mayoress also ,to §aY that she was extremely pleased at the way in which the re- sponse had been made, and she hoped that in the future an even larger number of dolls would be forthcoming. Her thanks were also due to the staffs at the Town Hall and the Education Office, who had worked hard to make the event a success.

div.head: United Irish _League.
div.p: United Irish _League.

_ A special meeting was held at the Club Rooms, 25, Winwick-road, , on 'Thursday evening, the President, Mr. D. Currie presiding. Councillor Joseph Hawthorn wrote to tke President: "Will you please convey to the members of the United Irish League my sincere thanks for their assist- ance during my election in Whitecross Ward. They helped me considerably in canvassing and bringing voters to the polling booth, and I trust that the triumph we gained over our opponents will be some recompense for their efforts. I hope it presages a still greater triumph at an early date, when the members of the United Irish League will have realised to the 1111 their dreams and desires for Home Rule." The rca d- ing of Councillor Hawthorn's letter was re- ceived with great applause.—The Secretary, Mr. J. Fay, gave a synopsis of the work done during the past six months, which, he declared, was one of the most successful periods in the history of the club.—On the motion of the Treasurer, Mr. E. Kelly, seconded by Mr. Handley, -t was agreed to send' £lO to the Executive for mem- bership cards.—Messrg. Ryan, Mahoney and Hughes addressed the meeting, expressing the desire that this the last year of the U.I.L. would be an unqualified success.

div.head: "Buff." Ball.
div.p: The "Buff." Ball.

There was much gaiety at the Parr Hall in Thursday evening on the occasion of the annual ball of the Antideluvian Order of Buffaloes: The Mayor and Mayoress were present, And Mrs. Peacock presented the prizes to the winners of the whist drive.—Mr. 'James Walsh, in asking the Mayoress to present the prizes, said that be was sure that everyone would agree with him that the choice of the Mayoralty of Warrington could mot have have fallen upon a worthier nern than Councillor Peacock,: (Hear, hear, and applause.)—The Mayor said that he was very glad to be aivongst his brother Buffs, and he took that opportunity of thanking them for their slipport during the last month or two, and 'especially for their support the previous Sun- day.—The exhibition of dancing by Professor H. Boyle and Mrs. Boyle was a decided success. They executed the Tango, and the Boston Waltz, but it was in the early Victorian Lancers, in cos- tume, that they called forth the greatest praise. They were assisted by Master Fred Boyle, Miss Vera Woods" Mr. and Mrs. .T. Jolley, Mr. P. Gardner and Miss C. Bostock. The dancing M.C.'s were Messrs. Clare and Bruce, and those for the whist, Messrs. Walsh and Gordon, whilst the Buffs' Band, conducted by Mr. Robert Smith, played excellently. The winners of the whist drive were :—Ladies: 1, Miss M. Williams; 2, Mrs. Bruce; consolation, Miss Hackett., Gent's: 1, Mr. H. Davies; 2, Mr. J. C. Houghton; con- solation, Mr. Berry.

The Borough Treasurer. Mr. John Fairhurst, the Borough Treasurer, was amongst the Corporation officials present in the Mayor's procession on Sunday, his name accidentally being • omitted from the list on another page.

Congratulations! We heartily congratulate Mr. H. S. Essenhigh, of the Town Clerk's Department, who has been articled to Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, upon having successfully passed the final examination of the Law Society, held November 3rd and 4th:

div.head: Museum Committee Lecture.
div.p: Museum Committee Lecture.

Mr. J. H. Phythian delivered the third of the series of lectures on "Venice," under the aus- pices of the Museum Committee, in the Co- operative Hall on Saturday evening, taking for his subject "The power and splendour of Venice." Councillor Henshall, who preaided, said in the story of the rise and expansion of. Venice they could see lessons of every-day value, to them all. It was full of deep and abiding lessons for their own and all other 'generations._

Etchings and Pictures. All those who are in any way attracted by good etchings, anpi in particular those who have any recollection. of Mr. Hedley Fitton, RE., once A resident in• Warrington, and now one of the most popular exponents of this branch of art, will welcome an exhibit which has just been added to the Museum. . Mr. Henry Roberts has recently formed a collection of Mr. Fitton's prints, which includes examples of his most important plates, and has kindly lent the whole series, 19 in number, to the Museum Committee for a few weeks. In return for the loan of two of the comraittee's pictures, the authopities of the Nottingham Castle Museum have lent a couple of oil paintings, which should prove very interesting, viz., "Accepted," a Venetian episode, by E. von de Blass, in the popular style characteristic of the artist, and "Child- hood's Treasures," a charming interior scene, representing a group of young children watching a litter of puppies.

Landmark to Disappear. An historic landmark of Warrington is about to disappear. As will be seen from our adver- tising columns, Mr. Robert Lowe will hold, his last sale on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday next, when a large quantity of household effects and other goods will be sold, in his noted Swan Sale Rooms, Bridge-street The property will be pulled down, and the site Will be occu- pied by new pKemisep of the London, and City Bank. The Swan Rooms are 'very ancient, and leading to them is an old archway, upon which is carved a swan with two necks. This was the original fro%itage to Bridge-street, the shops hay. ing been erected on the garden in front of the old inn. Before Mr. Lowe altered the pre- :nises there were a number of quaint rooms, and around the roof light of one were depicted characters from Shakespeare. The premises were at one time in the, possession °fib!**Ph Maxwell, and the inn had its own brewery attached. The licence was lost some 15 years ago, and Mr. Lowe has been in occupation of the premises for nearly ten years.

div.head: OBJECTED TO PUBLICITY.
div.p: OBJECTED TO PUBLICITY.
Property Owners and the Press.

A question which troubles the property owners of Warrington a great deal is, whether the Press should be allowed to report their meetings. There was a heated discussion on the point at the annual meeting of the War- rington and District Property Owners' Associa- tion in Toft's Assembly .Rooms on Wednesday evening. Mr. H. J..Longton presided. _ _ _ _

- - The committee was elected as follows: Coun- cillor J. Pemberton, Messrs. H. Bridge, W. Dain- teth, G. T. Diggle, E. England, T. Hewitt, J. Hill, P. Lawton, G. E. Mackey, W. Throssell, H. Winstanley, F. W. Wright, D. Cooper, W. Cooper, T. Cooper, W. Furness, E. Hough, G. T. Wilding, A. B. Marsh, G. Ashton, R. W. Cook (secretary), and R. Lunt (treasurer). Mr. LaNGTON said property owners should work hand in hand, but as long as property owners were over-burdened with rates they would not be able to do repairs, or make their tenants as comfortable as they would do otherwise. Thei e was no antagonism between that association and the Corporation. They worked in the interests of the people, to the best of their ability. Mr. SMITH at this stage proposed that the Press retire.
The PRESIDENT urged that they should be pub- lic men and discuss their matters from a public, straightforward, and fearless point of view.
Mr. SMITH contended that no- firms let the re- porters take notes of their business meetings. He might propose something to which the tenants would not agree, and they would report it.

Mr. ENGLAND said they should let the tenants know why the rents had gone up. He sup- ported the amendment that the Press remain. Mr. SMITE: The people/know why rents have gone up. Seven members voted for the amendment and the resolution was carried. The reporters retired.

div.head: RATIONAL HOURS OF LABOUR.
div.p: THE RATIONAL HOURS OF LABOUR.

• Mr. A: H. Crosfield and the -..llayor attended the annual- prize distribution in connection with the Warrington District Bowling Associa- tion in the Cemetery !Hotel Club Room on Saturday evening. Mr. Crosfield presided over a fair number of members and a most enjoy- able evening was spent. The prize-winners in the Individual Merit Competition were; T. Bolton, G. Ball, sen., W. Roughley, J. Gleave, W. Bridge, R. Sunderland, 11. Bennett and W. Barton. The Senior Con- servative Club team won the Association Com- petition, and the Cemetery Hotel team were runners-up. In the Consolation Competition Penketh Tannery won the first prize and Cros- field's the second.

During the evening songs were ably rendered by Mr. J: Willett and Mr. T. Humphries. Mr. 'Trciiv was the accompanist and gave a musical monologue in a clever manner. Mr. CROSFIELD proposed the toast of the "King, Queen and Royal Family."

of labour, and if he had a fair modicum of health and energy, and if tne fates were reason- able kind to him, he (Mr. tdrosfield) could not understand any man hying in this modern civilisation of ours ever haring a dull hour. (Hear, hear.) Speaking as a married man, he hoped that, as far as recreation went, they would always put home first. (Hear, hear.) The First Thing After Home.

Outside the home, he thought the most natural thing for a man living in a busy town like War- rington was to think of seeing a bit of the coun- try, whether he took Shank's mare or a bicycle, They could not come in contact with "earth, air, sea and sky," without wanting to learn at least a little of the teachings of science, of chemistry, of the microscope, and the telescope, in order to know, even in the most general way, something of the astounding and transcendent marvels of the universe in which we lived. (Hear, hear.) That made one of the first claims on their leisure hours. Then they wanted to know something of general history, even_if it were in its broadest outlines.. He was not, at- tempting to. give them any stereotyped order in whicb one subject or another called for their attention. They could not recommend exactly the same choice of study, culture, or public activity to any two men in the room. It all de- pended on a man's capacities and faculties. One man might do patriotic and manly service in his leisure hours by joining the Territorials. Inother man might add a little happiness to his mites in the way Mr. Willett, Mr. Humphries and Mr. Trow had done that night by giving them a great musical treat. Music held a high Place in the culture and recreation of England to-day. (Hear, hear.) • Others would turn to literature and languages, or make a special study of history. Some men would devote them- selves to charitable work, others to local govern- mentor to politics in a general way—and so on. There was no end to it. Given health and energy to follow one or another of those pur- suits, no man need have a single dull hour. (Hear, hear.) It was only fair; then, and abso- lutely just and necessary, that every man should have a reasonable amount of leisure, and therefore an opportunity to take advantage of the wider opportunities which modern civilisa- tion offered them. (Cheers.) Rational Hours of Labour.

rte had always opposed excessive speeding up of any industry, but let them have brisk, alert work during rational hours, rather, than jaded and inefficient work during hours longer than any man ought to be asked to work. (Hear, hear.) If they looked round the country they could see_ that the trend of events was in that direction. As Britishers they would all be glad to see that England was gradually, but surely, progressing in the right direction, And beyond that, if they were good Imperialists, they would rejoice to see the same progress throughout the whole Empire. (Cheers.) He would go further than that, and say if they were good citizens of the world they would not be content till they saw more rational conditions of work adopted throughout the world. (Applause.) When they had got that, which meant the regeneration of Western civilisation, then, even if it were only to be realised in a dim and distant future, they would still go forward and work for the progress of the same regeneration of the good cause throughout the whole world. (Loud applause.)

div.head: Except!onal Facilities,
div.p: Except!onal Facilities,

51r. W. PATRICK gave the Town and trade of Warrington." It was, he said, 32 years since he came to Warringten. as a boy, and went to the old standard soap firm and boilers of Windsor's. With a population over 70,000 Warrington could :ioast of trades providing matarials for a' hew- horn child, and anything from the .birth of the child up to death., (Hear, hear.)', Warrington, as a town of trade, was second to none to any in the country. (Hear, hear.) He believed ‘Varrington could quite well look after itself, i i respective of any part of the country. There were so many indnstries, and he could speak personally on the matter, because he had been, for eleven years, the secretary of the Works Bowling Association, in which 32 different works' took part. It was a pleasure to him to think that the *representatives of all those works valued his services so much as to appoint him again as secretary. During the last ten years , Warrington had jumped up by leaps and bounds. It had been simply owing to the working men putting their heart and soul in the work. They in Warring- ton seemed to have a class of working men who knew the right way about. They believed in giving to their masters a fair day's work, and it was only by such means that they in War- rington were able to hold their heads above water. (Hear, hear.) Warrington would, Very soon have to be taken into account in the com- mercial world. They could have their Man- chesters and Liverpools, but it was towns like Warrington that made the .Manchesters, Liver- pools and Londons. If there were no Warring- tons there would be none of the Liverpools, Sie. As working men, they could take some credit in making Warrington what it was to-day. (Applause.) "Bogey of Heavy Rates."

In reply, the MAYOR said it gave him great pleasure to meet the Warrington District Bowling Association members, because he was a vice-president of the association. He was also pleased to be there in the capacity of Mayor of the ancient borough. (Hear, hear.) He agreed with Mr. Patrick that Warrington enjoyed exceptional facilities owing to the diversified trades. We never suffered from any particularly keen distress for the reason that all the trades worked together, and if one trade was bad another was good, and the latter helped the former. With a population like Warring- ton's, practically a democratic population, they were always ready to help each other in dis- tress. It was a characteristic of any borough like Warrington, but such was not the case in towns depending almost entirely on one trade. When distress was acute all over the country we _scarcely felt it in Warrington. We were progressing admirably, and his hope was that we should have more prosperity in the future. (Hear, hear.)
He was proud of his official position, and he was also proud to be in that gathering, which knew no politics. (liear, hear.) _

With the bogey of heavy rates they had got to be careful in talking of the town's affairs. They had the question of the Town Hall exten- sion before them. That was a matter they could mention only in a whisper. If he had his way he would concentrate all the offices of the Gas Works, Health Department, Board of Guardians, Insurance Committee and Insurance Offices on the site at the Town Hall. He would have the quadrangle complete. If he had hib way he would go in for better arrangements for the public in regard to the Library, which was not sufficient for the commypity of War- rington. They must give the young men and women of Warrington sufficient facilities for enriching their learning. With all the objec- tions to the proposal he would approach Carnegie in regard to getting a Library which would he worthy of the name of Warrington. If they had the concentration completed it would not mean any actual increase in the rates. They had some doubt as to the Insur- ance Commissioners staying in Warrington. If they could get them and the Board of Guar- dians to come in with the other municipal offices they could sell the sites of the Education, Health, Gas and Water Offices, and they would 'make a little bit of money out of the transac- tion.

div.head: Scheme for the Future.
div.p: A Scheme for the Future.

That was a scheme for the future, which they could - only whisper about now, in the Council Chambes. They ought to consider War- rington-as a whole, and, to his mind, concen- tration was one of the finest things they could do. Workers and .masters understood the need for concentration, and he did not see why the Corporation should bq above it. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the Bridge would be completed this year. He was a little bit sore on that point. If he had had anything to do with the wording of that contract he would have had something to say about the bridge being completed within a reasonable time. He had no fear with regard to the prosperity of Warrington. Everything was looking very fine, and he hoped when his term of office was Completed that the members ,of that association would say that their. vice- president had done his work well. He would do all he could to merit their confidence. (Ap- platse.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE CONVENIENCE
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE CONVENIENCE
OF BOWLS.

In presenting the prizes, Mr. CROSFIELD said it was always a great pleasure for him to say a few words about bowls, which he thought so much of. as a national game. Amongst our most cherished forms of national out-of-door pas- times it went back further in English history Ithan any other English game. It had been his lgood fortune to see many a good finish at the game, and to watch the marvellous skill with which critical ,ends were played, and the won- derfnl acCuracy with which hand and eye had irsrot7tci go .together if a man was to. Win victory for himself or his side. The game brought out .many 'excellent moral qualities, and did a great deal for the physical fitness of a man. In our thickly populated towns bowls was such a con- venient game. Cricket and football were glorious games; but they took up far more room than did' bowls: (hear, hear.) In golf, if one of the cracks got well hold of the ball—a really good belt off the T—he expected to go at least 130 yards. If they carried that Out drive by drive they were going to get over a good deal of territory. Mr. Patrick had made a very interesting speech, and they had had an exceptionally in- teresting, fruitful and suggestive address from the Mayor. (Hear, hear.) He would say with reference to the immense number of artisans in the great organisation to which Mr. Patrick had referred, "More power to their elbows. lta.y they have a fair remuneration for fair work, and may they have fresh and alert work while they are at it, with rational hours of labour. (Hear, bear.) May they have their fair share pf leisure, and may it be agreeably and profit- ably spent." He often thought of the marvellous contrast between the circumstances ,of to-day and the conditions in which our ancestors lived. (Hear, hear.) Nowadays, if a man got a reasonable remuneration for fair work, with rational hours

div.head: CIIAIRNIAN FOR 20 SUCCESSIVE YEARS.
div.p: CIIAIRNIAN FOR 20 SUCCESSIVE YEARS.
Mr. A. IL Crosfleld's Remarkable
Record.
A FEAST OF REMINISCENCES.

Twenty years ago Mr. A. H. Crosfield presided I at the annual prize distribution in connection with the Cemetery Hotel closing bowling main. Year by year since then he has been at the head of that festive board, and it was appropriate that at this year's distribution, which took place on Friday night last in the Club Room, that Mr., Crosfield should, be reminiscent in his speech. An excellent dinner, catered for by Mr. and Mrs. Denham, was partaken of by a large num- ber of members, and afterwards an enjoyable social evening was spent. On the proposition of Mr. CROMPIELD, the toast of the-" King, Queen and Royal Family" was honoured in truly *loyal fashion. In presenting the 'prizes, Mr. Crosfield said the win of Mr. Young was a very popular one. (Alsalause.). The prize-winners were: 1, R. Yotirie; 2, T. It. Fielding; 3, A. Forster; 4, C. Jordan; 5,6, 7 and 8, equal prizes were,wen by A. Penningtoo„, W Drury, G. Ball, jun., and P. Dale., The prize for the best average in the , playing competitions was won by R. Antrobus, • Mr. Youxo suitably replied. Mr. J. Wn.zrer proposed the toast of 'The President," and said that was the first time he had had that privilege. Mr. Crosfield had been with them 20 years. He had shared with them, in their successes when they had won the top trophy, and he had sympathised with them when they had had their reverses.- At great sacrifice their President had come down from London that night to attend that meeting and one the next night. (Applause.) He had known Mr. Crosfield from childhood, and it was a great honour to him to propose that toast. He saw that Mr. Crosfield was following in the footsteps of his uncle, George, a man who was highly respected in Warrington; in the footsteps of his uncle, Morland, a man who always tried to do good; and, another thing, he was following in the footsteps of his good old dad, whom War- rington would never forget. (Applause.)

div.head: BOWLERS AS "GOOD FELLOWS."
div.p: BOWLERS AS "GOOD FELLOWS."

Replying to the toast, which was accorded with musical honours, Mr. CROSFIELD said there was an old saying that practice made perfect, ‘butiMjecrild-,noFt,Pristend to be perfect, for he wa's 'in his way a bit of a politician, and there were not many of them who were perfect. (Laughter.) Although not perfect, he could claim to have had a fair amount of practice in reply- ing to toasts connected in one way or another with the game of bowls and in discussing that time-honoured game in that room. (Hear, hear.) But '-he never felt more pleasure in speaking there thin he felt that evening. They had always had an air of good fellowship in that club, and seeing that that was the 20th anniversary of his first enjoyable evening there, he cciuld not help being a little reminiscent. They were all exceedingly pleased to see Mr. Allison and Mr. Willett there looking so fit and hearty that evening. (Cheers.) It had been a great pleasure to rejoice in the victories that the club had won in the last 20 years. (Hear, hear.) _ _ _

They had all been, very proud to see the 'club occupying quite a premier position in all Lan- cashire. They had, watched the development of bowls in Warrington with satisfaction. 'He thought bowls one of the most ancient games in this country. It was like another garne he was interested in, it was a game that had 'Come to stay. It was not like one of the fashions created by the dressmakers, which came out one year and were dropped and superseded by some now fangled, fantastic folly the next. div.head: CARETAKERS' WAGES.
div.p: CARETAKERS' WAGES.
Complaint of Those Who Look After the Schools.
ARE THE MANAGERS TO BLAME?

The caretakers of schools in Warrington have asked, as already announced in The Examiner," for extra remuneration on the occa- sion of the use of schools for social parties and elections.. At a meeting of the Education Com- mittee on Monday evening the Finance Com- mittee reported that they could not accede to the caretakers' requests. Mr. A. J. Jolley, who presided in the absence of , the Chairman, Councillor H. Roberts, said the matter had received anxious consideration from the Finance Committee, for they were much interested in the hours of the caretakers, Particularly those. in Council schools, and they had endeavoured to give fair treatment. People who used the schools outside of school hours should also endeavour to give fair treatment, but the Finance Committee felt they could do nothing more in the matter than they had already done.

COUNCILLOR BROADHURST INDIGNANT. Councillor BROADHURST moved the resolution back for further consideration. School man- agers were reaping profit from the social func- tions which entailed a great amount of extra work upon the caretakers. After such func- tions it often meant work till one or two in the morning getting ready for the school next day. In such circumstances he thought the care- takers were worthy of extra remuneration. At elections the school managers also reaped profit. He watild not say the Finance Committee were .exploiting .the, caretakers,- but they were cer- tainly 'increasing the Work, and he demanded that the caretakers should have some considera- tion.

If it was the case of an official they would grant an honorarium, spelt with a capital ll— (langhter)—without inquiry. Even such hum- ble servants as the caretakers should be treated in a similar manner, for even a caretaker ought to receive that to which he was entitled. • Councillor PRIHIRRTON : I would like to know if what Mr. Broadhurst has said is true? Councillor BROADHURST : Every word.

div.head: TO AVOID DISCUSSION.
div.p: TO AVOID DISCUSSION.
The CHAIRMAN : I made an explanation to avoid discustion.

Councillor PEMBERTON: I am sorry I didn't hear your explanation. If they are liaid for this extra work I'll not second Mr. Broadhurst. The CHAIRMAN: It is not so. Councillor PEMBERTON : We want to know if they are paid for the extra work?
The CHAIRMAN: f-e-annOt have .a conversation. Does anyone second Mr. Broadhurst; if not, his amendment falls to the ground. The Finance Committee were absolutely unanimous in the matter.

Mr. JARMAN said if the school managers made profit out of the functions they were the people to give the extra money. That was the reason why the resolution was put in that form, as the Finance Committee had nothing whatever to do with the extra duties.

Councillor BROADHURST said he understood the whole of the caretakers came under the Finance Committee as regarded wages, but now he thought, in fairness to the committee, he ought to withdraw his amendment.
Mr. UPSON thought if the managers did not pay the caretakers for the extra work, the care- takers had a just grievance. (Hear, hear.)
