div.head: RYLENTSS CONCESSIONS.
div.p: RYLENTSS CONCESSIONS.
Increased Wages, Shorter Hours and New Overtime Rates.
THE CHESHIRE LINES TROUBLE.

BY 'A WORKER." , A satisfactory settlement has been reached in the question of increased wages and lhorter hours sought by the labourers em h,,kl at the oi works of Messrs. Rylands Broth - The new terms, which come into -operati on Monday, bring that firm up to the level established at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' works, and at Monks, Hall Forge. __ _ _

The -firm have agreed to a minimum wage of 225. per week, with a working week of 53 hours, a reduction of -nearly five hours per week, and, on the average, an increase of is. per week. .As I exclusively stated some weeks ago the matter was raised as .soon as the other inns named had made the concessions. Mr. C. Dukes, the local -secretary of the National Union of Gas Workers and General Labourers, has thus once more successfully acted on behalf of the men. Increases In Three Years. _ _

In addition to the new minimum and the hours reduction, overtime is to be paid at the rate of time and one-third until May next, when, as the Warrington area comes under the terms of the Manchester and District Employ- ers' Federation, overtime will be paid at the rate of time and, a half. The new conditions have given a certain amount of satisfaction to the workers concerned, and the shortening of the hours are an indication that the time is coming when a 48-hour week will become the rule in, the iron trade.

In three years Some interesting concessions have been secured. The wages- have been advanced, in this section of the iron trade from 17s. 10d. per week to a minimum of 225.; and the hours have been reduced by at least five per week. Surely that alone ought to drive home to all the value of trade unionism. Cheshire Lines Trouble.

The sensation of the week in the local indus- trial world has been the trouble which arose on Thursday upon the Cheshire Lines at War- rington. Platelayer - Cosgrove was suspended because he declined to do duty outside that of plathlaying. He was ordered to act as flagman to 801110 drainers, and as this work was special, and would have been contrary to the resolution of the men on Sunday, Cosgrove declined, and the consequence was suspension. The work was so unimportant that the drainers were withdrawn.

There are not a few members of the public, who; in their ignorance, look upon this as in- subordination. The platelayers are at present miserably paid. About 20s. per week is paid for a long stretch of hours, during which the men's lives- are at risk. The Cheshire Linea men have asked for an advance of 25., and then they would be prepared to do all extra duty, as they have done cheerfully in the Past, but three of the wealthiest companies in the country have declined the request, so the men have resolved to work at their legitimate duties, but not undertake extra work until the wages are ad- vanced to 225. Every fair-minded reader will say there is nothing unreasonable in the men's demands.

div.head: Unanimous.
div.p: Unanimous.

I find the utmost unanimity amongst all grades of the Cheshire Lines employes in srp- port of the action taken by Cosgrove. Ile is a man with a sound record, and never before, in his 15 years' service, has he declined to do any special work, but now when he'feels, like others feel, that he cannot exist on 20s. per week, he has taken, as others have done on the system, steps to show that he, and they, cannot be regarded as wage slaves. The railway companies have increased fares, raised the rates for con- tract tickets, and made a huge increase in the rates for the carriage of goods. They did this, at least they told us so, to improve the wages of their .employes. Some platelayers were raised to 205., but is 20s. a living wage for these semi- skilled men, who hourly risk their lives on the ,iron-way?

"It wants a good fog to bring the matter to a crisis," said an official yesterday.-- That iS just .what it wants, and the service will be held 'up. Already arrangements have been made to knock off, many trains in the case of fog, and the Committee are calculating on porters, ware- housemen and others to fog signal. These are unanimous that they will not blackleg. The whole matter is a grave public question, and if the public make its voice heard through the Press, justice will soon he done to the over- worked and underpaid platelayers. Meanwhile the suspension of Cosgrove and others is mak- ing the settlement more difficult.

div.head: SIXTY YEARS A QUEEN.
div.p: SIXTY YEARS A QUEEN.
A Great Picture at the Park Palace.

The Park Palace had a grand re-opening on Monday with Mr. Arthur Bourchier and Miss Violet Vanbrugh in Shakespeare's "Macbeth." This film had a great reception. Since the ex- tensive renovation the Park Palace is exceed- ingly cosy and comfortable. The "star" films for next week are "The Uphill Climb" and "The Gangster."

The grealest achievement in cinematography is to be shown in Warrington during the next few weeks. The film referred to is "Sixty Years a Queen," the life and reign of the late Queen Victoria. Sole exclusive rights have been secured by the Park Palace at a record price, and we are informed by the manager, Mr. Tom R. Bibby, that this is an enormous attrac- tion.

His:laTst word was that there they could meet, Tory and Radical—and he did not know how many other political opinions were represented by the members who were that evening gathered round the board—in an atmosphere, of whole- hearted good fellowship. Let them be proud to keep up that kind of tradition in which old England excelled—the tradition by which men differing so widely, and often so strongly, in political opinions, could sink those differences and meet as friends and good fellows for purposes of sport ati4 social enjoyment. div.head: "The Red Herring."
div.p: "The Red Herring."

Colonel Alan J. Sykes said he political situa- tion of the day was serious.. He did not want anyone to think that he put anything in, the way of importance before the Irish question'. The man who robbed henroosts was attempting to draw a red herring across the trail, and to draw the attention of the people of this country from the, all-important question of Ireland, and he had tried to do it by his usual methods of promising all that he was going to do in the future for the people of the country.

div.head: Mr. Lloyd George's Promises.
div.p: Mr. Lloyd George's Promises.

When Mr. Lloyd George made all those won- derful promises of what lie was going to do for the agricultural labourer, to make the land blos- som again, and cause hundreds of more men to be employed upon it, they should look back and see what his promises had meant in the past. div.head: BRIDGE OF SIGHS.
div.p: BRIDGE OF SIGHS.
Those Long Waits a Nuisance.
MORE COMPLAINTS.

The great grievance of Stockton, Heath resi- 'dents is that they have to wait too long at the swing bridge. The matter was again discussed at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday, when it was stated. that. the officials at the bridges could help a great deal in the matter. Mr. E. Latimer; general superintendent of the Manchester,Ship Canal/Company, wrote in reply to the ConncirS,complaint regarding the length of time that the Chester-road swing bridge at Stockton Heath had been -kept closed, stating that upon the occasion under notice three steamers -passed on the' one swing. The bridge was closed 15 minutes in all, and the delay aris- ing therefrom was altogether exceptional. Any: attempt at closing the bridge would have been to curt disaster.

div.head: Gates Shut Too Soon.
div.p: Gates Shut Too Soon.

Councillor Mawdsley : I think the officials at the bridges could help us a great deal in this matter. They shut the gates before they ought to do. Many times thy shut the gates and you cannot find a steamer. (Hear, hear.), In lily opinion they think alnint the canal, and not about the public at all. (Hear, hear.) The ChalisMan (Mr., C. E. I4inaker): It may have been as you say, and I am inclined to thin kit is so. I suggest that you should in- struct, the Clerk to point out to the Company that oho of the faults of which we complain is that the bridge keepers open the bridges long before there is any necessity to do so. Councillor Mawdsley : I move that. Councillor Hayward: I second. This was agreed to.

div.head: Another Fault.
div.p: Another Fault.

Councillor Mclntyre:. Formerly pedestrians were allowed to.get oit the,bridge..before it had settled; and had not tO wait for the traffic to go on first. They don't allow that now, and pedes- trians have to Wait until the bridge is settled which takes a few minutes. They ought to let pedestrians on and get on their way before the vehicles..

div.head: Received Many Complaints.
div.p: Received Many Complaints.

The Chairman: There might be some element of danger in that. Councillor Lister Kayo: I agree with Council- lor Mclntyre. In Latchford it is just the same. Councillor Mclntyre: I have had many com- plaints. People say they can go on at the Stag and Latchford bridges, but at Stockton Heath they are kept back. It was decided that Otis matter also be men- tioned..

div.head: RIGHT OF WAY. Parish lfeetinu Favours the Remova of Obstructions.
div.p: THE RIGHT OF WAY. Parish lfeetinu Favours the Remova of Obstructions.

AN IMPORTANT GATHERING. Judging by the attendance and the speeches at Tuesday evening's parish meeting in the Stocks-lane Council Schools, Penketlf, there is .good deal of interest manifested' in the dis- puted right of way from the Fiddlers' Ferry Locks to the Fiddlers' Ferry Hotel, and a vote at the conclusion showed a majority in favour Of having,-the obstructions reMoved. Dr. T. A.,Mufray, the chair Man of the Parish Council, presided, and said that the object of 3alling the .meeting was to' ascertain the feel- ings of the district upon this matter, and whether they Should- proceed, and, if necessary, take legal proceedings, or drop the matter alto- ;ether. On October 9, 1911, a *resolution of pro- test was- passed by that Council against the Aosing of the footpath by Capt. Michaelliughes, when it was pointed out that the residents had had the uninterrupted use of the footpath for upwards of 70 years, and that it- had been a fatourite resort of children. After a deal of discussion it was decided to ask the Rurs.l Dis- trict Council to take the necessary action.

div.head: Aged Witnesses.
div.p: Aged Witnesses.

Mr. James Woodward said they had witnesses to prove that it had been a public right of way f or 70 Year, and he proposed : "That this meeting of the electors or Penketh in parish meeting assembled do. authorise, and instruct the Warrington Rural District Coun- cil to, remove the obstructions erected by Cape. Hughes at each entrance to the footpath- along the River Mersey known as the Fiddlers' Ferry footpath." 'Mr. Faulkner seconded...

'Hie following letter, which was addressed to the Surveyor of the 'Rural District Council, and written. by Mr. Joseph Monks, of Egremont, Cheshire, was read: sir,—There has been a right of way along the riverside from Fiddlers' Ferry Inn to Canal 'Lock to my knowledge since the year 180, when along with my father and Admiral ,Evans,- the then river conservator, we walked along the river bank from Sankey Brook to the bottom of Ferry Rgach. In that year I was appointed. by tdmirarTvans river inspector, from the above date' to 1901„ and no person, at any time, ever objected to me, and thousands more, walking along the riverside at that place or along the river bank from Runcorn to Warrington. Also there was a right of handling barges at tide time. "For 30 years I was employed as captain of Crosfield's vessels. "Yours trt,lly,
"JOSEPH MONKS?' An amendment was moved and seconded by Mr. R. Aldcroft that the matter be dropped.
A Lively Discussion.

Mr. P. C. Garnett said that as their repre- sentative on the 'District Council he had gone fully into this matter, and 'he proposed at the last Council. meeting that the surv.eyor be in- structed to remove the obstacle, but, an amend- ment waS put forward that the feeling of the district .of Penketh be ascertained and he was in accord, with this. - Mr. Hunter said that Capt. Hughes must have something to base his claim upon, to which Mr. Woodward replied that it was handed down to him. • Mr: Faulkner : We need to understand how

div.head: All the Money in the Village.
div.p: All the Money in the Village.

Mr. Hunter: If it costs all the money in the I village, we ought to pursue our claim. Mr. Mainley complained that there was no tangible evidence upon-,which to vote, and although he was not against the claiming of the path, he would like to say, perhaps Capt. Hughes had a greater claim to the land than those present supposed. A Parishioner asked if they won the ease if it was taken to law, would they be losers in the pocket? The Chairman: Yes. Another Parishioner : So far as the village is concerned, it is not worth powder and shot. The Chairman said the rates in the village were es. in the X, which was equal to the rates in many large towns. To him it appeared that the footpath under dispute was of more import- ance to the Fiddlers' Ferry Inn than to anyone else. • . _
The resolution was carried by 28 votes to 17.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM LYNIM.

Is Lyrnm's fate to become A large industrial. town? Prophets predict such possible. Developments go on apace. The new salt works mean much Extra population will be .brought in. Already the shopkeepers are rubbing Their hands in gleeful anticipation- Lynlm monopolised Warrington County Court. The case of the nurse of the late Mr. Richards Attracted a great deal of interest. The Junior Unionists have organised. Already we've had a touch of " Ulsterin." There was, however, a much larger • - Attendance at the ;Women's Liberal- meeting. The Church choir concert was a success. The clerical vocalist proved. to .be One of the greatest of the many attractions.
No Name.—At the. Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday: Harold Johnson, of Lymm, was fined 2s. 6d., including costs, for being the owner of a dog which was without name and address on the collar. •

On the Bench.—The magistrates at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday were Mr. G. W. Gould (in the, chair), and Messrs: John Coxon, Henry Holden and S. Davies. Unparliament;ry.—Thomas Leigh, a labourer, of Red Hut, Statham, Was fined 55., including costs, at Lyn= on Wednesday. ,for using bad language near the Lymm Post Office. He pleaded that he was drunk and did not' remem- ber.

Young Unionists.—The recently formed Lymm branch of the Junior Unionist Associations held a meeting in the Conservative Club., Mr. G. Parker presided.. Mr. W. Dawson, .Manchester, who was the chief speaker. dealt. principally on the Irish Home Rule question.

The Poor Rate.77At,the Altrincham Petty.Ses- Sions on Monday, the magistrate's apprdved of a poor rate for the township of. Lrinm for the next half-year of 9d. in the on agricultural land, and Is. 6d. in the ot on buildings and other hereditainents, this being the same rate as for the previous period.

. A Knowing Dog.—At the.LYmni Petty Ses-- sions on Wednesday, a charge against Thomas tone,. of Kilniver, Reatiry, of keeping: a dog without a collar was dismissed. The defendant explained by letter that the dog had slipped its collar, wki:eli was,. found attached to a chain, by' the Side of the kennel:

Women Lbera I s.—The Lymm Women's Liberal Association on Thursday 'held a meeting in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. Miss Welford ' presided. Mrs. Barton, Manchester, delivered an effective address on "The present „political situation," dealing chiefly with Welsh Disestablishment and Home Rule. Broom Edge Missionary Sermons.—The annual missionary sermons were preached on Sunday at the Broom Edge Primitive Methodist Church by the Rev.. R. W. Ferguson, whose, topic in the morning-was "A-Divine Commission." In the afternoon he delivered an interesting and helpful address .to the teachers, parents -and scholars on "An ugly corner Made. beautfis'uL"- The evening subject was " God,.'the God of the living," special reference being :made 'by the preacher to the late Mrs. Lawson, who was an ardent ,missionary 'worker. On' Wedriesday evening the missionary meeting was presided over by the Rev.. it W. Ferguson, who•condUcted the devotional exercises, and opened the meet- ing with a few remarks. The Rev. W. Daw gave the Connexional report. An inspiring ad- dress on missionary work, especially in Central and Western Africa, was given by the deputa- tion, the Rev. W. *Overton. On the proposition of the Rev. R.. W. Ferguson, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to all who had helped to make the anniversary a success and to Mr.- and Mrs. H. Champ for their gift to the trustees of a beautiful pulpit Bible. The total amount raised, including moneys collected by, Miss Mary Blease and the late Mrs. Lawson, was again in advance of previous years.

Lymm Developments.—Lymm 'at present appears to be in the hands of, the builder and contractor, for, in, addition to., the erection of: several houses, there are the :following under- takings,-whiCh are of public interest. Messrs, Henry Thomason and Sons are making quick headway with 'the erection of the new salt works OIL Boarded' Barn Farm for Messrs. Verdin Cooke. and Co., Ltd.; whilst, pipes have been Put under the roadway for conveying the brine from Birchbrook pump to the above works. Messrs-. Bentley and Ju`bb are constructing a railway siding which is to: join up the new works with the L. rand N.-W. Railway and .the Manchester Ship Canal; this, of course, entails a railway crossing over the Birchbrook-road. The con tractor for the disinfector washhouse at the Isolation Hospital, Mr. Levi Thomason, has made rapid progress, with the result that the building is being roofed. Messrs. Bennie and Thompson are :progressing with the sewer- age scheme, and the task of laying pipes across the Bridgewater Canal, near the Gas Works, has been successfully accomplished, after several weeks of difficult work. As mentioned in our issue of November Ist, plans of a new road on the east side of the lake, which is to come out on Penny Hill, and bridge crossing the Upper Lake, have been prepared by Messrs._ W. and S. Owen, of Warrington, and accepted by Messrs. the Lymm Estate Development Co., Ltd., and we understand the, contract -has been let .to Mr. Harry "Fairclough, who has -been' busy getting the necessary plant on the spot.' '

Parish Choir Concert.—A splendid audience assembled in the Drill Hall on Monday evening ,on the occasion of a concert promoted by the officers of the Lymm Parish Church Choir. The programme was a most attractive one, and was delightfully varied in its scope. Miss Mary Brundrett was the only lady singer, and her clever vocalisation and perfect phrasing were beautifully exemplified in the songs "A bowl of roses," "Bird of Love Divine," and, "0 Flower of all the World." The Rev. Horace Gray is the possessor of a 'mellow bass voice, which he used to advantage in "Mandalay," and two songs by William ,Wallace, "The Rebel" and "Son of Mine." The solo pianist, Miss Marie Hawley, captured her audience by the same means .she used to capture the first prize at Blackpool Musical Festival last month—sheer merit. She is a pupil of Mr. W. Cooke, and ft pupil to be proud of; her execution of the Capriccio, "Scarltitti-Tausig," which was the test piece at Blackpool, engendered a.real regret that this clever young lady's name was. omitted from. the second part of the programme. Mr. John Lawson's violin playing was a revelation, and must have been at once the delight and despair of most of the aspiring amateurs pres- ent. div.head: NURSEMAID'S FEE.
div.p: A NURSEMAID'S FEE.
Caring for a Lymm Celebrity.

A CURIOUS COUNTY COURT STORY. A curious Lymm case, in which the .name of a late local celebrity was mentioned, come before Judge Stanger in Warrington County Court on Thursday. Margaret Ann Marsh, Booth's-lane, Lymm, sued David,Daniels, execu- tor of the late Charles Richards, for £5 125., the amount of wages due for nursing Richards dur-1 int the illness froni which he died a few months ago. Mr. A. Browne, for the plaintiff, said Mr. Richards Was a .very notorious character in Lymm, and he died at the age of 89 years. The young plaintiff had nursed him at his request for 14 we*. She lived next door to Richards' ,house, where Richards - lived by himself, and plaintiff was the only person' titteiiding Knocked on the 4Vall. Miss Marsh said she attended Richards from ' 29th May to 6th September, when he died. She had to get-up at all, hours of the night to attend to him. When he wanted her he knocked on the wall. Defendant had told her to send her bill in. She heard that defendant had paid other persons. She had no food from Mr. Richards. In answer to Mr. Steel, for the defence, plain- tiff said she was 18 years of age. She had no insurance card. Mr. Steel 2 And you are claiming for wages?— Yes, I aril. Mr. Steel: But you got no insurance card?— I have an insurance ,card, but there are no stamps on it. Plaintiff further stated that Mr. Richards said he would go down to Parr's Bank and pay her the wages. When he first asked her to nurse him he was in a state of collapse. sum of ..t1 had been paid to her solicitor. .
--Mr. Steel sought to prove that Mr. Richards went out several times during the period plain- tiff said she nursed him. Posted Bills Before He Died.
Plaintiff: He went out twice. on the day he died, and I went with him, to.stick bills, &c. Mr. Browne: He was the general factotum of Lymm.

-Plaintiff further stated that, she had distri- buted bills for Mr. Richards.. He always paid his bills straight away. He told her he would not pay her in shillings but in pounds. She had been to Warrington for him several times, and paid her own railway fares. , Mr. Steel: Why did you not claim for railway fares?
Plaintiff: I claim for wages. promised to pay me them. Mr. Steel: He ,went to Shrewsbury Show?— Yes, and he said he was surprised to get back alive.
Mr. Daniels

div.head: Richards'. Estate.
div.p: Richards'. Estate.
Alice Marsh, the grandmother, said the girl had a lot of dirty work to do, and when the nurse was told what she had had to do, she shuddered.

At this Point Mr. Steel said he had gone into all the figures in regard to the estate, and he did not know' from where they were going to get more than XL Mr. Browne : Here we are put to all this ex- pense. We know, where the money is, though, and we'll- get it.

div.head: Had Three Wives
div.p: Had Three Wives

Mr. W. G. Groves said he knew Richards had done distributifig work for the Council. He had known the deceased a long time. He had three wives, and he (Mr. Groves) had known all of them. Mrs. Phillips. a neighbour, said she heard Mr. Richards ask Miss Marsh to nurse him; Mr. Richards had said later that he had a let of money, and lie would be able to pay his bills when he got better. He also said he would pay "Maggie." Mr. Steel submitted that the '..tl paid for the period from the .T7th .August was. quite suffi- cient. Mr. haniels said he was appointed sole execu- tor of the will, under the terms of which every- thing should go to Sarah Campbell, his niece, Mr. Richards had had meals with him many times. He had also attended a funeral at Lynim since June. After the death Mr. Groves had said, "I should pay Maggie for what she has done the last five weeks." He heard she was going to send in a long bill, and he said he would like to have her account, which was de- livered before they got, back from church on the day of -the funeral. lie offefed her 344, OvhiCh sum he had fixed, after making inquiries,
"Everyone Knows About It."
His Honour: Who told you? Defendant : Everyone in Lymm knows abon

• it. Mr. Browne: ,What is your defence? Is it that you have paid more money out than you have received. or that you do not think Miss Marsh is. entitled to the money? Defendant: She was not there nursing him from May to August. I admit she was there from 2nd August to his death. Dr. Thorpe said he thought the girl was get- ting too much at 10s. per week. ' Mrs. Fogg, Mostyn"s-lane, Lynim. said she had done work for Mr. Richards. Plaintiff had told her that she was only keeping the man company. Mr. Richards had always paid her. Judgment for £4 was given in favour of plaintiff, lees the £1 paid.

div.head: GREAT SAN KEY.
div.p: GREAT SAN KEY.
PUBLIC PLAYGROUND. Sankey Gardener's Troubles.

-As to whether certain ducks-, geese or hens had, eaten a. crop of cauliflowers and 'potatoes at Sankey was the subject of a Curious County Court case heard by Judge Stanger at Warring- ton on Thursday. John Cowap, 414 Liverpool- road, Great Sankey, claimed '.25 15s. 6d. from William Keenan, Hood-lane, Sankey, as he alleged defendant's geese, ducks and hens had trespassed on his allotment and had done' the amount of damage stated. After Mr. Browne had outlined the case, Mr. .Cowap said he had planted three lots of cauli- flowers, and each lot had been destroyed. On the day of the King's visit he planted 40 more. He went to see the King pass the end of the road and when he got habit he found three of de- fendant's hens on the, land. .Thkold defendant, who said, "You can do .as you A fur- ther 40 also disappeared, as did also 40 drills of potatoes. He had spent £2 .on the allotment, and had got no return.

Cross-examined by Mr. Jenkins, plaintiff said he had never allowed men on the ground nor boys to play "shinty." He had not allowed Boy Scouts to put a tent on the ground. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, for defendant, said the potatoes were pot planted in a proper manner, and plaintiff watered the cauliflowers in sum- mer, when -lie should not have done. The crop was absolUtely worthless. Mr. J. 'N. Eastwood, Bewsey Hall Lodge, the agent for the allotments, said he would not.give Is. for the 40 drills of potatoes. Not the slight- est effort had been made to protect the crop from trespassers.

Joseph Keenan said he had seen cattle on the allotment, *licit had been open to all the world. It was used as a general playground. Plaintiff had watered the cauliflowers with canal water. The hens had eaten someone else's corn.
His Honour : I suppose they got tired of the canal water and preferred the corn. His Honour awarded the plaintiff £2 2s.

div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

The New Church.—Special services at the new Independent Methodist Church were continued on Sunday. A sacred cantata, tThe Day of Rest," was admirably rendered by the Brick- street Church Choir.. Mr. A. Trow presided at the piano and Mr. W. Tomkinson at the organ.

div.head: SEWERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: THE SEWERAGE SCHEME.
Stormy Council Scene.
MR. LISTER KAYE'S LAST STAND.

A breezy scene was witnessed at the fort- nightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tu`esday between Councillor Lister Kaye and .Councillor G. Pilling over the Grap- penhall sewerage scheme.

The Local Government Board wrote, in reply to the Council's letter of the 6th inst., that ad- verting to the interview which representatives of the Thiral Council had with One of the Board's engineering .advisers with reference to the appli- cation of the Council for sanction to borrow £18,500 for purposes of sewerage and sewage dis- posal for. the townships of Grappenhall, Latch- ford Without and Thliwall, the Board thought that the site now propliosed appeared to be open to serious objection, and that the District Coun- cil should consider the desirability of \proceed- ing with regard to the Provisional Order in re- sped of the site originally proposed: The Clerk: In regard to that I have an order to come up for sealing later on.

div.head: Mr. Lister Kaye's Views.
div.p: Mr. Lister Kaye's Views.

Councillor Lister Kaye: May I say something as one of the deputation, or would the Chairman of the Sewerage Committee, like to speak first? Councillor Pilling: I don't know that I have anything further to say on the matter. Councillor Lister Kaye: I was one of the deputation of three members to appear before the Local Government Board. Mr. Ashton was first called upon to state our case, and, I must say he put .it fairly and well. The engineer of the proposed big scheme was, also present, and as he was continually, going round the table and pointing out different things on the plans, I sug- gested that Mr. Ashton should do this instead. as, naturally, the engineer, who is to be paid a large percentage on the total outlay, would not he altogether in favour of our cutting down the scheme and cheapening it. At least, that was the view I took Of it. However, the Inspec- tor said ho would conduct his inquiry in his own way, so.although I had made my protest I did no good. The Chairman of the Sewerage Committee was then called upon to give his views, and he said that although the committee passed a resolution to ask the Local Govern- ment Board to accept Lord ,Barrymore's site, it was not unanimous, as he did not vote, and that personally he approved of the big scheme. I was then asked if I had any figures to show that Lord Barrymore's scheme would save money. I said we had had an engineer on the job, whom we had engaged by private subscrip- tion, and he said it was much cheaper.
Grappenhall to Pay.

I also told the inspector that, our parish- of GrappenhAll. would. have to. pay two-thirds of the Cost of the scheme, and that what we wanted was the best scheme at the least possible ex- penditure, which we certainly did not get in the big scheme, which was suggested in the first instance, and which we hoped he would be able to modify for us by allowing and accepting our resolution.

I have been fighting for the modification all along, continued Councillor Lister Kaye, and I have been trying, as a representative of the ratepayers should, to save money for the rate- payers. All along, although I have not been on the Council long enough, my contention has been that something cheaper could have been done. It cannot be possible, it is against human nature, to get the cheapest scheme if you give a man so much percentage on what the full amount is. The whole principle and 'the way this scheme has been worked, has, been wrong. In Latchford Without they had a unanimous meeting ~asking their member to support a cheaper scheme.. In Grappeidiall they asked me to support the cheaper scheme and in Thelwall they resolved that they did. not want the scheme at all.

The Chairmu— n : Perhaps the most sensible resolution of the 10t. Councillor Lister Kaye: Perhaps so. I think that if you represent people, you ought to vote in their favour, which has not been done in this case, except -by myself. Although now it is too late to pro Pose a resolution, I still dis- approve of the big scheme.
Councillor Pilling's Reply.

Councillor Pilling: Councillor Kaye does not exactly put the facts of the case. He stated there that a resolution was passed by my Coun- cil going in for a cheaper scheme. Nothing of the kind. The other things he has said about my case are extremely wrong. If he had not interfered as he did at the Local Government Board office he might have got a cheaper scheme. It is only half a scheme about which he talks. It is ridiculous. The charges would be about one penny in the pound. That is the great cheap scheme he talks about. When he says that I have always talked about the big scheme he is making false statements. I say the original scheme is the best. I never said I agreed with it. although Councillor Lister Kaye and Councillor Hayward have both said I was sent here for the distinct purpose of oppos- ing it. I say it is net the truth.

A Little Breeze. Councillor Hayward: I did not say that. Councillor Piling: You did say so. The Chairman: Now, gentlemen. Councillor Hayward: I said he would never have come here unopposed if he had not given his pledge that he would support the cheapest scheme.

Councillor Pilling: I nover gave any,promise to anyone, and the gentleman who said that has not made a pioper stntement. The Chairman: Next business, please. At a later stage the seal of the Council was affixed to the petition to the Local Government Board relating to the acquisition of an outfall site in connection with the Grappenhall sewer- age scheme.

• -Councillor Woodward saick be thought that would be the most satisfactory in the long run. Councillor Lister Kaye was the .only audible dissentient to the seal being affixed. On the proposition of Councillor Pilling, it was 'decided that steps he taken to bring about an interview between the representatives of the scheme and the owners of land with a view to acquiring the land by amicable settlement, rather than by compulsury powers. ,

div.head: ST. HELENS YOUNG MINER'S DEATH.
div.p: ST. HELENS YOUNG MINER'S DEATH.

An inquest was held at St. Helens on Saturday on John Robert Mather, eighteen, 4, Norman's- road, Sutton, who died in the St. Helens Hos- pital, after suffering ,from a fractured spine since May 10th. The Coroner explained thett an action had been brought in the County Court ta recover compensation for injuries from the

Collins Green Colliery Company, but Judge Thomas, after very careful consideration, found that the man was hurt at a time he was doing inething that he ought not to have done. Evidence was given that Mather walked up the haulage brow at the time the rope was in blotion, which was against the rules.—The ver- dict was "Accidental death."

div.head: ST. HELENS' TITLED MAYOR.
div.p: ST. HELENS' TITLED MAYOR.

Sir David Gamble, Bart., the new Mayor of k Helens, attended the morning service on Sunday at St. Helens Parish . Church, when there was a very large congregation. The mem-- hers of the Corporation assembled at the Town also detachments of the borough police under Chief Constable Ellerington, the Lanca- shire Hussars Imperial Yeomanry,. the West Lancashire Divisional Royal Engineers, sth South Lancashire Regiment, and West Lanca- shire R.A.M.C. The service was conducted by the Rev. Albert Baines, vicar of St. Helens.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALISt
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALISt
The Mayoralty.

- - The Mayor's coming "At home" invites compari- son between Warrington's new Mayor and some others whom I have known ih the like position. For instance, on accepting the highest honour which his ,fellow-citizens have it in their power to bestow, Councillor Peacock immediately ar- ranged to dissociate himself from political officialism. 'For myself, I am decidedly of opinion that the view taken by his WorshiP ..is the correct one, and so far as my experience goes it is according to rule. I have :known .some striking exceptions, but I have . always been sorry to see the Mayor for he time being prominently taking sides in political strife and contention. Our present Mayor's decision as to this, and the real sacrifice inVolved, are en- tirely to his credit, and for these things he will he had in grateful remembrance, if not pub- licly commended, by partisans of variou§ Shades. • In Luck's Way. • '

The woman :against whom theft was alleged was singularly fortunate in being the first pris- oner to be brought before the Mayor on his first appearance on the Bench. it is, of course, well understood that on such an occasion the one heading ,the list of offenders is assured, of discharge; but 1.7 have never before known it apply to a case .of alleged larceny. Hitherto, according to my observation (and it goes back to mid-Victorian times), the police, anticipating the exercise of the Mayor's prerogative, have invariably taken care to call as the first case that of an ordinary " drunk " or of a carter summoned, on account of some trivial highway offence. In Warrington this time, the tradi- tional act, was not thus reduced to a mere matter of form.

Amusing Slips. . • We Warrington 4o -nOrmake_our•Nlayors and Aldermen of the staff that some large towns have occasionally- considered 'good enough for them, ort that is—well, comparatively seldom nodays. • I remember how, on a certain occa- sion elsewhere, & worthy alderman delivered himself with great pomposity of the graceful remark that he was not there to pour forth a paregoric on the recipient. Somebody whis- pered to him "panegyric," whereupon the alder- man continued,. gaily—" My friend says ' pane- but as4ht-.two words are ancinjiwis it, cannot matter very much !" Several stories of the kind are told of the late Alderman "Archie" Scarr, sometime Mayor of Leeds, whom I knew personally. During his Mayoralty, Mr. Jolliffe, deputy • town. ,clerk, -'acted as Aecretary to the Mayor. "What kind of alnenuard will you" have, Mr. Mayor?" :asked Jolliffe. "Some

, people like ther-n printed plainly; others elabor- ately, in 'blue and gold." The Mayor replied. "Well have 'ern in blue and gold, Jolliffe ; people like to take 'ern away for a momentum." At a committee meeting attended by a Mr. Woodhouse, that gentlenian •listened patiently to an excited gas debate, and then remarked :. "Mr. Chairman, I have listened attentively to the debate.' Much has been said, but I am not wiser than before. I have noted the idiosyncra- cies of Mr. Scarr--" Here the member alluded to jumped up, and indignantly repudiated what he called a "charge." " Well," he said, "that is a charge ;, and bnever was guilty of. such thing in my life!"

Guileless Indeed. On musical matters, too, Scarr was equally at sea. Going into the Festival Office one day he said, "My wife tells me I must take her to a Festivl COntert7 -NOVA have you got?" "Here's the programme, Mr. Scarr," replied the secretary. "Well, what do you recommend?" He directed attention to Sir George Macfarren's " Joseph." "What's that?" he asked.- "It's a sacred oratorio." "Nay," exclaimed ,Scarr, "I don't care for that. I..sulL hear enough sacred music heaven. Them Bells e'' Carnival suit me best." "Well," replied the official, "here's Mendelssohn's 'Scotch Symphony.' " "Ah I like Scotch bagpipes." And he took tickets for that concert. The Troublesome Aspirate. -

A servant girl in a play which I witnessed many years ago, apologetically remarked con- cerning her faulty speech that if she "dropped her h's in one place," she "picked 'ern up in another," so that matters were equalised. Alderpian Scarr,never dropped his h's, but used them all too freely. Questioned once as tO the large bank overdraft, he said they owed it partly 'to the laxity of Leeds ratepayers, and ended with this peroration: " Hin a borough like hours, turning hover hupwards of two -million and. a half per ,hannum there must be, hoscillation hup hand down." Whatever else may be said, Warrington cannot beat that.

"Lost—and not Wanted." May I briefly add to last week's editorial note under this heading? According to statistics of the lost jfroperty branch. of Scotland Yard, the articles received there as having been found in public conveyances in the course of one year numbered- 65,375, and about half of them were unclaimed and became the legal property of the finders. To be sure, most of the latter were of trivial value, .but among them were many that were not. They included sonic purses, several gold watches, jewellery that was neither cheap nor , tawdry, many‘ excellent opera glasses, first-class umbrellas galore, and a variety of other things that even a well-to-do person might consider well worth a journey to Scotland Yard to recover. The same sort 'of thing goeS on all over the country; Something over a couple of years ago, for example, I read of Birmingham that in public vehicles there One abstracted passenger left a glass eye behind, and false teeth were also mislaid, though the supreme height of forgetfulness was reached by the lady who absentmindedly left a marriage certificate behind. The passenger whe forgot to take two typewriters on leaving did the thing On the heroic scale. A ham and a Christmas tree also left behind suggests a festive mood tempered With oblivion:and it is, perhaps, just as well for those subject to such lapses that

• :hristmas comes but once a year. "Brass" V. "Wit." • Peter Cowell's statement, quoted in last week's "Literary Gleanings," that "there's not a pictur nor a frame nor a utinshill of any kyoin.d that Misther 'O'Donovan bruk an' red for," reminded me of more than one drunken mounte- bank of my acquaintance,- who, ihaving "more brass than wit," would go into a' public-house, sweep all the glasses 06 a table, and call in lopdly fashion for the bill. Such gentry are more: than tolerated because of the grist- they bring to the publiCan's mill—fools and their money being soon parted. 1 knew one of these unspeakable persons but for whose patronage a village alehouse Must have dosed its doors." He .would gather about him all the riff-raff of the district for an orgy, the details being alto- gether too filthy for description; and would then go home and turn:his wife and little ones out of doOrs. Once he met his match. Enter- ing his favourite haunt and finding' there a stranger with a glass of beer before him,‘ he look up the glass, emptied the contents on the floor, and called upon the landlord to replace it with "something better." The visitor wise, dealt the cowardly bully a tremendous blow, knocking himt down, and then, quietly ,resinii- ing his seat and his newspaper, ordered an- other glass of , beer, and paid for it himself. There are such creatures as the above, but it is ty pleasure to turn from them to a very differ- , ( Continued- in preceding column).

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22; 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22; 1913.
WHY DO WE WEAR MOURNING?
Ancieqt Beliefs awl the Curious survlvals they

div.head: harte Left BOind.
div.p: harte Left BOind.
DISGUISES FOR THE DEAD AND FOR THE LIVING

We are all conscious, in a vague sort of way, that we do certain things simply because our parents did them. We give, little thought to their meaning and less .to their usefulness. In a word, they are survivals, and not one person in a hundred thousand has clear ideas .about them. - It would he easy to, .administer a shock to a. . . student. (pCably to anvantiquarian) by .askini such a question as: "Why do mourners throw a handful of soil into the open grave?" or, "Why do we wear mourning?" In answer to the latter we tell ourselves that , when in sorrow we feel best in black. But :ttle feeling , has come from. habit. If it .be hattiral for bereft mortals to adopt black, why do the Egyptians take yellow and the Orientals white?' Possibly there is a common explanation behind all our mourning habits, whether the colour be yellow, white, or black. Let us see.

'frequently seen in old houses and their use can only have one significance. Our ancestors believed that a spirit could only cuter a house by the opening by which it had left it. .• At English funerals it was the common thing for a coffin to be turned round. .and round;: especially at cross-roads, in order-tonfUse the dead. as to the direction they were travelling

div.head: CURIOUS MOURNING HABITS.
div.p: CURIOUS MOURNING HABITS.
The custom of altering the appearance after a death has: occurred. is. universal. :low general .and how curious .our readers will see it we, give some instances.

-, In China it, was the practice with to cover the body pipe- clay after a relative bad • died. In Egypt the substance was yellow ochre, and, 'among people of low intelligence, tallow and soot. The Indians still daub their bodies in this way.

In Korea mourners wear big hats which con- •ceal their faces. In Papua the head is covered with banana leaves, and in New Guinea a .witlier „frame is -put over ,the body, which. is "alrhisa*umbrous 'enough 4gftprevent nibvetbent. Valerius, the ancient historian, says.that the. Lycians always changed dresses, the women wearing men's clothing and the men the .wOrnen's. The cutting of hair and the rending of ,c4otilesfisconinion, and in some lands` it is usual for mourners to sPend a period of hiding in pits.

-Confusing as these curious facts are upon first reading, they may prove to be the expres- sion of a single idea, possibly of a single fear. We think that they are. The various daubings and dressings are meant for disguise.

div.head: DISGUISING OF THE CORPSE.
div.p: THE DISGUISING OF THE CORPSE.

A more curious and very much more puzzling fact is that it was usual in time past (and among s,avage tribes still) to disfigure not only the mourners, but the corpse. A short time ago, 'When< some pt.ehistoric* tomb..- were opened at -Mentone, it Was found that the bodies were disfigured in an extraordinary way. Some were clailb&l 'with red oxide and some decked with ox horns.

The clue to this puzzle is with the . savage tribes who in-many 4hings lipep aliveTthehtiPits. of a distant past. Among savage tribes there is a deep-rooted belief that the ghost of the departed haunts the survivors; and it is always taken for granted that this haunting will be for evil. .However kind a person the deceased one may have been, it is supposed that death brings a. change for the worse; The kind husband- is believed to become full of vindictiveness towards his widow, and the wife to her husband, while children are supposed to become veritable imps and tormentors.
It is felt to be necessary to somehow keep the -spirit harmless, and this may be • done either by soothing it into quietness, by keeping it in ignorance, or by contriving to. deceive it.

div.head: DEVICES TO ,LSCAPE GHOST'S.
div.p: DEVICES TO ,LSCAPE GHOST'S.

With this piece of knowledge_before us let us now look carefully over some devices which have been adopted as means for dealing with the dead. Cairns of stones were piled over them; and they,rwere Availed 'in caves, placed „under the sea, or burned. Yet 'even these measures were not considered effective. The ghoSts came, chiefly, it was alleged, during sleep. There is no difficulty in believing this. After feasts such as followed ancient and savage funerals dream-ghosts would have come had the corpse been. buried under .a pile as high as Snowdon. Of course, in those innocent days they did not study psychology, or the Ik•prkings of the sub-con- scious mind. They saw ghosts, and did- not like them. ,So ingenuity began to operate and various solid prefautions were taken to keep the ghost from walking. Giving up the feast would have been the Most effective, but what ancient mind could have been expected to think of that? And what would a funeral have been without it?
- Let, us watch the working of the savage mind .as ,it grapples with this problem of ghostly interference.

div.head: SPIRIT DODGING.
div.p: SPIRIT DODGING.

In Siam and China flattery 'is used and eulo- gistic things are written for the ghost to read, presumably to make him happy and lieep him harmless. In Wurtemburg the mourners talk round the corpse, in suhi a way as to persuade the spirit that he will be happier if he dwells in the next world. Mexico supports profes- sional ghost movers, - who put spells and barriers ,for the Tghost. The Indians .carry the thing to grim lengths by breaking the back of the corpse to Prevent any further walking. Corning nearer home, there is an old belief that a ghost won't cross water, or, at any rate, that, like a blood-hound, he loses his trail. And so a corpse on its way to burial is carried through water. This. habit has prevailed in places as far distant asj3ritain, Italy an 4 among the .:Maories. 4! Another theory was that"- a ghost would not go through fire, so ‘fires were lit and the body carried through.

Many British funeral habits are based upon the same fears. Take the efforts at disguise. Middle-aged readers will not ncled to be told that the heavy funeral hat bands worn by men, and the crape worn by women were as effective as ever banana leaves could.be for misleading a ghost. _, _ _

And in the matter of confusing the dead and keeping .them n from being, troublesome. In country places ,we have noticed that coins are always placed over theleyes of the dead. Should the eyes be not quite ilosed a binder placed over them before the funeral. In Korea, it may be mentioned, such a bandage is always applied.
CORPSE DOORS.

In many old homes may be seen the; corpse door, a small opening walled up. Through the hole the coffin would be pushed on the occasiOn of a funeral, and, tee aperture- at once built up to keep out the ghost. These doors may be

div.head: AN ,ESVLINIO DEVICE.'
div.p: AN ,ESVLINIO DEVICE.'

The suppoSition in all this is that a ghost must come back by the way that the body had gone..„ 'lf the whole belief were not curious we !night be allowed to say that a peculiarly curious aspeet-of it is seen in the Esquimo idea that a ghost could only get back to the exact home from which he had gone. Under this conviction the Esquimos empty the house in which a death has taken Rlace, ,so that. the spirit finding no food there and no one to tor- ment will go away and not trouble to return. More extraordinary stilh they build special *death houses, to which .the,dyind'are _carried,

so that the ghost, when he returns, will come to a mere Mortuary: • Anything to baffle him. s ;Do we -not:here -,bit -Were* 44*the disguised and bedaubed bodies! The t!orpses werc disfigured so that they would not recog- nise themselves.

Stupid as this seems, it Was a serious belief. They placed a bowl of water in the tomb in the hope that the spirit would look at his reflection there, and, not recognising the figure painted red and in horns, would rest his perplexed:lml muddled brain In sleep and not venture outside the tomb. With the same object the Greeks put masks:over'the faces of the dead.
So'much for the disguising of the corpse. But what of the daubing of the mourners?
There is only one explanation. It was to deceive the rambling ghost and to escape his attentions.

div.head: TIIE ORIGIN OF MOURNING.
div.p: TIIE ORIGIN OF MOURNING.

Other habits fit the theory perfectly. White tribes daubed the body black, dusky Egyptians put on a coat of yellow ochre, and the black tribes took to pipe clay. As civilisation over- took them, while, 'Yellow and black raiment took the place of vulgar daubs. Time passed and the tribes (or some Of them) studied psychology, formed societies •1 of Psychic Research, and proved that among the things which certainly do, not exist are ghosts and _ . fairies.
Yet not the bravest of them dare go to a funeral without the modern equivalent for black daub.
It is now time to cast about for a gentle and unhurtfut conclusion to this article.. We- have all worn 'mourning.; we ,never knew why. • We shall all goon wearing mourning .now that we do know why. .

• No we are not superstitious. We do not try to deceive ghosts. Having abolished them, we can do no more. We are not superstitious. We are imitators of our ancestors in every- thing, good, bad, an indifferent. DeploraWe imitators', that. is ,all. A. M.

div.head: TABLE TALK.
div.p: TABLE TALK.
The World's Tribute of Interesting Items of News.
QUAINT AND AMUSING.

It is estimated that the annual catch of lob- sters in the world is 125,000,000, and of this Nova Scotia supplies 40,000,000, valued at two million dollars. The catch of cod and other fish by 'Nova Scotians brings the total annual value of the lisherieS to over nine million dollars.

Women's Progress in Germany. In Germany, women are • forging rapidly to ;he front as,publie servants. While in 1866 the ;otal number of Government Women employed .n .all the States amounted to 10,200, there are [low -engaged in positions of varying importance in the Post Office Department alone. no fewer ;han 166,000. women. •

Interest Calculating Machine. A Hungarian citizen has invented, an instru- ment which shows instantly the amount of interest due on any given sum for any period at any given rate of interest. The instrument, made in the size and shape of a watch, is of very simple construction, and inexpensive. All that is necessary to operate it-is to place .the hands in the pmper position on the dial and the exact amount of interest in each case is indicated on the face of the instrument.
Doctors' Best Patients.

Not long ago a famous foreign physician was persuaded IA watch some minor hospital oper- ations in -a zoological garden. The patients .were a chimpanzee, an orang-outang, and two or three plain monkeys. They were afflicted with various troubles. The famous man .watched the zoo experts at work for a couple of hours. When they: had finished, he heaved, a deep sigh, and 'observed : "If my patients had half as much sense as those monkey, I'd lose Rine- tenths of my practice inside of a week,."
A Woman Sea Captain.

On the bridge in 'command of a- steamer of neffrlY :3,090 tons which will shortly leave Copenhagen will be—a woman ! She is Mme. Von Bauditz, who, by passing an examination with the highest honours obtainable, has just become entitled to call herself sea captain. Mme.. Von Bauditz, whose husband, Dr., Von Bauditz, is a prominent scientist, declares with breezy vigour that she has not spent years in studying for her examination merely to gain an ornamental title of captain. She intends to make a start in her new calling at once, mid has already 'obtained the command of a steamer of nearly 3,000 tons, which will be the first of .a. new line to leave Copenhagen.
An Historical Prayer-book.

Thee is a remarkable history attached to the prayer-book which was used by the Archbishop of Canterbury at the Iloyal Wedding. It is the famous Hamilton prayer-book, which- has been used at 'nearly every Royal wedding ceremony since George HI. was married in 1761. It is kept, for 'sonic reason or other, in Scotland— in Biel House, Haddingtonshire—and is always brought to London in careful eustckly when any ,great wedding takes place. Dean Stanley used it, at the express request of Queen Vic- toria, at the late Duke of Edinburgh's wedding at St. Petersburg, in January, 1874.
Primitive Turkish Baths in Ireland.

The " sweating-hole " discovered by Mr. James Buckley,, near Schull, Southern Ireland, seem to be a primitive kind of Turkish bath, such as was very early used, and .such as has been known to be employed. by the. Irish peasantry not. )nore than half a century ago. This new- found specimen is in very perfect condition. It is nearly circular, 9 by 10 feet across, something like a lime-kiln, and was entered by a stone- lined creep hole two feet high and wide. The person using it took a pr;ofuse, sweat in it— sonielimes followed by a plunge into the ocean —after it had been made hot by a large fire.

STILL A FORTNIGHT.

My dear Children,— We are still a fortnight off the closing of our Christmas competition, the date of closing 'being 6th December. Already .a number of letters have reached me, and, of course, these have beeh put carefully away until the competi- tiOn closes.

For 'those who have not yet decided to enter ~perhaps I might repeat what is required in the competition. All you have to do is .to write and tell me what you would like that funny old chap Santa Claus to bring you, and tell why-. Then post it on to me. Prizes will be Oven for the best letters. Judging from-thJmmber of letters already received, I think we shall 'have a fine entry. Your loving • UNCLE JACK.

div.head: WHAT I SAW IN LONDON.
div.p: WHAT I SAW IN LONDON.

I am going to tell you -of a day I spent in London not long ago. Directly, after breakfaSt my mother and I walked to the station, and went .by train to Finsbury Park. From there we went to Russell-square by tube Then we walked to the British Museum. There Were a great many things there to interest me, of which one of the chief was a;tiny_watch -set in a ring. Beautiful pots of porcelain and china, besides drinking horns, were displayed in cases. Some seals (not the animal) interested me as well. We saw some beautiful bead work and afterwards the mummies. In the Students' Library I saw Magna Charta, also Shakespeare's signature affixed to a deed, believed to be the "only pieea Of Shakespeare's writing in existence. As we were going out we noticed Anne .Boleyn's and Lady Jane Grey's prayer-books, used at the scaffold.' -*

- After this we went by 'bus to the Bank of England. On the Way we saw a 'part of Old London; (Jog and Magog, Bow Church, the City Temple;- the New Old Bailey, the New Post Office, &c. Near .the Bank are the Mansion House and Royal Exchange. Walking toward.,, the Tower we saw the Monument, a column erected in inemory of the Great Fire. •

At last we reached the Tower, and as it was by this time one o'clock, we had our dinner For a few minutes I stood watching the rivet and the Tower Bridge. Not very far away Is descried London Bridge. We then went into the White Tower, built by William the Con- queror. In here were the armouries contain- ing, 'amongst other things, Wellington's, armour., The gun .carriage which carried King Edward's body and a model of Charles L's 'gold armour interested me most. After feaving the armouries we saw 'the •"Traitors' Gate," ,and then went into the Wakefield Tower to see'fbc: Regalia. I thought 1 had never seen anything so glittering .before. The -Piece I thought hes:, was a ,Avord of gold will nandle of jewels and gold. When we had taken a 'good look at the Crown Jewels we proceeded to the Beau- champ Tower. • There were many inscriptions of prisoners on the walls, one of whieh, I think. was "Thomas Eovill.",

After leaving the Tower we went: to St. Pau,l's Cathedra It i. the iros'. magnificent thing 1 have ever .seen. There were beautiful paintings on the inside of .the dome, and the roof .was inlaid with gold. Several small chapels were also 'ln the Cathedral. I saw the whisi;ering gallery, hut preferred to go into the vaults. Nelson's 'and Wellington's tombs were down there, besides several small chapels. There was also an erection, with the names of a good many battles on the sides, erected in memory of the men killed in battle. We saw General Gordon's tomb and many others in the Cathe- dral. As the evening service was at four o'clock, we stayed to it, and afterwards had tea 1n a refreshment room opposite St. Paul's. Then we came home.

First Principles of Evolution. By 1-leivbert, M.D., &c. riondork: A. and C. Black. Pp. N. 346. 7s. 6d. net.

This book, Dr. Herbert -explains in his .pre- :face, is the o.uteome.'of. a .series .of lectures. to working men and others. It is an attempt to present, in a form suited to the general reader, a complete account of the theory of evolution, not only as it affects biological questions; but in all its various aspects. Dr. Herbert takes a wide and Comprehensive view of the problem of evolution. It is -not a question merely of framing a hypothesis to account for the facts of variation and heredity, although the various theories relating to these subjects are reviewed' at great length, and with admirable impartial- ity. Evolution, ,as Dr'. Herbert very justly points out., covers a_very.much wider field, and Is coterminous withlhe whole range of cosmic phenomena. Darwinism has become so widely known as to be regarded as synonymous with evolution. It ,is particularly gratifying, there- fore, to find a present-day writer emphasising the fact that' the first application of. the evOlu- ,tionary .principle o the, totality -of, ,phenomena was the great achievement of Herbert Spencer. There is a tendency nowadays to overlook our immense debt to Spencer, and we are grateful to Dr. Herbent for reminding us of it. The book is divided into three main sections, dealing respectively with inorganic, organic, and superorganic evolution. Dr. Herbert re- views rapidly the main outlines of the various theories proposed to account for the evolution of the stars, the atoms, and life itself. In deal- ing with 'organic evolution, he very wisely separates the facts of evolution from the the- ories which are offered for their solution.

Dr. Herbert's general conclusion as to the adequacy, of the theory of natural selection to explain the progressive differentiation of the organic world is that, while it is the only accept- able theory of adaptation, it clitinot account for the "origin of the fit," and that though it "can be /looked upon as the efficient. caUse of the pro- gress Of evolutionary lines, their first begin- nings must be attributed to a still unknown factor in evolution.' "

In the section devoted to swerorganic evolu- tion, the present 'state of speculation as to animal behaviour, instinct and intelligence, is described veryjully, and this leads on to a brief but illuminating consideration of the evolution of Morals and society. The crude application of biological theory to political affairs is very rightly deprecated, the inimtance of the social factors in considering social evolution, being, emphasised, No Popular work on evolution would, Of course, be complete without sonic reference to M. Bergson's views, and Dr. Herbert gives a very, sympathetic account of the "Philosophy of Chance," reserving his judgment thereon, but- indicating at the same time that Bergson's theory of instinct cannot be accepted in its entirety. An excellent bibliography and an admirable glossary complete a work that we can very heartily recommend.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
A FUNERAL IN NAZARETH.

Each religious community has a separate cemetery, and the MO*IIIS ilti.ve two. A'deaLk in the household is immediately announced h) - the neighbourhood by the shrieks of the rela- tives who have been sitting around the death-' bed. If a Moslem, the dying man is turned so .as to !ace Mecca. No special religious cere- mony is performed then ; but if the last struggle.. seems to be prolonged, the " khateeb," or priest,' may be summoned to invoke Allah that the spirit may quickly leave the distressed body. It is believed to be the reward of a virtuous life to have a quick ending. The hands are lifted up at the very last, as a final adherence to the Moslem ,;creed. The moment '• that .-theA.death occurs the women scream, tear their hair, and rend their clothes, especially the covering of their breasts, and beat their chests. This frenzy brings all the neighbours, who crowd into the chamber of grief and add their voices to the tumult. Such a scene may last an hour, but sooner or later, order of a kind is achieved, The older women lay out the corpse, putting on the best clothes, and crossing the hands, and: then the formal wailing commences. The leader athong the women, who are squatted close to the wall all round the room, sets the rhythm n of the dirge. She begins to clap her palms together and the west join in, until the roomful are clapping in unison. Then the leader may sing a line in praise of the departed, , and the line is repeated by all in chorus. A sentiment is sung by the leader and repeated in unison, and' this, performance may go on for *ours.- '•

Burial,mustquickly follow death in this land, and presently a rough deal Coffin .-CoVered ith cloth is brought; in which( the body is placed lying on its side. The colour of a Moslem coffin is frequently green. Borne by relatives and male friends it is taken to the mosque for eere- moniousAvashing, after which the procession re-forms and proceeds, to the Moslem cemetery. Headed by several priests, the Moslem creed is repeated again and again as a monotonous chant. Shoulder high the coffin is borne along by relays of the younger men, for it is a good act to carry a true follower of the Prophet; to his last resting-place. So the edge of the coffin may be allowed to rest only a few seconds upon a man's shoulder before he is relieved of the burden by another. Meanwhile the women go straight to the cemetery, and form into a circle some distance away from the open grave. They resunie their, diite, but add to it a slow cere- monious dance, in,which each dancing woman takes a handkerchief in each hand and waves them in tune with the motion of her body. The rest look on, and keep time by hand-clapping. As soon as the procession of Men from the moue appears in the cemetery gateway, the women's dance and chant suddenly stop, and gives place to shrieks and screams and the rend- ing afresh of clothes, and this continues until the corpse is finally interred. The position-of the corpse is.such that the face is looking to vleeca. Later on a long low mound of .stones and mortar is built over the grave, white- washed, and painted in various strange de- signs in brilliant colciurs.—!" Nazareth of To- day," by F. J. SeriM geoui*.

BELFAST NOT THE WEALTHIEST CITY.

Music and politics _ proved to be a pleasing combination in the Co-operative Hall on Mon- day night, when a well-attended meeting was conducted under the auspices of the Junior Liberal Association. The vocal items were given in a very pleasing manner by Miss Ethel Austin (Liverpool), a soprano with a full-toned voice. who was accompanied by Miss Dorothy Kenyon of Liverpool. The experiment proved highb successful, the Chairman (Councillor Roberts) and speakers commenting 'Upon the innovation in a very congratulatory manner.

COUNCILLOR ROBERTS AND THE FORLORN PARTY. Councillor RosEnas,, who presided, said that a few days ago, when he had taken a similar posi- tion to that in Stockton Heath, he had ven- tured to make reference to some glaring prog- nostications by the leader of the Tory party. He (Mr. Bonar Law) had not 'up to that day ex- pressed himself in regard to any particular pro- gramme, but at Newcastle he gave utterance to what was undoubtedly the honest expression and conviction of his mind. Ile told ,his followers " years. ved to. be true. It *as hardly-the kind of speech one 'at that meeting that, in his opinion, unless thatss possibly y pro sometlting in the nature of a miracle occurred, if flie party to which he belonged would be very Llikibeelyralsinwooldponsoittiobne sof orrYr ex- pected from. the leader of a •Varty. As Mr. Winston Churchill said the previous night; you key a dog you expect him to bark and not to howl." A Tory Pledge. Since then Mr. Bonar Law had done some- thing else besides howl. Ile had Promised that in the event of the Tory party being returned to .power at the next election—an extremely re- mote contingency--one of the first things his party would do would be to bring in a Bill by which the compulsory conditions of the Insur- ance Act would be absolutely destroyed, and the people would return to a system of voluntary insurance. The Conservative party talked about compulsory principles as if they were a new thing. It was not a new principle, and any one of those present who had to pay his rates com- pulsorily realised that if he did not pay them he knew what he would get pretty quickly. In regard to education, the compulsory principle applied in regard to school attendance, and they saw that imposed not only in the interests and for the future welfare of the individual child, but for the permanent security and prosperity of the nation as a whole. (Applause.) That was the reason why the compulsory principle had been applied to that great measure of in- surance. Working of Insurance. Act. He knew something about its working, because he happened to be elidirman of the Sanatorium. and Medical Benefits Committees belonging tO the Insurance Committee, and he spoke Without hesitation that if it were not for the compul- sory principle and for that communion of in- terest the compulsory principle recognise...... principle which insisted upon the strong help- ing to bear the burden of the weak, which was in every way a. sound principle to follow—there were innumerable cases which to-day were not only a source of terrible physical pain and suffering to the individual, but wee an abse_ lute menace to the future of the State, and the Population could • not possibly have been dealt with at all. The objects of the Insurance 'Act were to enable them to stamp out the terrible disease of consumption, and there were men and women there who would live to see the day when the number of persons suffering from tuberculosis would be very small. Let Bonar Law go to the country on this policy of destroy- ing compulsory insurance and he thought 40 years would be a short period for the Tory party. (Hear, hear.)

"Homogeneous Counties." In tho four Ulster counties, the homo- geneous— or homoganeous—people. pronounce it differently--counties, the places which mean all the people had the same way a thinking, the rateable value of the four counties was lower than others in Ireland: County Down, the great, homogeneous, wealthy county of Ulster, stood fifteenth • on the list for rateable value. Antrim, the home of the wealthiest people of Belfast, was 20th on the list. Derry was 26th, and Armagh was 21st on the list. That was how they stood in relation to the other beggarly" counties of Ireland.

A-bout the homogeneous population, who were all one way of thinking,. and said they could not force Home Rule on those four counties who were determined, at the expense of their heart's blood, to remain citizens of the great British Empire, and at no cost would they be driven out, even at the • cost of becoming subjects of the German or some other Emperor—(laughter) —of those 'counties he found that in County Down there were 31.6 of the population Roman .Catholics and Nationalists. Of the men in Antrim 20.3, Derry 45,3, and Armagh 41.5 were Nationalists. Over one-third of the population of that homogeneous, little part of Ireland, were •opposed to being excluded from home Rule. If the two-thirds elected a provi- sional goVernment; the other one-thiTd would . . have to elect a provisional government, and thus the position would become too absurd to think about. OVERDUE REFORMS. Franchise Reform. •

Mr. W. A. BARTON, Liberal M.P. for Oldham' said it was unfortunate that British politics were involved in issues that should have been settled long ago. They wanted to tackle new and pressing issues, /and amongst these was the abolition a the plural voter. They wanted simplification of the franchise and the register. There were More votes, lost to the Progressive cause by the present absurd state of the regis- tration laws than by any other cause. In Lan- cashire manufacturing towns a large percentage. of working people were compelled to change eir res'lenee every 12 Or 18 months, which caused them to lope their votes: Liberalism must remove that, and give not only one man one vote, but' a' vote for every man. (Applause.) It ought to be the duty of the Legislature to make it easy. for every citizen to take his or her part in the life of the State. Home Rule was an issue that should be on the Statute Book. The cry had been raised that Rome Rule would bring about the ascendency of the Catholics in Ireland. It was no part of the Liberal policy to bring about the ascendency of any • Church or any body of men over the hearts and consciences of any other body of men. (Applause.) A Rome Rule Parliament in Ireland would have no power to favour, estab- lish Or endow any religion. (Applause.)

The Ulster Problem. The Ulster problem was all that remained of a Much larger problem. Where did the Ulstei problem stand? If it had not been shrouded in threats of illegality, of sedition and of rebellion,, it would have been easier for the .Liberals to deal with it, but it had been shrouded in lan- guage, which, if it was allowed to succeed, would shake the very foundations of the State and loosen the bonds of tile great Administrative Empire. Mr. Asquith and Mr. John Redmond wanted' a settlement by consent With Ulster, and if Ulster would not agree then the law must take its course. (Applause.) The men who spouted sedition must take the consequences. (Hear, hear.) • The Ulster question must not be taken on the value which some Ulstermen put upon it. They greatly exaggerated it, to mislead the people in England. Scotland and Wales. People believed that Ulster was the, great, progressive, wealthy, powerful province of Ireland, and they were told the other three beggarly 'provinces would overtax Ulster. There was no power under which a Home Rule Parliament could initiate taxation that would be unfair to Ulster or any other province.

Ulster Exposed. What was the real position of Ulster relative to the other Irish provinces? Contrast 'first of all Dublin and Belfast, and he quoted from Treasury returns, specially prepared on the sub- ject. In 1912 the gross annual Value of Dublin was .210,717,391; in Belfast, the great and only city in Ireland, according to -Ulster people, the gross annual value was £6,339,214. Pass to the income .tax. Belfast was a great comnlercial city, full of wealth and no sweated industries (laughter and applause)—the latter were down in Dublin—but what were the returns? In Dub- lin income tax amounted to £361,000 per an- num, and in the great ,Belfast to £206,000. The gross assessment per head in Dublin was £36 Ss. NI. per annum; in Belfast, £l6 is. 7d., 0r less

div.head: NO ONE TO FIGHT.
div.p: NO ONE TO FIGHT.

Mr. J. DAVIES, the Liberal candidate for Crewe, said he was astounded that a great and influential party like the Conseryatives should have pledged itself to support a handful of men in Ulster, who proposed •to rebel against the Parliament of the country and against the Crown of the British Empire. It was astound- ing that the one, great political party which prided itself on 'constipitional government should take such a course.' It would be a great misfortune if the Tories got hold of the reins of 'government before Home Rule became law, for, then the land would be faced with a rebel- lion in Ireland, to Which the proposed Ulster rebellion would be a mere nothing, and he•ven- tured to 'think if such an unfortunate thing did happen the last thing the Liber4s would do would be to back up the Nationaligts. If a rebellion came in Ulster the rebels would have no one to march against, and they would find no one to march- against them. (A Voice: "Then what about Carson?") He could not imagine a rebellion carried on under such -cir- cumstances. (Applause.) There was another _point in the Ulster ques- tion which amused. That was the • splendid threat of the great body of millionaires who met in Belfaat and decided they would not pay taxes unless Home Rule was withdrawn. He was not surprised by that resolution, for if there Was a set of men who Sought to avoid taxation it was the millionaire set, and if there was one thing the Conservative party sought to do, it was to put taxes on the poor men. (Laughter and ap- plause.) TO GET MR. H. SMITH OUT.

Mr. E. LLOYD JONES proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, speakers, vocalist and accom- panist. , Having detailed an excellent pro- gramme to be carried out by the Junior Liberals, he said they were anxious to shake Toryism in the ton—(hear, hear)—and wanted .to make a regular set 'march on. the Toryism of the dis- trict. They could not get Harold Smith out without banding together as one man in bring- ing him from the position as representative of the borough. .He hoped they would all help them in the great contest in which, they were engaged. (Hear, hear.) Personally, he ques- tioned whether he would fake the interest he did if it were not that•he, felt they had a man repre- senting.Warrington who ought not to represent it. Only a few days ago he had been out of town, and one of Harold Smith's speeches was in the paper. He felt ashamed to acknowledge to his friends that he lived in Warrington and was represented by a man who could deliver such a speech concerning the Welsh question and exhibiting such ignorance. But that was a characteristic, as well as want of thinking. (Hear, hear.) If they got hold of an intelltent eonception of the things before them. and gave the vote in the right way, they would have no doubt about the result. (A pplause.) Mr. HUGHES seconded, and said one Thing that upset him greatly was to be represented, by such a member .as they had got. • (Laughter and ap- plause.) It vas not a laughing matter yith him, but very serious. It was ridiculous to let Mr. Harold Smith get in the last time, but he thought it was a ,fluke more than anything. (Hear, hear.) They wanted to tackle the mem- ber properly. It did not need any advertising on his Part to say that they had a gentleman to fight their cause who would win at the • next election.. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The speakers haVing replied, The CHAIRMAN said he still found himself at home on a Liberal platform. He thought it would boa, long time before he would find him- self comfortable anywhere else. (Applause.)
