div.p: AT •DEATH'S DCOR WITH ULCERATED LEG. Full's( Summoned to Bedside by Telegram
ASTONISIILNG ZAM-BUR HEALING SAVES LIFE AND LIMB.
DAUGHTER CONFIRMS MARVELLOUS CURE!

Nothing could be more astounding than the miraculous way Zam-Buk rescued Mrs. Eliza Yeoman from ulcerated leg after the doctor had given up all hope of her recovery. Mrs. Yeo- man, whose cure by Zam-Buk has caused such a sensation, lives at The Hollies," Hackendown, St. Mary Cray, -Kent. To a reporter she said "I cut •my right leg 40 years ago with a rip hook while harvesting. Some time afterwards, on the very spot where the cut had been, there _came a lump as big as a walnut. Inflammation set in, so I' had the place lanced. As the lump returned, the place was blistered bY the, -doctor. This led to an Ulcer as large as a half-crown. Other sores also cable on the same leg: There must have been ten or eleveii of them. , "I went 20 years ago to St. George's Hospital. ' Later I went into Windsor Infirmary. I also had private treatment, but my case puzzled the medical men, who all failed to cure me. "About four years ago My bad. leg swelled up tremendously and became crimson. The doctor told my daughter that if I had any other chil- dren or relatives I should like to see, she had i better send for them, as my leg was n a very dangerous state. Mr DAUGHTER THEN REALISED THAT I WAS AT DEA'III'S DOOR.. Telegrams were sent to my children. When they arrived, I had been given up ..by the doctor.

"As I lay there, with my children expecting my death at any moment, my daughter came to my bedside and asked if I could bear my leg to be dressed with Zam-Buk. She had great faith in it and felt that it might at least relieve the awful pain. So my daughter dressed my sores with Zam-Buk._ _

• , " Sure enough, the pain was very much re- ' lieved. Continued dressings of 'the great healer, Zam-Buk '—as I call it—gradually drove the pain away, and to our surprise the swollen leg decreased in size. The terrible discharge ! from the iilcers slowly but surely ceased, and the sores began to heal. Even the chief place from which all the trouble had sprung yielded to Zam-Buk. A: few months after my serious ill- ness a new skin had formed over the places, which were completely healed. "That is three years ago, and although now 75 years of•age, I am, thanks to Zam-Buk, still able to go about among my family, entirely free from pain." Mrs. Green, a daughter of Mrs. Yeoman, living at 30; Inverness-road, Hounslow, Middlesex, has since written that her mother is still quite well, and adds :—" There is no doubt Whatever that Zam-Buk saved my mother's life. Everything else was tried in vain. The way Zam-Buk cleansed and healed the ulcers was marvellous." Zam-Buk, which alone could heal Mrs. Yeoman's terrible sores, is sold in sealed boxes by chemists, at 1/It and 2/9. Beware of worth- less imitations

div.head: LOW WAGES.
div.p: LOW WAGES.
An Artificial and a Natural and
Lasting Remedy.
"FREE THE LAND."
BY ARTHUR CHAMBERLAIN.

In view of Mr. Lloyd George's proposal to raise wages by a statutory Minimum Wage Act, the following views of Mr. Arthur Chamber- lain on the low wage question, written in May, 1911, will be of interest.

The cause of the fall in real wages during recent years and the remedy are, I venture to think, quite clear. In the first place I put on one side the increased gold production, because it is only in a very small degree responsible for the rise in prices; and I do not attribute it in any degree to a general rise in the prices of materials used in manufacture. In my experi- ence, which covers all the metal industries, and seine others that might be described as chemi- cal, I don't say there have not been some rises, but these have been more than balanced by greater economies in use. The average figure of percentage of material to total cost has not gone up. The real explanation of the rise in commodity values is this: The merchants and manufac- turers, pressed by various causes, one of the most important of which in recent years has been the oppressive nature of the Income Tax, have set themselves to obtain a quid pro quo by raising prices; and thereby increasing gross profits. Price agreements have certainly been on the increase, but even without any definite agreement there has been a consensus of opinion that competition was being carried too far. This aCcounts for the fall in real, wages, Sand this _might be met, Se far, as the present condition .concerned, .bx bringing the Iticts.. clearly -before both the masters' and the men. • Employers, as a.•rule, do not want to deal unfairly with their men; but I have 'foulid that very few, even of the employers, and, certainly, hardly one of the workmen, are accustomed to consider wages in connection with the price of commodities. Most people to-day' would say that men were well off—that their wages were higher than ever before, and. that no rise was justified.. If the case were properly put, and if tile trade union leaders were thoroughly to ex- plain the position to. their people by meetings and discussions in every local centre, they would understand that they had a moral right and real claim to such a rise in Money wages as would at least make them equal in com- modity value to the wages of, say, ten years ago. I doubt if the 'men are at present aware that they have such ,a claim. In the same way I feel convinced that, if the case were fairly put before the employers, the great majority would be willing to give a general advance to all trades, though not perhaps a special advance to a single trade.

div.head: PERMANENT CURE
div.p: THE PERMANENT CURE

This is one way—l should call it an artificial way—but there is a second and a better, be- cause a more natural and more permanent way. It is this: to free the land-4o enable the agri- culturists to have access to it. A small hold- ing of one acre and upwards, according to the position and value of the land, means an addi- tion of at least three shillings a week to the agricultural labourer's present weekly earnings. This would diminish the present exodus of the countryman into the town, and would increase the demand of the country for the products of the town. We should have, then, two natural forces at work increasing wages—namely, the smaller supply of competing labour from the country, and the larger demand for factory products by the country. The result would be inevitable. Without the machinery of strikes and lock-outs, wages would be bound to rise, because employers, having a larger demand for their products, and a smaller supply of labour, would compete among themselves for such labour as was, available.. The machinery to pro- duce this result is simple, an Imperial tax on the capitalised prairie value of the land, and, at the same time, local taxation withdrawn from the products of industry and of man's labour, and replaced by a tax raising the same amount on the prairie value of all land. In .both cases I mean a tax on all land, whether urban or agricultural, whether owned by the State or by kcal authorities, or by private individuals. To sum up, my . points are these:' Attention is repeatedly called to a most important fact showing an unreasonable inequality in. the dis= tribution of business earnings. The usual ex- planation is that of the 7,vicked capitalists and employers,, Who have by concerted action out- bargained trade unions, whose members are in consequence discontented .and depressed. I, on the other hand, do not think that any bar- gaining has taken place, 'and I think the urban population is far too much interested in foot- ball to be discontented or depressed about any- thing else. I deny that the depreciation in real wages is known, or, was known, as a subject of bargaining, either to men or masters, and I point out two methods by which it might he redressed, if the labouring classes could be induced to interest themselves at all in the matter. Finally, I strongly advise the use of the second method as being more general in its action and more permanent in its results, an(i dependent as it is on political rather than trade pressure, free from the violence, the sufferingsi and the want so often associated with great trade movements.
"THE LAND" BOOK.

Reproduction of the cover of the book, which is being eagerly read and'discussed in every part of the kingdom. Mr. Lloyd George speaks thus Of "The Land," the book published locally at "The Examiner" Office, in ' which appears the, evidence of the comMittee that will be the foundation of the land campaign upon which he. has embarked:—
"It is the biggest piece of work, I think, of the kind done in my day in Great Britain. Look out for the book. It is worth studying, but it will take some time."
"The Land," price 11-.

div.head: LIFE LOST FOR A CAP.
div.p: LIFE LOST FOR A CAP.

James Tinsley (41), labourer, was the victim of an unfortunate fatality at Lower Mill, Raw- tenstall, on Saturday. Tinsley was leaving the mill for breakfast when be turned back to get his cap, ascending to the spinning-room in the hoist. As he stepped out of the hoist he slipped and fell backwards into the hoist-well, 40ft. below, 'sustaining fatal injuries.

div.head: INSURANCE ACT CRITICS.
div.p: INSURANCE ACT CRITICS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. Linaker, jun., presiding. The Bucklow Board of Guardians wrote ask- ing the Board to grant to all widows, with chil- dren, deserted women, with children, and other women whose husbands were in the Asylum, is. extra for the, week ending .December 27th, and to.all old people in receipt of relief, 65 years of age and upwards, 6d. extra for the same period. They asked the Board to give effect to the reso- lution so far as it concerned the poor relieved in the Runcorn Union on their behalf. The City of London Union wrote stating that they had decided to grant 6d. per week extra to the, outdoor poor from the 6th Tiecember until 'February 28th. They asked the Board to make the same grant to any poor chargeable in the Runcorn Union on their behalf. The recommendations were adopted.
- Mr. Hallows moved that the .Runcorn Union give the same extra Christmas relief to outdoor paupers as last year. It was Is. for women and sixpence for the children. _ _
Air. Morris seconded and the motion was carried.

GUARDIANS AND INSURANCE BENEFITS. The Clerk read the following resolution : " That the Guardians of the Steyning Union are unanimously of the opinion that certain sections of the National Insurance Act are un- satisfactory and unfair in their application to Poor Law Institutions, inasmuch as without definite prospect of reimbursement. Guardians of the 'poor under exiting conditions are legally liable to receive into their ,institutions certain insured persons, who may become tem- porarily incapable, of following their employ- ment through sickness, or prospect of maternity, and they would therefore respectfully urge that the National Insurance Act be amended so as to provide: -
"-(a) That insured persons needing hospital treatment and entitled to sickness benefits under the Act shall not be eligible for admission to a Poor Law Institution

" (b) That any sick or maternity benefit which would in the ordinary course accrue to fully insured persons under the Act, and who. shall become inmates of a Poor Law Institution, shall be paid to the Guardians responsible for such institution during the period the insured person referred to remain Chargeable to the common fund."

div.head: " Rather_a Big Order."
div.p: " Rather_a Big Order."
_ The Chairman: That is ,rather a big order. It is a thing which needs some discussion, and some modification.

Mr. Morris: I move that it be sent on to the Parliamentary Committee. lam not doing so in a joking manner, for it is a thing that wants some consideration. The Parliamentary Com- mittee ought to 'discuss it.
. The Chairman You 'might suggest. a day when they could report. Mr. Morris: It is a long time since they had a meeting.
Mr. Lipaker : I thought that was coming. Mr. Gibbs: Say that they shall report in 12 months.
Mr. Morris: I move that the question of date be left in .the hands of the Clerk.
No- Hardships.

Gibbs: I was going to suggest that to my mind the Insurance Act has in no -Way placed. any hardships on Boards of Guardians. People had the same prh:ileges before the Act came in, and therefore it was no hardship, to the Board to take them in.

The Chairman: We are discussing the matter now, not leaving it to the Parliamentary Com- mittee. Have you .any amendment? Mr. Gibbs said that people had still the privi- lege to go into the Infirmary, as they did in the past. A point ,which had been overlooked in that communication was the great bearing such steps 3vould have on the working-class popula- tion. (Hear, hear.) 'Nine-tenths of those who went into hospitals left dependents, and they were going to be deprived of the benefit. It was decided that the matter be considered by the Parliamentary Committee.
BOYS AS GLASS WORKERS.

An important Suggestion .was made at a meet- ing of the Children's Home Committee to the .effect that boys over a certain age could be em- ployed at Messrs. Pilkington's Glass Works. Messrs. Spruce, Wood .and Morris had been appointed by the .committee to visit the works and see what, arrangements could be made for the care of the boys. The question of over:. crowding at Dutton Schools was considered, and the committee referred the matter to the Board for consideration. The tender for rainproof coats from Mr. Alfred Dodd for 12s. each was accepted. " The Ladies' Committee still sug- gested that additional help was needed in regard to the cooking, and still suggested that lockers be provided for the children's clothing, and the committee suggested a meat safe for the home. Mr. Morris: Is that meat safe to, put the
ts

div.head: "The Offer a Good One."
div.p: "The Offer a Good One."

Mr. Stiruce : Three of them are old enough. Messrs. rilkington's oiler is a good one, and the lads have the prospect of being put to a trade which will be of use to them When they get older. I think we ought to appreciate the ofter. it will, be an outlet for the lads when they have got past school age: We •sometimes send boys out and they have had to come back. At Messrs. Pilkington's they ill be in tt. hostelry and will be well looked after. The remuneration is also very good for a start, and we think the opening a good one. • I know there is an expres.: sion on the other side, but here these lads have an outlet, which is not always the case. It is not always that these boys fall in with the agricultural life, and: we thought it would he the best thing if further inquiry were made, and the deputation reported to the Board. We have not 'yet committed- ourselves. I move the adoption of the report. Mr. Morris: Don't you think discussion on the matter ought to be deferred until due in- quiries have been made?
The Chairman: The scheme is only in embryo at present... Several members asked that .the letter from Messrs. Pilkipkton's be read. -

div.head: Firm's Offer.
div.p: The Firm's Offer.

The Deputy Clerk (Mr. -W-":7E. Hough) read the letter as follows: "We are in want of about 15 boys for work in the glass trade at St. Helens and would be glad to receive any boys you could recommend to us. We have a boys' hostel, where strange and homeless lads are housed- and properly cared for. We have now over 80 boys resident there, boys from all over the country, from homes.- and institutions, and a few from the Isle of Man. We have a master. matron and servants to -care for the lads. We take them with a view to apprenticeship and we like boys from .14 to 16 years of age. The commencing wage is. Bs. 9d. to 10s., according to plus. money for good work and good attend' t.l ance, with periodical rises afterwards, accord,- met firm A )o ,loastt e which liiact si ing to progres......• tvery boy is self-supportia bracing fbevem .11 trl ee t e de o byill e c e n ri meu t or 116 byos;s l home attention and comforts are provided, eni- sleeping, food and recreation. Special care is also exercised in regard to the mental. physical and moral welfare- of the boys. As to the future of the boys, if they prove suitable in the way of health, strength and willingness, tkey are apprenticed to glassmaking between the ages :of 15 or -1.6 After this they become either glass-blowers, glass-gatherers, or glass- flatteners, callings which are well paid. If, however, they are not so bound outlets aro found for them in other departments. Employ- ment at the glass works is not a blind-alley employment. If a boy leaves when he is 16 it may be looked upon that it iS of his own wish, or that he has 'proved himself quite unsuitable. During times of sickness, holidays, stoppages. &c., boys are kept free of charge to themselves and receive pocket Money when off sick. Boys are, kept in clothing until able to provide for themselves."
Mr. Wright: The, terms seem very good, but the difficulty will be in getting the boys there. Mr. Morris : They bring the lads from, Widnes in a motor van.

The Chairman: That does not affect the pre- sent proposition., They want the boys at St. Helens, where they will be in the hostelrY. Mr. .Morris: ,They have also a recreation ground. It was decided that the deputation report on the matter as early as possible. • DUTTON SCHOOLS DIFFICULTY.
The difficulty at the Dutton Schools was fully discussed..

Mr. Morris said that if the 'Guardians would bring theip"-minds back to the time when the Children's TlOnies were first .discussed one of the reasons why they decided on Dutton was its claw proximity to Dutton Schools. The Chairman: And the Workhouse.

Mr. Morris said it was the close proximity of the Dutton Schools. He did not know whose authority it (tame under, but be did not think it was fair for the children of the Homes to be sent all the way to Aston Schools, across the fields, and especially in the winter time, when there was snow and mud. They should not be debarred from attending Dutton Schools. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Spruce said they could not see any other way out of the difficulty. If some persuasion could be brought to bear on .those people .out- side to send their children to Aston and those on the other side to send their children to Little Leigh, the situation would be saved. He sug- gested that some of the older boys should go to Aston. They did not see why the poor children from the Home should be sent from Dutton whilst the children from Aster' came to Dutton. At the same time they did not wish to bring any pressure on the management of the Dutton Schools which would necessitate-them increas- ing their building space or their staff. If the few children could be got in the Dutton Schools it would be preferable to sending them to Aston- Time the Remedy. Mr. Woodward • said they had control over their own children, but they had no authority over those from Aston and outside. The then would not have to go when it was Ho suggested suggested that they should wait for a time and the difficulty would remedy itself. div.head: "A's" AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE "A's" AT WIDNES.

Warrington "A" take a strong team to Wid- nes to-day, when they hope to secure points, which will make their position at the top of the Combination table more secure. The Warring- ton team will be: J. Brown; Baker, C. Brown, Howard Davis and Waywell ; A. Brown and Young; Fearnley, Green, Naylor, Critchley, Harmer and Board- man.

RYLANDS' CUP-TIE FEAT. A 39 Points to Nil Victory. \ Rylands' again proved themselves remarkably clever cup-tie fighters and won the third round tie...in the Lancashire Jupsior Cup. They beat Sherdley Athletic at Gorsey-lane with a clear margin of 39 points, after a game of a one-sided character. .

Sherdley kicked off before a fair attendance. Morris returned. From the pack formed Floyd passed to Warren, and he to Carter, who gave Griffiths a. nice opening. He scred in the first few tuiriiites. The' goal-kick 'failed. Morris scored' on-the- other wing. Tries quickly followed by Griffiths, Carter, Horrocks and Morris. Half-time arrived with the score 1 goal 7 tries (23 points) to nil. The second half was a repetition of the first, the passing of the Rylands' backs 'oimpletely outclassing the opposition. Although the visit- ing forwards were the heavier.lot, they were-no match for the " Wiremen." ....Further tries were scored by Griffiths, HorrOCks and Warren. The latter' also dropped a. goal _. and. converted one of the. tries. . Thus ended fl easy journey for RYliindehy 3 goals'il tries' (39 Points) to nil.

Teams for To-day. Bylands' Recs. v. Pendleton, at Pendleton :-- F. Horrocks ; J. Griffiths, S. Carter, A- Hor- rocks, P. Morris; G. Warren, G. Floyd; A. Stret- ford, J. Whittaker, H. Morris, F. div.p: PICKS OUT OF THE SCRUM. Pithy Pars About the N.U. Games.

All oyes were turned Young-wards. There was no disappointment there. Stan. did very well in his first match. his dives were particularly good. Ii he can keep up that form Perhaps he may change the style Of play in the senior thirteen. Who says but he may soon become • Another "Diver" Young of long ago. It was a wearisome match at the Cliff. Warrington certainly should not have been beaten. They were the better of two wretched sides. •

coo eer Ruddick, the Manchester critics say was The best half-back on the field. Nicholas had hard lines in being Hurt early in the second half. \lt was after that incident the Complexion of the game changed. Where was Cheaters •on. Saturday? We' missed the use of his weight. Jolley did not need his goal-kicking boots. He never got a chance to use them, Therefore they were of no use—a pity.

a Critchley did not have his kickers either. He missed quite a number of goals For Warrington against the Rangers' - "A" team. This is not like the usual performance Of the goal-getter-in-chief for the Warrington reserves. He had a day oft. Shaw shaped well at threequarter. Prophets say he will be seen in The first team before very long. Dainteth is coming slowly back To the form he disclosed late last season. It islithe he got a wriggle-n.

div.p: ao a a ao

The`Wilderspool crowd gave Young A most cordial welcome to Warrington. When he came put to be photographed By The Examiner" camera man He received quite an ovation. All this was nice and very pleasant. Just what it should have been. For a novice to the N.U. game, Young played particularly well, And gave promise of doing big things. When he comes along with the first string lie has the making of a N.U. half-back.

A correspondent Says: "Young and Nicholas At halfback; and the three'quarts ishould be Bradshaw, Shaw, Dainteth and ituddia."

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
Warrington Workingmen's
Association.
N.A. CENTRE.

The elements were so unkind last week-end, that few anglers ventured out, and those who visited the dithirent waters had a very bad time, several returning home without a fish. Whether or not the attraction in town last week-end had anything to do with so few members turn lag out, those who staied away from their. 'favourite spots had the belt of the argument, for at least one week-end. Members are worry- ing as to what bait to use at this tline of the year, as we are about in between the season for baits, and it seems that pike fish is .the only thing left until we have a frost or two, then ,bread, paste ,and, stone halts ay have a-.better chanc3.

The board yet remains unaltered, and those who are the winners are likely to remain so, as, we have not long to go, and the way our waters are fishing they are not likely to yield anything better than we have at present.

div.head: POOR SPORT.
div.p: POOR SPORT.

We heard of one member visiting Llangpllen, hut spot was not up to the standard, although he managed a road' over 11b. .Then the pike Caine on feed and upset all, one strjking right 'ft:ress his line, that finished his fishing in that hole, as he had not another Stir.

, There were only about half a dozen at the Gowy from Warrington way, and they said things were going very had. As we, expected, the, low-lying grounds around here were under water, and some of the most favoured spots could not be approached. The best we heard of was a catch of five roach, the largest about 10Oz. Others did nothing, but. to venture to the Gowy after the recent downpour was worthy, of better results, as it is ~not one of the dryest places after a long spell 4if weather similar to that we have had this last summer. Stout boots and leggings are necessary here at all times.
Those who visited the canals had poor results, and beyond a roach or two ang up to 40z., nothing was done. AS.

A keen ,enceunter.was witnessed on the Thel- .enelosure. Latchford and Oughtring- tdn were in opposition, as on the previous Saturday, only on this occasion it was in the League Competition. There were several alter- ations in both teams, but this did,not detract any interest from the game, which resulted in a win for the home teani,,,thus comPensatillg them a little for the set-back they received in the Senior Cup Competition. On the Latchford side two new players were tried in Webb and Green, the former a brother of the home club's centre-half, and the latter hailing from the Stalybridge district. Both players performed creditably and will be given further trials, whilst Kay, of the visitors, was the best player on view, his: kicking and tack- ling being splendid to watch. tiughtrington United received a visit from Altrinclram St George's, and .the latter had to return defeated by -three clear goals. .Blease; Lord, Haddon and Burrows were the pick of the home team.

The Latchford team reversed the previous week's result by defeating their cup-tie victors by three goals to two. Smith was the best forward in the home quintet
But Kay, the visitors' full-back, was the beet player on the field.
The home club gave a trial to two new players in Webb and Green.
The Oughtrington United Reserve defeated Altrincham St George's 3—Q. - Stanley Craig, last.' season with- Stockton Heath, has joined the Adult School. '•
_ He was always a favourite with the sup- porters of the Stockton Heath-Thth.., _ _ _
Hunter played a very good game agiti.nst the Soldiers,
And .Morrison gave a good exhibition between the uprights.. at Barnton, now 'of the;Weave Refining Co., scored both goals for his new club last Saturday:
Dan Woodward played a good defensive game for the Itaners.
Denny was the best player on view.
Evan, the Refiners' centre, and Denny, the visitors' centrehalf were a - contrast—the long and. the short.

Ths-3*Divex Club, by cancelling their fixture with The Great Sankey Club on the Saturday, morning, caused much disappointment up Pinketh way. - - When Lees missed scoring with the easiest of chances everybody laughed they could not help it. On Saturday there were no fixtures in the Warringfon and District League—Second Divi- sion.

The Juniors were taking the rest cure. The Stockton Heath Reserve have, been accepted as members of the Widnes Alliance, And they won ,their first match,. Widnes St. Paul's, 3-1. - - C. Bailey was the best half-back on the field. What do.prford St. John's and St. B,arnabas' think of it?

The Lads at Wilderspool Brewery have formed a club and have sent in application to the Warrington and District League. Hawthorn and Shakeshaft turned out again for Hindley last week, the former scoring twice. The Witton Club. officials were watching the match at Acton Bridge last week :(not fishing match), and were angling for players. One, I understand, signed a form. There were also some other club touts came to watch two or three local players I know. So club secretaries, look out!

There are also rumours about that if so many Warrington players go out of town to play with other clubs it should be possible to raise a town's club and apply for admission to the Lancashire Combination.
J. Broadhurst and T. Woodhead, two stalwarts of the defunct Latchford Rees., have signed for Stockton Heath.

div.head: LATCHFORD DEFEAT MANCHESTER
div.p: LATCHFORD DEFEAT MANCHESTER

- UNIVERSITY. Latchford had Manchester University as visitors on Saturday, and, a good game was the outcome of the visit Uniyersity said they had a weak side compared with those previously fielded this season, but their play did not suffer in the least.

, The game began at a very brisk pace and Latchford were soon attacking, several shots at goal being saved and others going narrowly past. However, the 'Varsity were the first to score, Bruhl having no chance with a shot at close range, after the backs shad been beaten, owing to good combination between the visiting forwards. The home team equalised through Pearson, who picked °up a centre from the right wing. This represented the state of affairs at half-time; although it did not represent the run of the play. '- When, the, second half opened the visitors went away aa though they were going to play havoc with the home defence, but a very strong clearance by Fletcher put Latchford on the attack again. From this point onwards, the combination between flie home men was very good and easily the hest display, of the season. Knight was constantly turning defence into attack,- in_fact he reduced the visitors' right w,ing to almost a nonentity. - 'lsherwood was also giving a good display, and through his judicious feeding and keen vigilance the home right wing was constantly attacking, with the result that ' three more goals • were put on, One by Travis and two by Pearson. Still the 'Varsity had their spell of attacking, but their forwards were. not very thrnstful, although Bruhl had one or two anxious moments. On of these was when ther visitors' ontside7left put in a fine oblique shot, which Struck the foot of the far post-and was deflected to the right wing. The winger pounced on the ball, pushed it into the circle to_ his inside man, for the latter to score with a brilliant first-time shot. The score of 4-,2 in favour of Latchford Was rather flattering to the University, who , were saved from --a -bigger defeat by the splendid display of their goal- keeper.

In front of him were two hard-hitting full- backs and a very good left-half. • All round;.. the University have a good team, and it is, no *en- der they have already defeated three other. University teams. laatehford gave a sound .diSplaY; and it is iteiy pleasing to see a safe goalkeeper between the uprights, two hard- hitting backs, halves that can both defend and attack, and forwards, who combine, prettily in raid-field, but are always moving goalwards.

Crosfield's Beat Latchford Reserves. The second eleven should have played ' the University Second at Manchester, but the match was cancelled late on Saturday morning, owing to the Manchester ground being flooded. Crosfield's First happened to have a vacant date and a match was fixed up between the two teams at Hood-lane. Considering the heavy rains, the ground was in very fair condition, with the. exception of a few patches round one circle, which were water-logged, and . conse- quently hindered both forward lines in their shots at goal. Crosfield's opened the scoring from a shot by Bloomer, and play ranged very evenly till half-time, when Crosfield's had a lead of 1-0, although Marsden,; for Latchford, had hard lines on at least two occasions. When plarwas•resumed 'Latchford's forwards opened out the otme and finally C. Newbold 'equalised; ' Then Crosfield's carried- the play down the fielkl and Hudson scored a good goal through being prompt in his following-up. Vernon added a third for Crosfield's, and time was called with the score 3-1 in favour of Crosiield's.

Bloomer and Vernon played a good game for Crosfield's, while bean, their right-half, was the best defender on the field. For Latchford, Fletcher, at centre-forward, and his two wing men, Marsden .and McCawley, gave a good exhi- bition. Altogether it was a very enjoyable game, and the hope was expressed on both sides that this -match was only the first of a rgular series of games together.

div.head: An Extraordinary Incident in the Warrington Match with Broughton.
div.p: An Extraordinary Incident in the Warrington Match with Broughton.
STAR! YOUNG'S FINE FIRST PERFORMANCE.

-What goes wrong with Warrington when they 04y away? While they can win matches at home, they are ..always beaten away, and not lince the match at Batley, early' in September, have they -secuivi, a, . win on., foreie soil. ,--TSO they suffer from the nerves when 'away from their own supporters, or what else is the matter? Personally, I am at a loss to understand what wrong. On the play at the Cliff, Warring- ton certainly should not have been beaten. Broughton only scored after Nicholas had to tetire with an injured hand, and they were hicks in scoring as they did. On the other hand, Warrington had quite their share of the -88.m.e, but it was the old story Of•Swinton, Old- and Rochdale. They could do everything '74l3De e p t.score. Again and again:-_the visiting . threequarters got on the run, and the way' was ' °Pen,' .but not one ot :them had the required BPeed and 'enterprise to make use of the open- ings. In the end Warrington retired defeated by 12 points to nil, made up of three goals and t'wc, tries.

Young, too, was only inches short, after a great " dive." Bater also got well away on the right, but was .pilehed intdtouch at the critical moment. Broughton were 'penalised, and this time Critchley landed a fine goal, but just before the whistle blew for half-time he was unsuccess- ful with another penalty. This was all the scoring in the first half, which had been hard and fast throughout.

In the ,second half Warrington were unable to add to their score, although Waywell should have been over on at least two occasions. Baker on one occasion looked like a certain scorer, but was brou:ght down just on the line. Critehley had one, dr AWE) attempts at goal from penalty but-4,as unable to put the ball over the bar. div.head: REFEREE LAID OUT.
div.p: THE REFEREE LAID OUT.

A. most unusual accident occurred in the Ilecond half. The referee, Mr. Crabtree, of Hud- fl, ersfield4 was the victim, and he was completely 44ocked out .of the game. The Rangers'.' for- Wards were having an exciting tussle with the Warrington forwards near the Warrington line. The referee, in following up the game, got Itrrialved in the melee, with the result that he tot mixed up with the two sets scrambling on t,115. ground. When the players got up, it was leen that the referee was lying helpless on the Ditch. The ambulance men hastened to his 441, and found that he had sustained a displace- lent of a cartilage in one of his knees, and his "liuries were so severe that he had to be car- lied off the ground. . Mr. Moore, of Oldham, one (It the linesmen, took on the task of refereeing the rest of the play. The injury sustained Y Ur. Crabtree was purely accidental; in fact, alone of the players realised that he was in their Itlidst until after the melee was over..

div.head: AN UNINTERESTING GAME.
div.p: AN UNINTERESTING GAME.

The game all through was dull, uninteresting, rtud extremely scrappy, and Warrington were certainly not beaten by a superior side. There i/taa little to pick and choose between them, as uoth played a very indifferent gaine. It turned :!lustly to a duel amongst the forwards. The Kerae sextet packed better and were more active Tian the Warrington six, but the visitors &tro- unced more bustling tactics, and thus upset the calculations of the home half-backs consider- ably. The half-backs on both sides were lacking, It_nd of the four, Ruddick was easily the best, 1418 individual work being at times brilliant. E nee more the absence of an understanding be- ,,weSn him and Nicholas was very evident, and Li• Was apparent that this line will have to be I'ungthened. Stan. Young, the new Welsh half-back, nay 111,,rove a more useful partner for Nicholas, and uen it is possible that Ruddick may be given trial at threequarter. He ought to be a use- man there, provided he gets the opportu- nity and is fed -with the half. The threequar- tars were very badly fed on Saturday.

CHANGE AT HALF-BACK WANTED. Every match shows how hopelessly Warring- are at present placed in the two back divi- *lons. Nicholas can play a good game, but he pee not seem always to rise to the occasion. Young comes in will the pair work together? dlidging of what was seen of Young on Satur- his style should about fit in with that of iilleholas, and if such proves the case, then I,"e may be a change in the half-back play. Oung has, of • course, to learn the ,N.V.• game, tit't it should not be long before`he accomplishes ,t, for he plays with his head. the Warrington threequarters ,were disap- lZkinting. Their game was fitful all through, „ one moment they would waken up and give `ll4 brilliant display, then they lapsed into the i:diocre, and so it went on all through the 4teh. The two wing men did not show to itciltantage. Bradshaw is not playing the game did earlier in the season.

I3ICKENSON MOST IN THE PICTURE. 032nwn does not partner well with Bradshaw, ftt4.c he brought off some fine tackling, if, he kilted in the initiation of runs. Dickenson was (Ist in the picture of any of the Warrington ti3Oartet. There seems to be plenty of life in the 'eteran but he cannot stand the pace as he " to do. Brookes was not the success anti- *Jolley was more reliable at full-hack than he g 4 in the match with Batley the previous 40,,,44turday. Some- of his >stops, were partiCUlarly i ‘5,7, but he s not up to the form he showed gilier in the season. taken all over Warrington's display against 4 Itangers was very disappointing, and there tj have to be a marked change if matches are '3le won. There is no prophesying when that 0,40ge will come, but the sooner it does come `e'hetter it will be. •

div.head: 4t,
div.p: THE NEW PLAYERS.

Chief interest, of course, was centred in the two .new players—Young and Shaw. Both, in my opinion, made a very-creditable first appear- ance, and I am of the opinion that the War- rington Committee have done a good stroke of business, and that the half-back and centre threequarter positions will be greatly strength- ened. Considering that this was Young's first game in N.U. football, I think he shaped re- markably well. He is very .speedy, and knows how to take the ball, and some of his, passes are really brilliant. Like Nicholas, when near the line, he will be a most dangerous player. Of course, he. will want a little more practice before he thoroughly gets intQ the N.U. game, but, taken all round, his exhibition on Satu,r- day pleased the critics, and he certainly had hard lines in not scoring, as he was 'brought down by superior numbers only inches short of the line.

div.head: SHAIN'S SUCCESSFUL DEBUT.
div.p: SHAIN'S SUCCESSFUL DEBUT.

Shaw, the new centre, made a very success- ful debut with the Combination team, and did ,many smart things. .11e seems to be a "glutton" for "work, and I was -greatly 'impressed by • the way he tackled. With a little more practice I don't think it will be long before we see both Young and-him operating with the seniors, and I think the Warrington Committee will be well advised if they play Nicholas and Young at half, and Bradshaw, Shaw, Dainteth and Ruddick in the threequarter line.

Of the other players, J. Brown played a mas- terly game at full-back, and some people think he is quite equal to Jolley. Undoubtedly he is developing into a " class " full-back, and the way he repeatedly bluffed Beetham, the inter- national forward, greatly tickled the home spec- tators. It was a. great effort of his when he almost scored, and certainly he fully deserved to.

div.head: DAINTETH IN FINE FORM.
div.p: DAINTETH IN FINE FORM.

Dainte-th played a fine game, and was the pioneer of many of the passing movements, and ought to be seen in ,better company. Baker, too, was,very resourceful, and showed his speed to fine advantage. Waywell, on. the other wino' did not play up to his usual standard, and cer- tainly should have scored on two occasions. He was, however, rather unfortunate in the way of receiving "knocks " and at one period was laid ," hors de combat" for some time. A. Brown, at half, played his usual consistent game, and every credit is due to him for the way he served Young and helped him to open out the game. These two players completely overshadowed the Broughton pair. • • • The forwards had a great share. in 'Warring- ton's victory, and each man gave. of .his best. It would be unfair to ,pick out anyone .for special mention, .as each ope was continually in the picture. _ _ _

For Broughton, Harris was a good full-back, but, taken all round; the team could not com- pare with the Warringtonians, who are a smart lot, and their prospects of winning the Com- bination championship are at present very rosy.

MORE CHANGES IN THE .TEAM. Young Net Yet to Appear. There are several changes in the Warrington team to meet Widnes in the "local Derby" at Wilderspool to-day. Young is remaining with the Reserves until he gets some more experi- ence in the N.U. game, and until Nicholas is better, when the two Welshmen, who under- stand each other's game, can join at half-back. Renwick, Dainteth and Tra.nter are back again in the side. Teams:

div.head: WARRINGTON LEAGUE NOTES.
div.p: WARRINGTON LEAGUE NOTES.

In the Warrington and District League there werq only three games down for decision, the most interesting being that at Acton Bridge, between the Weaver Refining Company and Stockton Heath. The home club bad a strong eleven out, including Haspell, late of Barnton and of Latchford. He scored both goals.'- The ,yisitors relied on their usual team, and were very unfortunate in not securing both points; the equalising goal being obtained just before the close of play. The match between Orford Barracks and the Adult School was verY interesting and keenly contested. It resulted in a victory for the school, who, after being in arrears at half-time, managed to obtain the verdict in their favour by the odd goal in five. The Great Sankey Club and their supporters were very much disappointed with the Divex Club cancelling their fixture on Saturday morn- ing, thereby giving the club no opportunity of fixing up a friendly game for the convenience of their_players.

NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. First Division. Latchford V. Oughtrington United. •Played at Thelwall-lane, and, owing to the United having ,the previous week defeated the home team in the cup-ties, there was a good crowd present. The follcrwing players turngd out for Latchford: Kite; Robinson aricrßards- ley; Downs, Webb and Carter; Smith, Webb, Lees, Green and Siddall. Lees set the ball rolling, and after several even exchanges in mid-field the home players were the -first to become .aggressive. Smith made a grand run- on Ale_ extrerne right, and finished by scoring a grand goal. The visitors had a spell of attack on the home goal and several chances were missed; the forwards fin- ishing very poorly. The game new opened out and the exchanges in mid-field were even. The home forwards made .a rush down the field, and during a scramble in front of the visitors' goal press •the visitor? defence, but no goals were Green scored a second. Latchford continued to two goals down. - visitors added, and half-time arrived with the visito On resuming, the home team again carried the play into the visitors' quarters, but Bur- rows and Kay defended in grand style, and from a huge clearance by Kay the visitors got possession and made a grand combined run up the field, when Holt reduced the arrears. The game was now faster and more keenly contested and both goals were visited in turn, the de- fenders being equal to'the attack in their determination to beat each other. Lees, when in a good position, missed, scoring—a very unusual thing for him to do. The game con- tinued to be evenly • contested until a few minutes from the finish, when the same player made _funends for his previous failure and scored the third goal' for 'Latchford. Result: Latchford, three goals; Oughtrington United, one goal.

div.head: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Second Division.
div.p: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Second Division.
Oughtrington United Reserve v. Altrincham
St. George's.

Played at Heatley. Altiincham won the toss and Haddon set the ball in motion. - Burrows, receiving a nice pass, initiated an attack on the visitors' goal: but was driven back by good defensive play. Lord tried a long shot, but sent the ball, wide of the goal. Burrows opened the ware with a shot across the goal-mouth, which `went just inside the post. The visitors now retaliated, but they could not beat the home defence. Owen scored a second goal for United, and. at half-time the game was in their favour by two goals to nil. On changing ends the visitors had more of the play and, soon began .to attack the home defence, a, line effort by Bremen .just Missing, by inches, and Blease made a good run for the United, only to see his final effort spoilt by Haddon getting offside. The ensuing free-kick brought relief to the visitors, and they now took up their posi- tion in the home portion of the field and caused the home defence a lot of trouble, Ogden; in ! goal, bringing off some very, good saves.. The ' home half-backs began to assert' themselves and transferred the leather to the opposite end, where Lord made a grand opening for Owen to increase the score.. Onghtrington United, three -goals; ,Altrincham St. George's, 'none.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. First Division.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. First Division.
Weaver Refining Co. v. Stockton Heath.

This match was played at Acton Bridge, when there was a good number of spectators. Jones set the ball rolling and the game *com- menced at a fast pace, the visitors being the first .to become aggressive. The home backs Were' quickly" called upon to assert themselves, D. Woodward kicking finely, but the visitors set about their work in a determined fashion and forced Woodward to concede a corner. The, flag-kick was taken by Magill and placed well in front of goal, where Denny headed the ball against the cross-bar, and from the rebound he. sent the' hail through, out of the 'goalkeeper's reach, and scored for the visitors after five minutes' play. From the centre kick the home team tried to force the visitors' defence, but Simcock, Gosling and Woodward would not yield, and. off-.side against Evans sent the home team back to their own lines. Play continued in mid-field, the .half-backs on both sides :play- ing a very strong game. Hands" against Woodward resulted in a. penalty kick, from which Haspell made the scores equal,. and at half-time the score. was ;one goal each. On.. resuming, the game was . just as .keenly fought as in the first 'portion, and the home forwards, finely led by Evans, laid siege tq_ the visitors' citadel, but the "Heathens" defded resolutely and gradually sent their opponents back. The home quarters were invaded and the Refiners had to bestir themselves to stave off defeat. •The players were urged on by the cheering of their supporters, and the game was very exciting, both teams striving hard for the lead. A fine pass out to Gerrad on the visitnrce

right was taken up,, splendidly, and...from his centre Smith headed. a second point for the visitors. Roused- by this reverse, the home players set off with renewed vigour, but .were- met with a stout defence. A free-kick against Gifford gave the home team their thence, and Respell again beat Simcock -and equalised. Result: . Weever"Refining Copapally, two, goals; Stockton Heath, two goals.
Orford Barracks v. Adult School.

Teams representing the above met on the ground of the former, when the following players turned out :—Orford Barracks—Mor- rison; Staple and Lonnen; Callow, Stevens and Topping; Procter, Hicks, Roberts, Spicer. and Trafford. Adult School—Welsby; Spilsbury and 'Garnett; Leigh, Hinter and Clarke; Rhodes, Rowe, Banner, Dykes and Craig. Referee, Mr. C. S. "ESsenhigli. 'Dykes kicked kicked off for the visitors, and Stevens, intercepting a pass, initiated an attack upon ,the visitors' goal, Hunter nipping in and clear- ing. The game proceeded.very evenly, both ends being visited in turn. Some fine combination by the home front line led to Roberts opening the score. Encouraged by this success, the home team had the best of the exchanges and Procter increased the lead with a good shot well out of Welsby's reach. Nettled by these reverses, the School opened out more in • their ganw and attacked strongly and were awarded a penalty. Dykes took the kick, but failed to utilise. The visitors were not dismayed;' but kept up the pressure, and Rowe reduced the margin with a beauty. When the interval was called the .Barrackateam were leading by two goals to one. The visitors, gaining possession, set the game at a very fast pace, and Staples and Lonnen were severely tested, and, kicking strongly, they cleared the danger. The visitors were not to be outdone and they came again.. Craig, playing a fine game on the wing, passed to Dykes in a good position, and he made the scores leveL From the centre-kick the pace became ,hotter, atd some exciting play was witnessed, both goalkeepers being called upon to save, until the visitors gradually gained the upper hand, and Banner was successful in beating Morrison. The visitors thus took the lead. The game con- tinued to be-keenly contested, and the Soldiers tried hard to break down the visitors' defence, but failed. As the finish was drawing hear the honie team rallied finely and were nearly through in the last moment. Result c Adult School, three goals;, Orford Barracks, two.
WIDNES AND DISTRICT ALLIANCE.
Stockton• Heath "A" v. Widnes St. Paul's.

The home club opened their Alliance fixtures with a match at West-avenue, when the follow- ing. players , opposed each other :--§tockton Heath "A "—J. Vernon; Waller and Jefferson; Glover, Bailey and West; Parr; Marsh, Morti- mer, Rigby and Houghton. Widnes St. Paul's— Harris; Jones and Tilley; Brocklebank, Rev. Willetts and Parkinson; Helsby, Langford, Perry, Ward and Greenwood. Referee, Mr. J. Hollings. The home players were the first to press and good play by Jones and Tilley drove them back. The visitors entered the home territory, only to be treated similarly by Waller and Jefferson. The ensuing play was evenly contested and the defence on both sides proved too good for the attack. There was no score at half-time.

On resuming, the ?layers set about with earnestness, and the gime was .keenly fought until the visitors gradually worked their way towarcts the home goal Sand opened the score from a penalty given against Waller for hand- ling. This reverse gave the home team a stimu- lus and they set up a hot siege on the visitors' citadel, with the result that Marsh equalised. Encouraged by the cheers of their supporters, •the " Heathens " now had the best of play, the visitors only getting over 'the centre line occa- sionally. A good shot by Glover was fisted out by Harris, but the' home team would not be driven back, and Glover placed his side in front, sending the ball through a crowd of players. From the centre-kick the visitors made strong efforts to get through, but Bailey and then Waller drove them back. A long shot by Lang- ford was easily saved by Vernon, but he was penalised for carrying, 'and the ball being put into the net without a second playing touch- ing it, the score did not count. This brought relief to the home defence and the visitors began to tire. Play was transferred to the other end, when Parkinson handled a shot from Parr. Jefferson took the kick and scored with a low shot. Result: Stockton Heath, three goals; Widnes St. Paul's, one goal.
ST. HELENS AND DISTRICT THURSDAY LEAGUE.

Warrington Co-operative v. Collins' (St. Helens). At the King and Queen Ground, Warrington, on. Thursday. Collins'. were .the first to attack, and made a rnid on OA, home goal, but were driven back by the splendid defence of the hOme backs. The "Co-japers" took play 'right into the home half, and made strenuous efforts to net the ball, but the visitors' defence prevailed. After some mid-field play the visitors worked the ,ball into the home territory and were the first to, score._ The Co-op. tried hard to-equalise, but.no further scoring took place in this half.'

. Before the, game Wa five -minutes' old in the second moiety 'Stringer scored for the home team. This player immediately :afterwards put on goal number two for the " Co-opers." Here- abouts some fine combination was shown by both sides, and then the home side pressed and Cum- mins 'sent the ball into the goal-mouth for Rutter to net. Towards the finish Stringer again scored, thus completing the "hat trick." Result: Warrington Co-operative, 4 goals; Collins', one goal.. For the home team Cummins, H. Stringer and Rutter played well and were, the pick of a well- balanced side.'
FRIENDLY GAMES. Emmanuel Old Boys v. Orford Juniors.

At Victoria Park. Williams started. Cald- well, however, gained possession, and after a brilliant individual ,performance left Pickering helpless with a fast shot in the first Minute. After this reverse, Orfbrd tried hard to equal- ise, but their finishing was poor, although Jack- son hit the cross-bar with a fine shot. The Old Boys were playing a splendid game, and only .the brilliance of Pickering in goal prevented a complete rout. -Barnes led the. homesters Tin good-Style,. and Green, gaining possession, beat Pickering with a fine cross shot, while jmrae- diately afterwards _Wainwright secured a third, from a Corner. Interval Old Boys, three goals; Orford "Juniors, none. • • Orford had the wind at their backs on resum- ing, and Jackson, Redford and Williams tried: hard' to open their 'account, but the Old Boys held firm, O'Brier 3specially playing a fine de- fensive game. Jdckson broke through, but Whittaker saved from short range, while ft moment later he fisted•out a hot shot from Wil- liams. The Old Boys continued to show fine de- fence, and the Juniors were held in check. Cald- well secured another goal with a long shot. while O'Day managed to get through in the last
minute for the Juniors. Final: Old Boys, four goals; Orford Juniors, one goal. Padgato Wesleyans v. Latchford Juniors.

This -match, which was played at Orford-road, resulted in a win for the visitors by three goals to nil. Padgate, who were a much heavier team to Latchford, could make no impression on the visitors' defence. The scorers were Howard, Llewellyn and Yates.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1913.
GUILDERS' RALLY.
The Wesleyan Guild a Force of Good in Warrington.
GREATER NUMBERS WANTED.

Taking the meeting at the Bowsey-road Wes- leyan Church on Monday night as a criterion of the enthusiasm of the members of the Wes- ley Guild in the Warrington Circuit, it would seem that they are truly devoted to their work and growing, as the various secretarial reports showed.

The occasion was the annual Guild Rally, when addresses were given by the Rev. Theodore Bishop, of Crewe, who was, eleven years ago, a well-known Warrington preacher; and Mrs. Stevens, wife of Dr. Stevens, both of whom are active missionary workers in West Africa. The Rev. W. A. Beckett presided until the arrival of Dr. Bennett, of Padgate, and supporting him were, in addition to the two speakers, the Rev. R. Morgan, the Rev. H. Middlewood, and Mr. Duckworth, of Padgate.

div.head: WORK ABROAD.
div.p: THE WORK ABROAD.

Mrs. STEVENS said she thought the English people did not know enough about the part of Africa where her 'husband and herself had been sent. Of all the places that wanted help she thought Africa needed it the most, and if they were going to do anything at all they must do it at the present time. Christ and Mohammed were fighting for the lordship of Africa: Pagan- ism was dead and the idols meant nothing to the natives. They were discredited in nearly all the towns and most of the villages. They could see the land was waiting, and there were only Christ and Mohammed to compete for it, and, said the speaker, ~" I am afraid Mohammed is winning. But *here Christ jets His foOthOld Islam stands no -chance, so that it is necessary that we should get there first. If we don't within the next ten years it Will be centuries before Africa is won for Christ."

WANTS 1,000 MEMBERS. Mr. KENNETH F. B/SHOP, the local general sec- retary of the Guild, presented his report, which showed that the membership of the circuit was, 825, an increase of 68. He hoped to see the number reach 1,000 for the next Guild Rally. During the year two new Guilds had been formed, one at Whitley and the other at Antro- bus, which brought the number up to twelve. The shield competition was again won by the Latchford Guild. It was rather hard lines upon Moore, who were only beaten by just over one per cent., which showed that success depended upon every individual member. The house-to- house collection this year for the National Children's Home and Orphanage realised £32 2s. 6id., an advance upon last year of £4 12s. 3d.

div.head: POWER FOR GOOD.
div.p: A POWER FOR GOOD.

The Rev. THEODORE BISHOP said he was de- lighted to learn that they had 825 members in Warrington. What a wonderful power for good there was in the Warrington Circuit! How their ministers ought to thank God every day, and many times a day, for having all these chances of furthering their efforts! The Guild nursed all sorts of sickly and delicate children, and turned them into vigorous and robust men and women. When a man grasped the Guild spirit he did not mope in the corner, but told people what God had done for him, and tried to comfort them. The Guild was a nursery for local preachers, for class leziders, because those who were earnest attenders at the devotional meetings made good class leaders, and good class leaders were very scarce, but when thPy had 825 Guild members there should be no diffi- culty whatever in finding class leaders. The Guild was, in fact, a nursery for every branch of Church work. THE SECRETARIES' REPORTS.

The various Guild secretaries made individual reports, which; summarised, show that the last year's workings had been successful. Bold- street, for the first time, reached three figures, their total membership numbering 107, and they were third in the shield competition. Bew- sey-road showed no great increase in member- ship, their figures being 78 active, 18 com- panion, and 17 associated members, total 113. Latchford t maintained their high position, and again won the shield. No increase in member- ship. Sankey Bridges bad been in a very poor condition, but had a slight increase in the figures. Padgate were wakening up to the possibilities of their strength, which stands at 05, composed of 67 active, 40 companion, and 75 associate members. Their Children's Guild was doing splendidly, although they had a decrease in membership. Penketh showed that they had been almost dead, but by the aid of a, few 'workers they pulled together and were suc- cessful in gaining 48. members, mostly active. Moore continued to make progress, whilst Stockton Heath reported the most successful year they had ever had,

Successful Ambulance Men.

At the conclusion of the parade at the Central Police Buildings on Monday, 24 employes of Messrs. Crosfield's Works were presented with ambulanceitertificates. Dr. Adams, the lec- turer, deserves a meed of praise, for there was only one failure out of the 25 who entered for the examination. Mr. T. Cawley, in presenting thsi certificates, said that the inspecting officer had certified that the division was in a very high state of efficiency. They wanted to keep that up, and if possible attain to even a higher standard of efficiency. (Applause.) That would rest largely with the recruits, and he had no doubt they would do their utmost to uphold the reputation of the division. The following were the winners of the certificates: Messrs. H. div.head: People Who Sent Out Fire-water and Firearms Alc.)no: With Christianity.
div.p: People Who Sent Out Fire-water and Firearms Alc.)no: With Christianity.
REMARKABLE WARRINGTON GATHEI%ING.

In the furtherance of any object, practical demonstrations are far more convincing than the most eloquent oratory, but when the two are combined the result is bound to be satis- factory. Those two essentials are features at the gigantic ten days' Missionary Exhibition (S.P.G.), now open in the Empire Hall, War- rington, for not only are there exhibits of the various articles used by our friends abroad, and specimens of the idols which the unchristianised worship, but special missionary workers, who have been in the "field," give explanatory addresses and illustrate the ignorance of the heathens by worshipping blocks of wood, &c. The Empire Hall lends itself admirably for the purpose, and each of the various courts, repre- senting different parts of the world, are espe- cially attractive. The exhibition has been organised by the Rural Deaneries of Winwick and Frodsham, with help from the Wigan Deanery, under the auspices of the S.P.G., and will be open until November 29th. The platform represents a settlement in Canada, and the other scenes lend local colour to the .various exhibits. A chapel for private devotion is always open behind the West and Central African Court. In conjunction with the exhibition pageants and lantern addresses will be given each evening in the Patten Hall.

ities the better for us as a nation, as Churches, and as individuals. (Applause.) A spitit of unity and good fellowship was fostered by such an undertaking as that. They said people should not be parochial, but there was a danger of them becoming too diocesan, and an organisation such as that workeil in the right direction of all 'being united. (Hear, hear.)

THE OPENING PAGEANT. The first pageant, "England's Call," given in the Patten Hall on Wednesday night, by chil- dren of the Parish Church, typified the whole Spirit of the Missionary Exhibition. . A speaker, Dorothy Wilson, accompanied by a cross-bearer, choir and company of British, first claimed the attention of a crowded audi- ence. Then a party of Syrians demanded if the British were fulfilling the command of Him who trod with sacred step the land in which they lived. "Go ye into all the world and preach the Gospel." At the request of the speaker, these Syrians stood aside, while Christian delegates from foreign and colonial countries, came to ask for help. In rapid succession delegates from China, India, Japan, Africa, America and Australia, each in distinctive costume, sounded the call for help. Solemnly and prayerfully the British accepted the responsibility and answered the call. The whole company, kneeling reverently, asked for- giveness for previous neglect, and grace for future determination to obey the call. Then a delegate stepped forward to take two British missionaries back to his own country. To the rousing strains of "God is working His pur- pose out,' these missionaries were escorted by the delegates to the respective sections, andv finally, the speaker reminded each and all of the great need, and the correspondingly great duty, privilege, and responsibility, of this England of ours to the lands beyond the seas. The whole pageant was inspired with devotion and solemnity. The children seemed imbued with the spirit of it. The singing and reciting were exceedingly well performed, and the move- ments dignified, while the spectacular effect was. brilliant in the extreme. One left the Hall with the feeling inspired by the Great Master: "It is good to be here." HERITAGE OF MAN. There was a very encouraging assembly for the opening on Thursday by the Bishop of Whalley.

Councillor G. W. JOSEPH, who presided, said the human race, in its relation to God, was one huge family, some of whom enjoyed the blessed heritage which Was contained in a knowledge of God, and there were other members of the family wh6 were still ignorant of that heri- tage. Did they think it right to conceal this knowledge and keep their brothers and sisters in ignorance? If it was -an earthly heritage, and they were keeping it from their brothers and sisters, it would, in all probability be accounted a fraud, morally and legally. In sharing this heavenly heritage it woUld not be like sharing an earthly one, because they would not be losing T , anything Bingisbn f wyopito.( (Hear, hear, and applause) EY said God taught them they could not be saved unless the help of man was called forth to assist. NARROW-MINDED OBSERVERS.
There was a •larg6 attendance yesterday, when the Bishop of Burnley opened the exhibition. Canon Willis presided. _ _

The BISHOP of BURNLEY thought exhibitions were a good thing for laying before the people things as they actually were. In too many. cases ears had been open to the stories of ignor- ance and prejudice, which had too often been spread from foreign lands by superficial and narrow-minded observers. (Hear, hear.) On the other hand, they were full of gratitude to the men who had come back and told them the truth.

That exhibition was no mushroom effort. Not a week's work, and forgotten in another week; and he hoped it would have a lasting effect, for the very hard way they had worked deserved a good result. (Applause.)

ENGLAND'S RESPONSIBILITIES. Bishop of Chester Opens Exhibition.

. _ ..... The exhibition was first opened 'on Wednes- day afternoon by the Right Rev. Dr. Jayne, Bishop of Chester. Lord Shuttleworth pre- sided, and the Rector, the Rev. and Hon. C. F. Cross and other clergy supported. Lord Sutrrnswowia spoke as a layman, and said there was no part in the work of the Church in which laymen ought not to take part. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that men in the drama of life had to play different parts, and what was true of men was true of missions, and Great Britain had a very special part to play in the world as the greatest coloniser amongst the modern nations of the world. (Hear, hear.) It was the lot of the British race to come in contact more, probably, than any other race, with the less civilised races, and also to control, to a large extent, those less civilised races. Britishers went out into all parts of the world, and what did they- take with them? He was afraid that there was one class of ex- perts we took to foreign lands, gun powder, fire- arms, and fiery drinks, which did unmitigated harm. Happily the question as to whether we should take nothing better than that had long ago been decided in the affirmative.

div.head: Natives as Fellow-Subjects.
div.p: Natives as Fellow-Subjects.

• Natives were often our fellow-subjects. Still more •often they were customers to a great ex- tent for our wares, and, alas! very often also they were the victims of the very first fruits of the advent of civilisation, and we had to take grgat care that the evils brought by the advance of civilisation were corrected and transcended by, the good. We were guilty of three things. First, shocking selfishness; second, neglect of the obvious duty about which he had been speaking, and, thirdly, we were guilty of dis- obedience to the Divine command. Some people made the excuse that with the slums, &c., mis- sionaries were needed at home, but he would ask those people were they liberal contributors to home mission work, or actual workers in it? Those who objected or made excuses for them- selves were apt to remind them that charity began at home. That was true, but charity did not end at home; and especially so .with all the responsibilities about which he had been speak- ing. (Hear, hear.) He dongratulated the pro- moters of the exhibition for the excellent work they had done. (Applause.)

div.head: FIRE-WATER AND FIREARMS.
div.p: FIRE-WATER AND FIREARMS.

The BISHOP of CuP.sna said they should trot mix up the unchristian things—fire-water, fire- arms, &c.—with the name of Christianity. (Hear, hear.) They ought to do all they could to overcome those evil agencies, keep them short if possible, and not allow them to come in. But if they must come in in any shape or degree to overcome them, and, as far as possible, obliterate them. Our nation, with its Imperial responsi- bilities, must be missionary, and the sooner we realised the true character of our responsibil-

div.head: XMAS CHEER OR BEER P
div.p: XMAS CHEER OR BEER P
"Guardians With Kind Hearts Beneath Their Expansive Waistcoats."
EXTRA OUTDOOR RELIEF REFUSED.

Warrington Guardians were described at the monthly meeting on Wednesday as persons "with kind hearts beneath their expansive waistcoats." The Rev. A. M. Mitchell made use of this phrase to cajole the Guardians into granting extra relief at Christmas to those in receipt of outdoor relief, but the gentlemen of the expansive waistcoats declined to be parties to what one member declared would prove "aS glorious burst up." The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL proposed the follow- ing resolution "That a special Christmas grant of Is. Gd. for each adult, and .9d. for each child, be made to all .entitled to receive out relief during Christ- mas week."

He was too late last year, he said, but he thought he would be in time now. They ought not to begrudge a little extra to those people at that season. There was always something done for the people inside the workhouse and the children at the homes, but when it came to those outside, they were left without a Christ- mas gratuity. He believed the Guardians had kind hearts beneath their expansive waistcoats, and would support the resolution or perhaps make an amendment that the amount was not sufficient. (Laughter.) Mrs. SIMPSON seconded.

div.head: "A GLORIOUS BURST UP."
div.p: "A GLORIOUS BURST UP."

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said he felt a little amused at the suggestion made by so staunch an advo- cate of temperance, that those people were to be allowed facilities for a glorious 'burst up. (Laughter.) It was not a laughing matter, but. a• serious matter.'
If Mr. Mitchell thought those people should have a glorious fuddle he was at liberty to do so, but it meant about Bs. or 9s. going to be spent on drink.

-Mr. MITCHELL: I will refer Mr. Jolley to the Rector of Warrington for his decision. Mr. IicKINLEY : We ought to discern the de- serving from the undeserving. Mr. DALE supported the Rev. A. M. Mitchell. If they gave extras to those in the house, they ought to give them to those outside. (Hear, hear.) He did not think they should judge those in receipt of out relief so unkindly. He knew some who would not spend the money in drink.
Mr. MAI-ITER agreed that they should discern between the deserving and undeserving, and if there were deserving Cases give them a little help at Christmas time. _ _
_ - - The CHAIItiAN (Mr. E. L. Bent): We are not supposed to give anyone who is undeserving outdoor relief. We cannot differentiate between the two .people.

div.head: OUT OF THE POCKETS OF THE POOR.
div.p: OUT OF THE POCKETS OF THE POOR.

• • • •• • ••• ,••• ••• Miss BROADBENT : Mr. Mitchell talks as if the money were coming out of the pockets of the Guardians. Much of it comes out of the pockets of people who are only just above the pauper line themselves.

Mr. BILLINGE said that the granting of the extra amount would probably interfere with the giving of assistance from doles or the Church, &e . One might think there was going to be an election in Burtonwood.

_ Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : There might be. Mr. BILLINGE : Let us be true to our princi- ples. If a member is not satisfied that certain persons are not being relieved sufficiently, let him bring the matter before his committee. Mr. FLANAGAN though* they ought not to differ from what they had done in previous years.
Mr. MITCHELL ItSeems to be Bogging a dead horse. We have had this matter over and over again. I know a great maioStv of cases which are not adequately. relieved. The resolution was not passed.

div.head: NEW SCHOOL REPAIRS.
div.p: NEW SCHOOL REPAIRS.
Mr. Upson's Complaint to the Build- ings Committee.
SUPERIOR OLD SCHOOLS.

Mr. Upson, at a meeting of the Warrington Education kdommittee, over which Mr. A. J. Jolley presided, on Monday, complained that the more modern schools were continually re- quiring repairs. The discussion arose over the provision 'of air gratings- for Beamont Council .School and the repair of a boundary wall at the Secondary School. It had been his custom, said Mr. UPSON, periodically to call attention to the sums of money the Education Committee had to pay On these wonderful buildings--the new schools- (Councillor PEMBERTON : Hear, hear.) He did not like to speak of them individually, but he would say, speaking generally, that the Site!! and Buildings Committee had spent more money on the three new schools upon repairs than had been spent in repairs upon all of the old schools putT together.hey wj asked to make more-repairs at t); Beamont Council School, erected, six or years ago. Where were the men responsible le' that building? He would ask them why they did not at first put in such simple things- as air gratings. At the Secondary School a wall, erected a short time, now required repairing- He could point out walls, put up 20 or 30 years ago, at the older schools, which had never re- quired repair. Was the cost of these continual repairs because the committee had cut down the cost per head 611 the newer schools, that consequently they had to put in rain gutters they would not put on a humble cottage? t Was it the case that they put in lead than ran to only 21b. per square foot, whereas it should have been 51b. or 61b. lead?

Councillor PE3fBF.RTON : It is a very serious matter is this constantly recurring expense for repairs. The committee was as stubborn over these jobs as they are now over the new school. Alderman BOLTON: You are one of the cool' mittee!

Councillor PEMBERTON : T know that! " Blaming Yourself." Alderman BOLTON: Then you are blaming yourself. Mr. G. WALKER Some of the details are the result of recent practical experience. It hag been discovered that decay has arisen in Bei!' mont School through the want of proper ventl- lation, and it is now suggested to remove that; Alderman BotaoN said that several causes ha n arisen to make the alterations necessary. Virile° they had a large quantity of , property, as the committee had in the schools, they should have a special man to go round and periodically el!" amine the property. It was not the committee fault, as they carried on the building at as lovi a price as did any committee of the Corporation' Mr. UPSON : Exactly; my point is that Yeil build them too cheaply. The minutes, authorising the repairs, were adopted.

Applications are invited from married couples, between the ages of 25 and 45, for the Appoint- ments of Tailor and Boys' Instructor and Foster Mother of one of the Homes respectively at the Cottage Homes and Schools, Padgate, near War- rington. • Applicants must be active, energetic and will- ing to make themselves generally useful. Salary, £35 per annum for the position of Tailor and £2O per annum for the position of Foster Mother, together with apartments, rations, washing, &c. Particulars of the duties may be obtained upon application to the Superintendent of the Homes. Applications must be made upon forms, to be obtained from me, the undersigned, and must be returned duly completed not later than 10 a.m. on Tuesday, the 2nd December, 1913. Canvassing the Guardians directly or in- directly will disqualify. By order, ARTHUR BOTTOMLEY, Clerk. Union Offices, Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, 19th November, 1913.
